Introduction  Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide  1  , primarily driven by metastasis  2 , 3  . Lymph nodes (LNs) are critical anatomical checkpoints in cancer progression  4  , serving as initial metastatic sites and immune regulatory hubs orchestrating host-tumor interactions  5  . Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) status is therefore paramount for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types  6  . However, current clinical management relies primarily on crude quantitative approaches—predominantly pN staging  6  —which fail to capture crucial biological features such as lymph node ratio (LNR), metastatic tumor burden, and diverse spatial growth patterns of metastatic cells within LNs. Recent evidence explicitly links elevated LNR to decreased survival rates and shortened recurrence-free intervals  7  , while highlighting how spatial distributions of metastatic cells can modulate the immune microenvironment, potentially facilitating immune escape  8  . Despite these insights, pathologists now face an unprecedented surge in LN specimens due to rising cancer incidence  9  , rendering such detailed, multi-dimensional analysis practically unfeasible in routine workflows.  Deep learning has rapidly advanced pathological diagnosis, with numerous artificial intelligence (AI) systems gaining regulatory approval. However, existing AI approaches for LNM detection  10 – 15   typically follow cancer-specific paradigms. This fragmentation hinders widespread clinical adoption by necessitating multiple, disparate systems  16 , 17  , conflicting with the need for operational efficiency and unified diagnostic standards. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity manifests as a “long-tail distribution”  18 , 19  , where common metastatic patterns coexist with diverse rare variants. Standard deep learning models often struggle with these outliers, prone to “overconfident errors” where the system makes incorrect predictions with high certainty on out-of-distribution data. The reliable detection of these rare but clinically significant variants is crucial for patient safety  20 , 21  , yet remains challenging even with large datasets. While emerging foundation models  22 – 27   offer powerful representational capabilities, their effective application across the pan-cancer spectrum requires substantial annotation resources. Thus, there is an urgent need to transcend these limitations and establish a unified, robust, and safe diagnostic framework capable of not only high sensitivity but also reliable failure awareness across all cancer types.  To address these challenges, we developed UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware AI platform integrating a pathology foundation model with uncertainty-guided active learning and robust uncertainty estimation (Fig.  1 ). Trained and validated on an extensive multi-center, multi-cancer LN dataset, this study demonstrates UPATHLN’s capacity for highly sensitive and safe pan-cancer LNM detection with robust generalization. Ultimately, this study represents a critical step towards establishing a unified, trustworthy diagnostic standard for AI-assisted pathology. Insets highlight thyroid-type colloid-like material and other non-specific patterns that may be prominent in metastases from the indicated primary sites, including mucin pools, stromal fibrosis/desmoplasia, and keratin pearls.  d  Uncertainty-guided active learning framework: system leverages clinical pathology database with iterative refinement where pathologists review high uncertainty (HU) predictions, verify challenging cases through IHC staining (CAM5.2, AE1/3), and exclude poor-quality samples. In clinical practice, uncertainty estimates guide pathologists' review to prevent rare subtype misdiagnosis and enable continuous system improvement.                     Results   Establishment of the UPATHLN platform and active learning optimization  To establish the UPATHLN platform, we curated a large-scale, multi-center pan-cancer dataset comprising 26,229 lymph nodes (LNs) from 8294 whole-slide images (WSIs) across 2738 patients, spanning tumors from 14 distinct primary organs. The dataset was rigorously partitioned into a development cohort and an independent test cohort, with seven rare primary origins strictly held out as unseen primary-origin holdouts to evaluate generalization to previously unseen origins (SFig.  1 ). To ensure high-quality input to the platform, our automated LN extraction pipeline achieved robust performance, with YOLOv8-s demonstrating a recall of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection and nnUNet achieving a Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for tissue segmentation, effectively excluding non-target tissues (Fig.  2a  and SFig.  2 ). Rather than relying on static training, we optimized the platform using an uncertainty-driven active learning strategy. Misclassified tiles were enriched in the high-uncertainty (HU) tail of the tile-level uncertainty-score distribution (SFig.  4a ). Accordingly, we summarized tile uncertainties into a slide-level ambiguity score and ranked candidate WSIs for expert review (SFig.  3 , “Methods”). Through five rounds of human-in-the-loop iterations, this active optimization substantially improved discriminative performance on the internal validation set, increasing the tile-level AUC from a baseline of 0.953 (95% CI: 0.932–0.974) to 0.986 (95% CI: 0.976–0.996), with consistent gains in both PPV and NPV (Fig.  2b–d ).  To rigorously attribute this high performance to architectural design rather than data accumulation alone, we benchmarked the final model against alternative architectures trained on the identical dataset generated from the final iteration. The multiscale architecture significantly outperformed both the single-scale UNI baseline (AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.910–0.946; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001) and the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.901–0.935; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001; SFig.  4b ).    Uncertainty-aware classification achieves high-sensitivity LNM detection  Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a clinical fail-safe. While the optimized multiscale classifier achieved a robust intrinsic sensitivity of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.985–1.000; Fig.  2e ), it erroneously classified three metastatic cases as negative when relying exclusively on diagnostic probability scores (false negatives, FNs). In the uncertainty-annotated confusion matrix (SFig.  5a ; HU-flag counts are shown in parentheses), all three FNs were flagged as high uncertainty and therefore routed for mandatory pathologist confirmation. This capability to “rescue” potential false negatives effectively neutralized the risk of missed diagnosis, underpinning the system’s 100% conditional sensitivity and ensuring that ambiguous but critical lesions were correctly routed for pathologist confirmation.  To evaluate clinical workload, we quantified the review burden at the LN level. Here, each LN was counted at most once, regardless of how many false-positive or high-uncertainty subregions it contained. Across iterations, both the LN-level false-positive (FP) rate and HU rate steadily declined (Fig.  2f, g ), reaching final values of 0.112 (95% CI: 0.070–0.155) and 0.156 (95% CI: 0.110–0.202), respectively. The model’s progressive refinement was visually corroborated by prediction heatmaps (Fig.  3a  and SFig.  6 ), and it precisely identified diverse metastatic burdens, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cell clusters (Fig.  3b ). Final validation by pathologists on the remaining development cohort confirmed a 100% positive detection rate with minimal review overhead (1% FP rate and 0.16% HU rate at the LN level). Validation of pan-cancer robustness and safety  Performance evaluation on the independent test cohort confirmed the system’s robust discriminative power (Fig.  4  and SFig.  7 – 10 ). To establish a baseline, we first evaluated the standalone classification module without uncertainty intervention. Operating strictly on diagnostic probability scores, the module achieved a robust sensitivity of 98.7% and a specificity of 88.0% (SFig.  5b ). Although this represents a high level of diagnostic accuracy, relying solely on this conventional probability thresholding still resulted in 60 FN predictions (missed LNMs). Crucially, the parallel uncertainty estimation module functioned as a decisive fail-safe mechanism to address this residual risk. It successfully intercepted all 60 initially missed instances by classifying them as HU. This “rescue effect” secured a 100% conditional sensitivity across the entire test cohort, effectively neutralizing the clinical risk of missed diagnoses. Accounting for the union of FP and HU predictions, the effective RBR-N was 26.8% (3180/11,873). This indicates that 73.2% of negative LNs were safely excluded from manual review.  Subgroup analysis revealed remarkable consistency across organ origins, with a weighted average FP rate of 7.5% (SD: 2.1%) (Fig.  4 ). For the seven cancer types included in training, performance remained stable regardless of sample size. Notably, although Stomach cancer LNs were overrepresented in the training data (35.6%), their performance (HU rate: 5.2%; FP rate: 6.6%) closely mirrored the cohort average, indicating that the model maintained balanced discriminative power despite the non-uniform training distribution. While robust to sample size variations, the model exhibited sensitivity to specific non-neoplastic histological features. LNs from the lung and cervix exhibited higher HU rates (32.6% and 26.0%, respectively). Pathological audit confirmed that in lung cancer, these flags were predominantly triggered by anthracitic pigment, indicating that the model correctly identified non-malignant confounders as HU regions (SFig.  11 ).  Most notably, the system demonstrated exceptional adaptability to the seven cancer types entirely unseen during training. The fail-safe mechanism remained fully effective even in these out-of-distribution domains, with zero missed diagnoses recorded. Regarding efficiency, the model maintained consistently low LN-level FP rates for the majority of these unseen origins (6/7), ranging from 2.4% (kidney) to 10.8% (thyroid) without fine-tuning. The sole exception was penile cancer (SFig.  8 ), a rare type with complex morphology, where the system exhibited an adaptive increase in review rates (HU: 30.2%; FP: 20.0%). This reflects a cautious inference strategy that prioritizes diagnostic safety when encountering highly atypical histological patterns.    Interpretability and pathological characterization of uncertainty  To elucidate the interpretability underlying this robust performance, we deconstructed the uncertainty landscape. Multiscale feature fusion dimensionality reduction analysis (Fig.  5a, b ) clearly delineated tumor and normal regions, with HU areas concentrated at the boundaries in feature space. We were able to effectively extract these areas through uncertainty quantification. As shown in Fig.  5d , the model assigned high HU scores to two patients with distinct atypical cytomorphology: one with lymphocyte-like tumor cells featuring scant cytoplasm and naked nuclei, and another exhibiting plasmacytoid/histiocytoid features with moderate cytoplasm. Discussion  This study addresses the limitations of current organ-specific AI paradigms by presenting UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware framework for pan-cancer LNM diagnosis. While previous deep learning approaches have validated LNM detection in organ-specific cohorts, they often operate as “black boxes,” lacking the safety mechanisms required for broad clinical adoption  20  . By devising a specialized Multiscale cross-attention framework to effectively contextualize features from the pathology foundation model, UPATHLN establishes a robust clinical safety net. Notably, this architectural design demonstrated a definitive “fail-safe” capability in a large-scale independent cohort: the uncertainty mechanism successfully intercepted all initially missed metastases, securing 100% conditional sensitivity. This achievement marks a significant advancement: moving from algorithms that prioritize raw accuracy to safety-critical systems that effectively mitigate the risk of FNs in metastatic screening.  The parallel uncertainty estimation branch underpins the technical integrity of this safety profile. Classical uncertainty estimation methods—such as uncertainty-prediction model co-training  28 , 29  , multiple model ensembles  30  , or repeated dropout strategies  28 , 31  —increase computational burden and often flag large unnecessary regions for manual reassessment. By contrast, our independent bypass architecture provides precise localization of diagnostically uncertain regions without compromising inference speed. This decoupled mechanism acts as a reliable diagnostic filter, specifically designed to handle the inherent biological heterogeneity of metastatic disease. It respects the ambiguity of “long-tail” rare variants and non-neoplastic confounders (e.g., anthracotic pigment), routing these cases strictly within the system’s competence boundaries. This “rescue effect” ensures that algorithmic limitations do not translate into diagnostic errors, maintaining high reliability even when encountering complex morphologies that typically confound conventional models.  Furthermore, we successfully navigated the data annotation bottleneck that typically constrains the scalability of foundation models. By coupling high-level feature representations with an uncertainty-guided active learning framework, we efficiently captured a comprehensive spectrum of metastatic morphologies across 14 cancer types without necessitating exhaustive annotation. This strategy proved vital for addressing the diverse patterns of metastatic pathology. Consequently, the system maintained robust performance even on LNM samples from primary sites entirely unseen during training. This demonstrates that uncertainty-driven learning provides a practical, scalable pathway to generalize pathology AI, enabling adaptability to domain shifts and rare cancer types lacking large-scale training data.  UPATHLN reconciles the critical tension between rising diagnostic volumes and the demand for granular prognostic assessment. By safely automating the exclusion of 73.2% of negative LNs, the system liberates pathologists to focus on complex cases. Crucially, this efficiency renders detailed “multi-dimensional analysis”—specifically the precise quantification of tumor-to-lymph node area ratio  12   and spatial distribution patterns—feasible in routine practice. Moving beyond crude pN staging, UPATHLN provides the quantitative depth required for modern precision oncology that is practically impossible to achieve manually.  Despite these advances, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study is retrospective, and all training/validation data were sourced from hospitals in China; therefore, real-world deployment requires prospective multi-center evaluation and external validation across diverse populations, institutions, and scanning protocols. Second, although many artifacts are appropriately flagged as high uncertainty, future work could incorporate dedicated artifact-suppression or quality-control modules to further reduce review burden without compromising safety. Third, while the pipeline is designed to be compatible with different pathology foundation models, we only evaluated UNI and did not empirically compare performance against alternative encoders.  Collectively, UPATHLN advances pan-cancer LNM screening by introducing a risk-aware architecture that balances automation with expert oversight. The synergy between its decoupled uncertainty “fail-safe” and active learning framework ensures robust performance and scalability under heterogeneous clinical conditions. This approach not only streamlines routine triage but also provides a quantitative basis for assessing metastatic burden, potentially informing prognostic insights beyond standard pathological staging.    Methods   Dataset collection and cohort definition  We established a large-scale, pan-cancer dataset combining clinical data from three independent medical centers, with heterogeneous clinical workloads and patient populations, enabling evaluation across varied real-world settings. The primary clinical cohort included 2738 patients (8294 WSIs, 26,229 LNs) covering 14 distinct solid tumor types (SFig.  1a ). We applied specific exclusion criteria to ensure data quality: WSIs exhibiting severe artefacts—such as tissue folding covering >20% of the area, significant out-of-focus blurring, or extreme staining inconsistencies—were removed prior to analysis. In addition to the clinical cohort, we utilized an annotated gastric cancer dataset from our previous work  12   (GLN21) and the publicly available breast cancer dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge  11   (BLN16) for model initialization.  Crucially, to prevent data leakage, we employed a strict patient-level splitting strategy, where all WSIs and LN sections from the same patient were assigned exclusively to a single cohort. As illustrated in the study design flow (SFig.  3 ), the clinical data were stratified into two independent cohorts. The development cohort consisted of 683 patients (2547 WSIs, 9729 LNs) from 7 common cancer types and was further subdivided to support the active learning workflow (SFig.  1b ). The multi-center multi-cancer test cohort comprised an independent set of 2055 patients (5747 WSIs, 16,500 LNs), serving as the held-out standard for final performance evaluation (SFig.  1c ). To rigorously assess the model’s generalization capabilities, the test cohort was stratified into two groups: the 7 cancer types encountered during training and a distinct set of 7 cancer types (thyroid, pancreas, bile duct, kidney, prostate, penis, and anus). Crucially, samples from these rare origins were strictly excluded from the training pipeline, ensuring that their evaluation represents a true test of the model’s ability to generalize to completely unseen primary origins. For LN counting, pathologists manually reviewed the slides to identify spatially distinct LNs; serial sections of the same node, if present, were identified based on morphological continuity and excluded from the total count to ensure each observation represented a unique LN.  This retrospective, multi-center study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Changhai Hospital (CHEC2024-276), the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Wuxi (2024Y-125), and the Ethics Committee of the 960th Hospital of the People’s Liberation Army (2024-087). The requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymized data.    Lymph node contour recognition  To increase the training accuracy of LN metastasis detection models, we first developed an LN contour recognition model. The WSIs of LN tissue include not only LNs but also muscle, extraneous fat, and cancer nodules. The presence of these nontarget tissues can adversely affect the accuracy of metastasis detection.  Our model comprises two stages: initially, the YOLOv8-s model is employed for LN detection due to its high efficiency and rapid localization capabilities. The detected regions are subsequently input into the nnUNet  32   model for segmentation to remove impurities from the LN periphery.  We processed images using 1024 × 1024 pixel tiles at 1× magnification and utilized a 256-pixel sliding window for segmentation. The YOLOv8-s model was trained with default parameters, using the annotated contour coordinates as ground truth labels. The nnUNet model was similarly trained with default settings, using the bounding box of annotated regions to cut tiles at 0.25× magnification and employing annotated contours as masks.  During inference, a staged strategy was employed: YOLOv8-s model-predicted coordinates were used to cut local tiles, which were then input into the nnUNet model to obtain precise contour masks. These masks were mapped back to the full 0.25x thumbnail based on relative coordinates. For overlapping sliding windows, an averaging method was used to smooth boundaries.  We annotated 200 WSIs with 721 LNs from various tumor types for the YOLOv8-s model and nnUNet model training. After initial training, predictions of unannotated WSIs in the development cohort were manually reviewed. We reviewed 918 WSIs (comprising 3528 LNs) and reannotated 132 WSIs with incorrect predictions. Then, the YOLOv8-s model was retrained on a combined dataset of the initial 200 annotated WSIs and the 918 manually reviewed WSIs (total 1118 WSIs; randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing). Ultimately, the YOLOv8-s model achieved a recall rate of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection.  Since nnUNet requires contour-level annotations, we used the initial 200 WSIs along with the 132 fully corrected WSIs (comprising 1245 LNs) for retraining. Finally, the nnUNet model achieved a mean Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for LN contour segmentation. A manual review of inference results from the development cohort confirmed the ability of the two-stage model to accurately delineate LN contours and exclude non-LN tissues. This process provides high-quality input data for subsequent metastasis detection. As illustrated in SFig.  2a , we effectively identified and extracted LN contours from complex pathological images, facilitating high-quality input for further metastasis detection. Some missed LN diagnoses are due to atypical morphology (e.g., indistinct capsules) or small nodal size (SFig.  2b ). In clinical applications, missed LN identification is rare, so it does not increase the workload. Pathologists can easily add annotations during the review process. As missed diagnosis cases continue to be collected, this situation will become increasingly rare. The annotation and review process was conducted by two senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience: Y.C. and C.Q.    Data preprocessing for the classification model  Following the extraction of LN contour regions from WSIs, we tiled tumor metastasis areas on the basis of annotations to train the classification model. Given that accurate diagnosis of some LN metastases requires multiscale observations, we applied multiscale tiling to the annotated dataset. This process involved extracting image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both 10x and 4× magnification, as shown in Fig.  2a . The center coordinates of tiles at both scales were aligned to ensure consistent observation of the same region at different resolutions.  By integrating the LN contour mask with the tumor mask, we cropped regions of interest into tumor and nontumor areas. At 10× magnification, a sliding window of 64 pixels was used to divide the region into extractable tiles, with each grid classified on the basis of the proportion of the tumor area annotated by doctors. Specifically, if more than 25% of a grid area was annotated as a tumor, the tile was labeled positive; otherwise, it was labeled negative. To ensure category balance, if the number of tiles in any category exceeded 100 within a WSI, we randomly selected 100 tiles. This sampling strategy maintained balanced categories at the tile level.    Feature extractor  In this study, we utilized UNI  23  , a Vision Transformer (ViT-Large  33  ) foundation model pre-trained on over 100,000 HE-stained WSIs, as a frozen feature extractor. UNI was selected as it represented a leading solution for pan-cancer feature representation at the time of study implementation. Importantly, our proposed multiscale architecture is designed to be foundation-model agnostic. While UNI was employed here as a representative high-performance encoder to validate our framework, the system is compatible with and can readily incorporate other emerging pathology foundation models  22 , 24 – 27  . For feature extraction, we processed image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both the 10× and the 4× magnification levels and randomly cropped them to 224 × 224 pixels. The resulting feature matrix for each tile maintains a shape of (196 + 1, 1024), where 196 represents the length of the patch-tokens, and 1 represents the class token.    Multiscale feature fusion and classification module  By extracting features from the same local region at different magnification levels and then fusing them, the model can capture both global and local pathological morphological features, better locating and identifying tumor areas. Specifically, we adopted the cross-attention module proposed by Zhou et al.  34   to multiscale image feature fusion. As shown in Fig.  2a , the entire cross-attention module consists of two cross-attention blocks and two self-attention blocks. The cross-attention blocks learn the intrinsic connections of multiscale image features by dynamically weighting features from different spatial scales. During training, the parameters of the UNI pretrained ViT-Large feature extractor were fixed, and no backpropagation optimization was performed. We used ColorJitter from Torchvision for transformation with the following parameters: maximum increments of 0.1 for brightness, 0.2 for contrast, 0.2 for saturation, and 0.15 for hue. The tiles were also randomly flipped and rotated by 15°. To address the imbalance between positive and negative samples, we perform balanced sampling of positive and negative samples at the initialization of each epoch. We calculated the loss via cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities and the true labels and optimized it via adaptive moment estimation with weight decay (AdamW) during training, with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate was managed via a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and ending at 1e-6 over 40 epochs. All training and testing were performed on six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.    Uncertainty estimation module  Deploying deep learning models across multi-center pan-cancer cohorts inevitably introduces challenges related to histological heterogeneity, variable data quality, and out-of-distribution inputs that essentially differ from the training distribution. In such scenarios, enforcing deterministic predictions often leads to high-confidence errors. To address this, we incorporated a parallel uncertainty estimation module into our diagnostic framework. The primary objective of this module is to quantify the reliability of region-level predictions, serving a dual purpose: guiding model optimization through active learning during development and acting as a trigger for pathologist review during clinical inference.  Diverging from conventional approaches that rely on computationally expensive ensembles or require joint training with classification objectives (which may destabilize the primary task)  28 – 31  , we implemented a sequential optimization strategy. Specifically, the uncertainty branch is trained as an independent architectural bypass only after the multiscale classifier parameters are frozen. This design ensures that the uncertainty mechanism is specifically calibrated to the fixed decision boundary of the main model. Consequently, this approach enables precise confidence estimation without compromising the original diagnostic performance, while incurring negligible computational overhead.  Specifically, we implemented this module by adapting the uncertainty estimation algorithm for pretrained models proposed by Kirchhof et al .   35  . As shown in Fig.  2a , using the same feature  F  as the classification model input, we passed it through the uncertainty estimation module comprising three fully connected layers with 512 hidden units and LeakyReLU intermediate activations, outputting a single value normalized by the Softplus function to ensure positivity. We used mean squared error (MSE) loss, comparing the uncertainty module’s predictions with labels derived from the classification model’s forward propagation loss, computed at runtime with backpropagation disabled. Crucially, this design provides an intuitive measure of reliability: a high predicted loss indicates that the model anticipates a likely error on the input, thereby flagging it as a “High Uncertainty” (HU) region for pathologist review.  The loss function is defined as:   8     L  uncertainty   =   1  N    ∑   i  =  1   N        u  i   −   L   pred  i       2      where    u    is the uncertainty module’s predicted value and      L    pred      is the loss from the classification model’s forwards propagation.  The training process employed the same data and sampling strategy as those of the classification module. We used the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate followed a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and decreasing to 1e-6 over 10 epochs.    Uncertainty-driven active learning strategy  To address tumor heterogeneity and optimize annotation efficiency, we implemented a human-in-the-loop, uncertainty-driven active learning framework structured into five distinct iterations (Fig.  1d  and SFig.  3 ). To facilitate this process, the clinically derived development cohort (683 patients) was partitioned into two functional subsets via random patient-level sampling: a large unlabeled candidate pool of 594 patients (2245 WSIs, 8832 LNs) available for selection, and a strictly held-out internal validation set of 89 patients (302 WSIs, 897 LNs). Notably, the internal validation set was comprehensively annotated at the lesion level prior to the active learning process. This set remained fixed throughout the study and served as a reliable ground truth to monitor model convergence and determine hyperparameters without biasing the training process.  The training workflow commenced with an initialization phase (Iteration 1), where the baseline model was trained solely on the fully annotated initialization datasets (GLN21 and BLN16) to establish foundational detection capabilities. Subsequently, we conducted four consecutive rounds of uncertainty-driven refinement (Iterations 2–5). In each round, the model performed inference on the unlabeled candidate pool to compute tile-level uncertainty scores      u    i      (derived from the uncertainty module). WSIs were then prioritized for expert review according to a slide-level diagnostic ambiguity score. Senior pathologists reviewed these flagged samples to correct FPs and verify missed metastases. After each review phase, the corrected samples were incorporated into the expanded training set.    Data annotation and establishment of ground truth  To satisfy the distinct requirements of model development and independent validation, we implemented a two-tier annotation strategy conducted by senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience (Y.C., C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.).  For the development cohort, pathologists performed exhaustive region-level annotations on WSIs selected for the expanded training set and the internal validation set. This involved delineating precise boundaries for all LNs and contouring all internal metastatic foci. This process ensured that the model received high-granularity supervision for distinct metastatic morphologies, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cells (ITCs). During active learning iterations, regions flagged as HU were specifically reviewed and corrected (C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.) to provide high-quality supervision for challenging examples.  For the independent test cohort, we established a rigorous diagnostic standard to evaluate clinical safety. Instead of pixel-level contours, we focused on the definitive metastatic status of each LN. Two senior pathologists (Y.C. and C.Q.) independently reviewed all WSIs. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by a consensus panel. To resolve diagnostic ambiguity in morphologically challenging cases, we performed confirmatory immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (CAM5.2 and AE1/AE3) on 52 challenging cases to determine the final ground truth (SFig.  12 ). This process ensured a non-ambiguous “Positive/Negative” label for every LN in the test set.    Statistical analysis  The detection (YOLOv8-s) and segmentation (nnUNet) models were implemented with probability thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50, respectively. For the classification model, the binary decision threshold was set at 0.50. The uncertainty threshold for each iteration was determined empirically using the Internal Validation Set. To balance the trade-off between the volume of regions flagged for review and FP predictions, we selected the threshold at the intersection point where the average High Uncertainty area per slide (HUavg) equalled the average False Positive area per slide (FPavg) (SFig.  13 ). Isolated positive predictions approximately the size of one tile (3600 μm²) were excluded from analysis owing to resolution constraints.  To comprehensively evaluate the system, we defined detection and classification targets at three distinct levels. Tile-level performance measures the fundamental classification accuracy of individual 256 × 256 pixel image patches, where a tile is labeled positive if tumor tissue comprises >25% of its area. Lesion-level (Region) performance evaluates the model’s ability to correctly localize and classify contiguous metastatic areas (including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and ITCs) within the LN tissue, distinct from simple tile-level accuracy. LN-level performance serves as the primary clinical unit for N-staging; an LN is considered positive if the model identifies at least one metastatic lesion within the nodal area.  We defined specific metrics to assess the safety and efficiency of the proposed human-AI collaborative workflow. Conditional classification sensitivity evaluates the classification performance specifically on all LNs successfully localized by the detection module. For performance evaluation, regions flagged as HU (highlighted in yellow in the prediction heatmaps) were considered positive for sensitivity calculations, as these areas require pathologist review in clinical practice. To quantify workload, we defined the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N) as the proportion of true-negative LNs that required high-magnification manual review. An LN contributes to this burden if it contains any region predicted as False Positive (FP) or High Uncertainty (HU).  Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) was performed to calculate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics. AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). evidence_text:
Multimodal alignment improves generalizability of genomic biomarker prediction in computational pathology. Computational pathology models that use digitized histopathology whole-slide images have the potential to become a cost-effective and scalable alternative to molecular assays for the prediction of genomic biomarkers, a key task in precision oncology. However, as new genomic biomarkers are discovered or quantified, large, labeled datasets must be prospectively collected to train new models. To address this challenge, we developed multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization (MARBLE), a multimodal contrastive pretraining strategy that integrates structured biomarker knowledge into representation learning of histopathology images. MARBLE aligns histopathology-derived representations with representations of genomic biomarkers generated by a large language model (LLM) and a protein language model (PLM). This biologically informed alignment enables data-efficient generalization to novel, out-of-distribution biomarkers. Using the MSK-IMPACT cohort of over 40,000 patients across multiple biomarker panel versions, we design experiments grounded in real-world data to demonstrate the value of our proposed approach. Introduction  Histopathology data, particularly hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained tissue samples called whole slide images (WSIs), are routinely collected as part of cancer care. These samples are increasingly being digitized, thereby enabling the development and application of foundation models,  1   ,   2   ,   3   ,   4   ,   5   which can be used to extract robust and general-purpose visual representations. Building predictive models using these representations has been successful for routine predictive tasks, such as cancer detection and subtyping  6   ,   7   and has shown great potential for expanding the utility of WSIs to novel downstream tasks. One such use case is the computational prediction of biomarker profiles directly from histopathology images as a replacement for screening for genomic biomarkers via molecular assays ( Figure 1 A). DNA sequencing is used to assess the presence of tumor-specific genomic alterations (e.g., mutations, deletions, insertions, duplications, and rearrangements), the results of which are used to inform prognosis and guide therapy selection.  8   However, as the sequencing procedures underlying these assays are expensive and challenging to scale, direct prediction from H&E images presents a cost-effective and scalable alternative. Several works have already demonstrated encouraging performance for both single biomarkers  9   ,   10   ,   11   and larger panels.  12    Figure 1   MARBLE uses pretraining with biomarker embeddings to improve predictive performance, as demonstrated on the MSK-IMPACT panel  (A) The molecular profiling and tissue collection pipeline in cancer care: a tissue specimen undergoes DNA sequencing, routine H&E staining, and digitalization.  (B) Biomarker panel size across MSK-IMPACT versions (v.3, v.5, v.6, v.7), distribution of patient-level biomarker counts, and distribution of biomarker positivity rates.  (C) Key components of the design of MARBLE. Aggregated histopathology embeddings from a frozen pathology foundation model (Path FM) are contrasted with aggregated biomarker embeddings derived from a frozen LLM (GPT-4o + Sentence-BERT [SBERT]) and/or a frozen PLM (ESM-2), enabling cross-modal alignment through contrastive pretraining.  (D) Supervised fine-tuning of the imaging encoder for multi-label biomarker classification.  (E) Pretraining and fine-tuning cohort setups with panel-specific sample counts.                       At the same time, advances in precision oncology continue to expand the catalog of actionable genomic biomarkers, both as new oncogenes are identified and new cancer-driving alterations for existing oncogenes and tumor suppressors are characterized. For example, the MSK-IMPACT panel, a test for tumor-specific genomic biomarkers, has grown by 164 genes since it was first released in 2017 ( Figure 1 B).  8   As new cancer drivers and therapeutic targets continue to emerge, predictive models face the challenge of rapidly integrating these biomarkers in a data-efficient manner while maintaining performance on existing ones. In practice, adapting these models to novel targets often requires a large amount of labeled data, which is time consuming, costly, and potentially infeasible to obtain (e.g., for rare alterations). Addressing this limitation requires approaches that can generalize while utilizing a minimal amount of labeled samples.  We hypothesize that multimodal contrastive pretraining can overcome this limitation by structuring the visual representation space around biologically meaningful relationships. To this end, we introduce “multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization” (MARBLE), a pretraining strategy that incorporates knowledge about biomarkers directly into the representation learning process, enabling downstream generalization to novel biomarkers ( Figure 1 C). Our approach aligns aggregated H&E-derived embeddings, created using a pathology foundation model (Path FM), with aggregated semantic embeddings of biomarkers.  To create biomarker embeddings, we use large language models (LLMs) and protein language models (PLMs), allowing us to explore the effect of representing biomarkers as different modalities and to exploit the specific semantics learned by their respective pretraining. Recent studies demonstrate the utility of LLMs in biological domains, from enriching protein representations via textual annotations  13   to modeling perturbations through structured LLM reasoning.  14   In parallel, PLMs encode latent information about protein function from amino acid sequences and are thus capable of capturing how mutations impact function.  15   ,   16   ,   17   PLMs have been leveraged to incorporate molecular priors into vision models, such as in the VirTues framework,  18   which fuses PLM-derived protein embeddings with image patch tokens to encode channel-specific marker information and guide multimodal representation learning in spatial proteomics.  Because tumor morphology often reflects the combined influence of several genomic alterations rather than just one ( Figure 1 B), traditional supervised approaches that treat each biomarker as an independent entity fail to capture the semantic relationships between co-occurring alterations. For example, KRAS, BRAF, and NRAS mutations all activate the MAPK signaling pathway.  19   By aligning H&E-derived embeddings with LLM- and PLM-based embeddings, we leverage the structured biological knowledge of these models to capture such relationships. This biologically informed alignment enables the model to learn that morphologically similar tissue patterns may arise from functionally related combinations of biomarkers. From principle, the construction of our method enables generalization to new biomarkers by recognizing their similarity to previously observed alterations with related mechanisms.  We evaluated the MARBLE strategy through experiments grounded in real-world data. Using earlier versions of the MSK-IMPACT panel, we performed pretraining to align image embeddings separately with LLM-derived embeddings and with PLM-derived embeddings, as well as jointly with both. The image-only component of the pretrained model was then fine-tuned to predict all of the biomarkers measured in the most recent version of the panel. Our results support the claim that alignment improves predictive performance for previously unseen biomarkers in a low-data regime and enables generalization to out-of-distribution samples. Overall, we demonstrate how our pretraining approach leads to improved, data-efficient generalization of biomarker quantification.    Results   Representing biomarkers with PLMs and LLMs  Contrastive learning aims to align representations of paired samples while simultaneously penalizing the alignment of representations of unpaired samples.  20   This approach has proven highly effective in improving the performance of modern deep learning systems and has recently gained significant interest in multimodal settings such as vision-language modeling. One example is the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) approach,  21   which learns a unified embedding space for images and their corresponding textual descriptions. Models with multimodal contrastive pretraining are becoming prevalent in computational pathology, spanning both vision-language  22   ,   23   ,   24   and vision-molecular  4   ,   25   ,   26   ,   27   settings. To date, the use of multimodal pretraining in computational pathology has focused on learning tile aggregation models that produce a slide embedding. In these works, the motivation rests on the assumption that the additional modality provides a generalizable supervisory signal for aggregating tile representations. Here, we investigate the distinct setting where we specifically hypothesize that pretraining will aid in out-of-distribution performance. This hypothesis is motivated by successes in representation learning from proteins and text to create PLMs and LLMs, respectively.  PLMs aim to learn rich representations of protein sequences, capturing the structural and functional properties of proteins through large-scale pretraining.  28   ,   29   The recently developed ESM-2 model  30   is a particularly noteworthy PLM because of its strong downstream performance in tasks like structure prediction and function annotation. Recently, PLM representations have been combined with imaging data in the context of spatial proteomics to capture both molecular and spatial information with the aim of enabling more accurate clinical diagnostics and biological discovery.  18   Building on this idea, we propose to leverage PLM embeddings of mutated protein products of tumor-specific genomic alterations and integrate them with H&E imaging to derive richer representations that are biologically grounded and predictive of molecular alterations.  We model in-frame variants of genomic alterations including missense, nonsense, deletion, insertion, and indel mutations. Combining the canonical UniProt sequence with the specific genomic alteration provides a sequence of amino acids. These mutated sequences can be used as input to a PLM, providing us a systematic mapping from genomic alteration to embedding. Given its recent success, we select ESM-2 as the PLM.  30   This approach produces fixed-dimension embeddings  d   P   per biomarker which are gathered into a set of      P  i   ∈   R    N  P  i   ×   d  P        where      N  P  i      is the number of embeddings for patient  i . Copy-number variations have no clear altered protein product and are excluded from the PLM representation. Additionally, MSK-IMPACT does not include data about altered protein product from frameshift mutations, so these are also excluded.  LLMs are pretrained on massive text corpora via masked language modeling or next token prediction, which implicitly encodes domain-specific knowledge in their weights.  31   Recent studies have demonstrated that this embedded knowledge can be retrieved through prompting. For instance, Med-PaLM, a variant of an LLM tuned to the medical domain, achieved expert-level performance on clinical question-answering tasks using prompt-based querying alone.  32   LLMs are typically used for their ability to directly generate text. In parallel, text embedding models provide compact vector representations of a text corpus.  We propose a systematic approach to transform biomarkers to text embeddings. Each biomarker present in the panel consists of a HUGO gene symbol (e.g., EGFR), high-level mutation information (e.g., copy-number amplification), and a cancer type (e.g., bladder cancer). For each gene, we obtain a canonical protein function description from UniProtKB,  33   an expert-curated protein knowledge base. The obtained description is then used to prompt an LLM ( Figure S1  for the complete prompt) to produce a concise description of the associated mutation and its role in the provided cancer type, including any known mechanisms of action. The resulting text description is then used as input into a text embedding model, specifically Sentence-BERT (SBERT),  34   to obtain a fixed-dimension embedding  d   L   per biomarker. This process is repeated for each patient biomarker to create a set of embeddings      L  i   ∈   R    N  L  i   ×   d  L        where      N  L  i      is the number of embeddings.    Multimodal alignment for biomarker learning and generalization  Our proposed contrastive pretraining strategy MARBLE aligns two types of biomarker representations with histopathology image representations from a patient sample ( Figure 1 C). We hypothesize and show that performing this pretraining step ahead of supervised fine-tuning improves performance, particularly when the number of labeled training samples is small. To use MARBLE, the following steps are applied. A foundation model is applied to each modality to produce instance-level embeddings. For histopathology, WSIs are divided into tiles, each embedded independently using a pretrained vision foundation model ( STAR Methods , embedding generation). For biomarkers, each genomic alteration is represented either as a textual description embedded via an LLM or as an altered protein sequence embedded via a PLM, as described in the preceding section. Both the number of tiles per patient WSIs and the number of biomarkers per patient vary across samples. Therefore, an aggregation step is performed per modality ( STAR Methods , aggregation model), and the resulting representations are used for contrastive alignment ( STAR Methods , multimodal alignment objective). After pretraining, the histopathology image-only aggregator is fine-tuned to predict multi-label biomarker status ( STAR Methods , biomarker prediction) for biomarkers that were observed and unobserved during pretraining ( Figure 1 D). Because our approach can work with LLM embeddings, PLM embeddings, or both, we evaluate the respective variants, MARBLE-LLM, MARBLE-PLM, and MARBLE.    Improving generalizability with language pretraining  We design our experiments and evaluations to mirror a real-world setting. Using the MSK-IMPACT panel genomic alterations as our target predictive task, we exploit the property that several versions of the panel have been released over time, each adding new biomarkers. This allows us to test the effect of pretraining with early versions and fine-tuning with varying numbers of labeled samples from the latest panel. Our experiments use a cohort of 40,300 patients tested with one of four MSK-IMPACT panel versions, v.3, v.5, v.6, or v.7, each with an increasing number of oncogenes ( Figure 1 B;  Table S1 ). The dataset is partitioned to use patient samples assessed with early versions of the panel, specifically v.3, v.5, or v.6, during pretraining ( STAR Methods , pretraining setup). The final predictive model is fine-tuned to predict all biomarkers from the v.7 panel, which contains 37 new oncogenes, corresponding to 53 new biomarkers ( STAR Methods , fine-tuning setup). Performance is reported using balanced accuracy for in-distribution biomarkers, those seen during pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, out-of-distribution biomarkers, those unseen during pretraining, and overall. To specifically assess sample efficiency, supervised fine-tuning is performed with v.7 samples of size 100, 1,000, and 10,000 ( STAR Methods , fine-tuning setup). Results are compared to direct supervision without contrastive pretraining (no pretraining) and pretraining with only binary presence/absence encoding of biomarkers without semantic embedding information, motivated by the THREADS  4   approach (multi-hot) (see  STAR Methods , comparison approaches for additional pretraining details). We add one additional comparison which uses an LLM to perform aggregation in place of the multiple instance learning approach ( STAR Methods , comparison approaches).  Our proposed MARBLE-LLM consistently improves out-of-distribution generalization, particularly in the low-data regime ( Figure 2 ; and  S3 ). For example, at  k  = 100, our method achieves a balanced accuracy of 62.7 ± 0.8, substantially outperforming both the supervised baseline (55.7 ± 0.6) and the multi-hot pretraining approach (57.0 ± 1.1). This advantage persists across larger sample sizes, where MARBLE-LLM continues to outperform alternatives in the out-of-distribution setting. The gains of MARBLE-LLM compared to the multi-hot and summarization approaches across all evaluation settings demonstrate the benefits of using embeddings and of learning to aggregate biomarker embeddings dynamically, respectively. Strong performance on in-distribution biomarkers is also important to consider, as it demonstrates that strong out-of-distribution generalization does not come at a cost of in-distribution performance. MARBLE-LLM also almost always has the best in-distribution performance as well. The only setting where another approach has better balanced accuracy is for the supervised model when  k  = 100 and on in-distribution biomarkers (67.4 ± 0.4 versus 66.6 ± 0.3 for supervised and MARBLE-LLM, respectively). However, because of the large gains of MARBLE-LLM on out-of-distribution biomarkers, the overall balanced accuracy of MARBLE-LLM is still higher.  Figure 2   Performance comparison of multimodal pretraining across generalization setups and data regimes  Balanced accuracy (BA) of in-distribution and out-of-distribution biomarker prediction at three data regimes ( k  = 100, 1,000, 10,000).  (A) Results for pretraining scenario 1, using v.3, v.5, and v.6 panels.  (B) Results for pretraining scenario 2 using v.3 and v.5 panels.                         Language embeddings demonstrate strong generalization performance  Detailed sequence information is only available for patients measured with the v.3 and v.5 MSK-IMPACT panels ( Table S1 ). Therefore, in a second experiment, we focus on the relative value of the different biomarker representations.  Figure 2  ( Tables S2  and  S3 ) presents the results of the three pretraining settings. For all representations, MARBLE improves out-of-distribution performance compared to the supervised approach, particularly in the low data regime. We observe that MARBLE-LLM pretraining provides stronger out-of-distribution generalization than MARBLE-PLM across all data regimes. For example, in the low-data regime at  k  = 100, LLM-based embeddings achieve a balanced accuracy (BA) of 62.7 ± 0.5, compared to 61.3 ± 0.1 with PLM-based embeddings.  When combining both PLM and LLM embeddings, MARBLE achieves consistently strong performance, often matching or surpassing the best individual approach. For example, at  k  = 10,000, the combined model achieves a performance of 68.6 ± 0.2, the highest overall and comparable to MARBLE-LLM, trained with all three previous panel versions, despite less pretraining data. These findings suggest that LLM embeddings are particularly effective for enhancing generalizability, while their integration with PLM embeddings yields complementary benefits that improve performance across both in- and out-of-distribution scenarios.  Comparison across the two panels in  Figure 2  ( Table S2 ) for MARBLE-LLM allows us to consider the impact of the size of the pretraining dataset. Generally, we observe a slight boost in performance with the larger pretraining dataset when considering overall balanced accuracy; however, it is small or even zero for out-of-distribution biomarkers. For example, at  k  = 100 in the out-of-distribution setup, LLM-based pretraining achieves 62.7 ± 0.8 on the full dataset and 62.7 ± 0.5 on the restricted subset. This observation highlights the robustness of LLM-based embeddings and suggests that the advantage in low-data regime fine-tuning can be realized even with only modest amounts of pretraining data. At the same time, using the full dataset provides a slight performance boost at larger  k  (e.g., 69.3 ± 0.2 versus 68.2 ± 0.2 at  k  = 10,000), indicating that LLM-based pretraining can still benefit from a larger pretraining cohort.    Pretraining results in improvements for many biomarkers  While the aforementioned results show the value of MARBLE at the panel level, we also wanted to understand how these improvements are distributed among the different genomic biomarkers. To do so, we conducted a paired one-sided  t  test on a per-biomarker basis ( Table 1 ). For each biomarker, balanced accuracy across five independent draws of  k  is compared between the corresponding pair of models. Overall, these results suggest that MARBLE and its variants improve performance for many out-of-distribution biomarkers with a minimal number of biomarkers exhibiting a degradation of performance. For instance, at  k  = 100, 47.2% of out-of-distribution biomarkers demonstrated significantly higher balanced accuracy with MARBLE ( p  < 0.05), while only 1.9% of biomarkers showed significantly lower performance compared to the supervised baseline. The remaining out-of-distribution biomarkers exhibited no significant difference between the models. Meanwhile, the in-distribution biomarkers had a comparable number of increasing and decreasing, resulting in an average performance that is approximately equal to the supervised baseline. Across larger fine-tuning sets ( k  = 1,000 and  k  = 10,000), the proportion of biomarkers with significantly higher performance for the MARBLE and its variants decreased, reflecting smaller gains as more labeled data became available. However, even when  k  = 10,000, MARBLE resulted in a net improvement for 24% of in-distribution biomarkers and 28% of out-of-distribution biomarkers. This statistical analysis confirms that multimodal pretraining yields the largest improvements when labeled data are scarce. Comparison between MARBLE-LLM, MARBLE-PLM, and MARBLE revealed complementary benefits, with each contributing significant gains for different subsets of biomarkers ( Table 1 ). To further characterize per-biomarker performance, we visualize the change in balanced accuracy ( Figure 3 ) and its distribution as a function of baseline performance ( Figure S3 ). The former shows the clear advantage of MARBLE and its variants: there are no settings where average balanced accuracy decreases. And although we do observe some in-distribution biomarkers decrease in balanced accuracy, they are offset by an approximately equal number of increasing biomarkers yielding no major change in performance overall. This matches our expectations, as the amount of labeled data for in-distribution biomarkers is large and therefore the effect of pretraining is more minimal. Plotting the change in performance as a function of baseline accuracy ( Figure S3 ) allows us to note that most biomarkers have predictive performance better than random and that MARBLE is able to improve performance across the range of baseline values.  Figure 3   Distribution of change in balanced accuracy for in-distribution (left) and out-of-distribution (right) biomarkers compared to the no pretraining baseline for MARBLE and its variants at the different levels of k  The distributions show the clear improvement of MARBLE for out-of-distribution biomarkers as well as its decreased effect as  k  increases. For  k  = 100, MARBLE results in a small decrease in in-distribution performance on average. This effect is not observed for  k  = 1,000 and  k  = 10,000.                       We also wanted to investigate possible trends in which biomarkers had the most improvement related to the underlying biology. We focused on understanding if increases in performance from pretraining with PLM/LLM embeddings could be explained by functional overlap between the biomarkers not observed in pretraining (v.7) and those observed in pretraining (up to v.6). To do this, we used Reactome,  35   a pathway database with strong coverage of signaling pathways, which we selected over more generic ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology  36   ,   37  ) as defects in signaling are common in cancer (quantification and statistical analysis). In all  k  = 100 settings, the results show a weak but statistically significant correlation ( r  = 0.29,0.13,0.21 for MARBLE-PLM, MARBLE-LLM, and MARBLE, respectively,  α  ≤ 0.001). For larger values of  k , i.e., more supervised fine-tuning samples,  r  decreases and is no longer significant in any of the settings (e.g., for  k  = 10000, r  = 0.11,0.04,0.19, respectively). We note that the correlations are likely low as our analysis is necessarily underpowered due to the small number of biomarkers. However, we did not want to change the splits of data to better power the interpretability study as we prioritized fidelity to the true versioning of the MSK-IMPACT panel.  Because the PLM embeddings cannot naturally capture copy-number variations, we investigated whether or not this could explain the difference in MARBLE-LLM and MARBLE-PLM performance; however, no clear trends were observed (see  Table S4  for the types per panel;  Figure S5  for violin plots comparing the MARBLE variants to no pretraining as a function of mutation type).  Figure 4  plots the change in balanced accuracy compared to the supervised baseline without pretraining. Most notably, there is a high correlation of the improvements for each MARBLE variant. Using a relative  t  test, we find that MARBLE-LLM outperforms MARBLE-PLM on in-distribution oncogenic mutations for  k  = 1,000 and  k  = 10,000,  p  = 0.011 and  p  = 0.019, respectively. MARBLE-PLM outperforms MARBLE-LLM on in-distribution tumor suppressor genes for  k  = 1000,  p  = 0.041. There are no settings with statistically significant differences for out-of-distribution biomarkers. In some cases, MARBLE-PLM performed better on copy number variation biomarkers compared to MARBLE-LLM, however, on average, MARBLE-LLM is better.  Figure 4   Comparison of the difference between MARBLE variants and no pretraining by mutation type  Overall, there is a very high correlation between MARBLE-LLM and MARBLE-PLM. Although there are no statistically significant differences for out-of-distribution biomarkers, MARBLE-LLM does outperform MABRLE-PLM on average for copy number deletions, a type of mutation that the PLM cannot encode, across all settings of  k . Similarly, for copy-number amplifications, MARBLE-LLM is not worse on average than MARBLE-PLM. For other types of mutations, one approach does not clearly outperform the other.                       It is also possible that confounders drive performance. To investigate this potential issue, we consider performance as a function of positivity rate, i.e., the number of positive instances of the biomarker, and cancer diversity, i.e., the number of cancers in which the biomarker is observed. Positivity rate ranges from 0% to 43% with a mean and median of 0.7% and 0.2%, respectively. The number of cancers ranges from 0 to 227 with a mean and median of 18 and 11, respectively.  Figures S6  and  S7  visualize the change in balanced accuracy compared to the supervised baseline without pretraining as a function of positivity rate and cancer diversity, respectively. MARBLE leads to improved performance across the observed range of positivity rates, with consistent improvement once the positivity rate reaches approximately 1%. Similarly, MARBLE leads to improvements across the range of cancer diversity, with consistent improvement once the number of cancers reaches approximately 25. This latter observation particularly suggests that tissue-specific short-cuts are not a driver of performance as MARBLE has more consistent improvements with greater tissue diversity.     Discussion  The assessment of genetic biomarkers is increasingly important for cancer care as targeted therapeutics become available. However, sufficient sample collection is not always performed  9   leading to measurement gaps. For instance, in lung cancer, it is estimated EGFR testing is not performed on approximately 25% of lung cancer cases despite clear clinical recommendations.  38   ,   39   Performing an initial assessment using routinely collected diagnostic samples could inform sample collection and triaging of cases for genomic biomarker testing.  In this work, we present MARBLE, a multimodal contrastive pretraining framework that aligns histopathology WSIs with biomarker representations derived from LLMs and PLMs. Our results demonstrate that integrating biomarker knowledge through contrastive pretraining substantially improves out-of-distribution generalization, especially in low-data regimes and without degradation of in-distribution performance. LLM-based embeddings proved especially effective for generalization, and their integration with PLM embeddings provided additional improvement. These findings highlight the potential of combining pathology FMs with structured biological knowledge. This integration is crucial for precision oncology applications, particularly as new genomic or molecular biomarkers are discovered and incorporated into sequencing panels.  The motivation of our approach is also supported by recent observations in the literature. Dawood et al.  40   have published a recent study critiquing biomarker prediction efforts using H&E as latching on to spurious correlations and simple co-occurrence. In contrast, by using LLM and PLM embeddings, our approach aims to avoid these issues by introducing stronger mechanistic knowledge of the mutations, which in turn allows for generalizability. The particular approach we use is further supported by the observation that multi-hot encoding performs significantly worse, highlighting that pretraining alone is insufficient for generalizability and structured relationships are required. Overall, our proposed approach offers encouraging evidence for the expanding use of H&E images in precision oncology applications, which has been highlighted as an important frontier for prognosis and therapeutic responsiveness.  41     Limitations of the study  Our study dataset is limited to one institution. The unique requirements of creating dataset splits that incorporate new biomarkers meant that we were unable to find a suitable cohort to replicate the application of MARBLE. To address this limitation to the extent possible, we performed a careful study design, making sure no patients spanned the train, validate, and test splits as well as maintained fidelity to the panel versioning to create a real-world example. We also performed subset analyses over mutation type, cancer type, and positivity to investigate possible sources of confounding. No obvious sources of confounding were discovered. Nevertheless, future work will need to validate that the results of our study generalize to other biomarker panels and institutions.  Interrogating the model to interpret or explain its predictions remains challenging. Although it is possible to investigate attention maps, it is unclear to what extent the morphological features that predict biomarker status are or should be easily categorized and human readable. In lieu of direct visual interpretation, we rely on predictive performance as the key evaluation measure.  There are many architectural design considerations that must be made to implement MARBLE. Future work could consider different aggregator designs or different weighting of the loss terms. Our study focused on leveraging protein-level and text-based biomarker representations, future work could incorporate other representations such as those from recently developed DNA foundation models.  42   ,   43   There may also be opportunities to select representations that are more focused on mutations. Incorporation of spatial information may be another direction for improving model performance. Our multiple instance learning approach did not leverage spatial relationships among the image crops. Recent work has shown the importance of tumor microenvironment’s spatial relationship on prognosis.  44   ,   45   Such information could have complementary value to LLM and PLM embeddings and is an interesting direction for future work.     Method details   MSK-IMPACT cohort  The cohort used in this study underwent paired tumor-normal targeted sequencing with the FDA-approved MSK-IMPACT assay at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Each assay sample is paired with one or more H&E-stained WSIs obtained from the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue block. Each biomarker is defined as a pair: a gene name and a genomic alteration. Genomic alterations are defined as one of the following: mutations (single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and insertions/deletions (indels)), copy number variations (amplifications and deletions), and structural rearrangements (fusions).  The cohort contains 40,300 patients tested with one of four MSK-IMPACT panel versions: v3, v5, v6, or v7; note that a v4 panel was never released. The number of patients tested with a specific version, as well as the number of oncogenes and biomarkers associated with this version, are shown in  Table S1 . During pretraining, only biomarkers from panels v3, v5, and v6 are used. This is critical to ensure no data leakage and test true out-of-distribution generalization. For supervised fine-tuning, in all experiments, 2681 patients with biomarkers measured using the v7 panel (all biomarkers) are used as the test set. An additional 2692 patients with biomarkers measured using the v7 panel are used as the validation set during supervised fine-tuning.    MARBLE  MARBLE is a pretraining strategy which aligns two types of biomarker representations with histopathological image representations from a patient sample ( Figure 1 C). It is comprised of four components: (1) embedding generation, (2) aggregation model, (3) alignment objective, and (4) biomarker prediction.   Embedding generation  Following typical workflows,  46   whole slide image crops, commonly referred to as tiles, are embedded using an image-only pathology foundation model, specifically Virchow2,  3   which is selected because of its superior generalizability  47   and strong performance on biomarker tasks.  48   The WSI is split into a grid of high-resolution, non-overlapping tiles extracted at 20× magnification. Each tile is processed using the foundation model to produce tile-level embeddings, specifically the CLS token. The resulting set of embeddings per patient is denoted      H  i   ∈   R    N  H  i   ×   d  H        where      N  H  i      is the number of embeddings and  d   H   = 1280 is the embedding dimension.  Details regarding the generation of the biomarker embedding are reported in the main text. Briefly, PLM-based embeddings are created using the altered protein sequence and ESM-2. LLM-based embeddings are created using functional annotations from UniProtKB, which is summarized using GPT-4o and embedded with SBERT. The text embedding model is specifically all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a lightweight 6-layer transformer model from the SentenceTransformers library, which produces sentence embeddings with a dimensionality. Concretely, each projection head linearly maps the aggregated embedding to a 256-dimensional space, applies GELU activation, a second linear transformation with dropout, and a residual skip connection before layer normalization. Pretraining setup  Based on data availability, we considered two pretraining scenarios.   Scenario 1: LLM only.  Pretraining was performed using all samples measured with versions v3, v5, and v6, spanning 24,257 patients in total. MARBLE-LLM, the multi-hot baseline, the alternative aggregation approach described in Comparison approaches, and a supervised baseline were evaluated.   Scenario 2: All settings.  Protein mutation data were obtained from the publicly available MSK-IMPACT 2017 cohort through cBioPortal.  52   Detailed annotations specifying the exact amino acid substitutions were available only for the two earlier panel versions (v3 and v5). This data was essential for constructing altered protein sequences, which were subsequently embedded with a PLM to capture the molecular changes in the embedding space. This same subset (v3 and v5) of patient samples was also embedded with the LLM approach. Consequently, pretraining using MARBLE-LLM, MARBLE-PLM, and MARBLE was performed on this subset.    Finetuning setup For both Scenarios, during fine-tuning, the pretraining data from Scenario 1 is combined with a random sample of  k  = 100, 1000, or 10,000 patients measured with the v7 panel to train the multi-label classification model for all 1611 biomarkers ( Figure 1 B). This procedure is repeated five times to ensure robustness. Although the samples are random, they are consistent across settings to create valid comparisons. For all pretrained settings, weights are initialized with the corresponding MARBLE or baseline model. In the supervised baseline, the architecture and training data are the same, but the weights are initialized randomly.  We measured performance using the average of per-biomarker balanced accuracy (BA), with stratification for in-distribution, out-of-distribution and all biomarkers. In-distribution refers to biomarkers included during pretraining (i.e., up to v6 of the panel). Out-of-distribution refers to biomarkers not included during pretraining and introduced only at the fine-tuning stage (i.e., the latest panel, v7). To calculate balanced accuracy, the binarization threshold for each biomarker was selected based on the validation subset using the Youden index criterion  53   to maximize sensitivity–specificity trade-off. The reported values represent the mean and standard deviation across the 5 trials.

title: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: FTU-Seek: Foundation Model-Guided Hard-Negative Learning for Sparse Functional Tissue Unit Segmentation. Background/Objectives: Functional tissue units (FTUs), including tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs), blood vessels, and glands, encode localized immune, vascular, and epithelial organization in histopathology. Accurate quantification of these structures is important for studying tissue architecture and disease-associated tissue organization. However, FTUs are frequently sparse, heterogeneous, and surrounded by large amounts of morphologically similar background tissue, making automated segmentation in whole-slide images (WSIs) challenging. We therefore developed FTU-Seek, a pathology foundation model-guided framework that treats morphology-aware negative-patch selection as a key component of sparse FTU segmentation. Methods: FTU-Seek uses frozen multi-depth features from the UNI pathology foundation model to train a patch-level classifier that distinguishes FTU-containing from FTU-absent tissue. Target-absent patches are subsequently ranked according to their predicted target-containing probabilities, and the highest-scoring hard negatives are selected through a static TopK strategy to construct compact segmentation training sets. The framework was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and internal test cohorts across TLS, blood-vessel, and gland segmentation tasks, with an additional independent 30-WSI held-out cohort for TLS. Positive-only, all-tissue, random-negative, and matched random TopK sampling strategies served as comparators. Segmentation-derived phenotypes were further explored in external TCGA cohorts. Results: The patch-level classifiers achieved mean validation AUCs of 95.92%, 90.11%, and 98.16% for TLS, blood vessel, and gland classification, respectively. For TLS segmentation, the pre-specified Top1000 configuration retained 27.6% of the all-tissue training workload and achieved a slide-level Dice of 76.69 ± 11.89% on the independent 30-WSI held-out cohort. Compared with matched random Top1000 sampling, it improved Dice by 3.72 percentage points (95% CI, 2.05-5.38). Blood vessel and gland segmentation achieved performance approaching all-tissue training while reducing the retained training workload by approximately one-half and one-third, respectively. Compared with matched random sampling, classifier-guided hard-negative selection produced the greatest improvements for sparse and morphologically ambiguous FTUs. Exploratory TCGA analyses further showed associations of TLS phenotypes with overall survival, vascular phenotypes with overall survival and microvascular invasion, and glandular phenotypes with clinicopathological characteristics. Conclusions: FTU-Seek demonstrates that pathology foundation models can support sparse FTU segmentation not only through feature representation but also through morphology-aware construction of segmentation training sets. By prioritizing informative hard negatives, the framework reduces redundant segmentation-training workload while maintaining competitive segmentation performance and supporting quantitative tissue phenotyping from routine histopathology.

title: A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

evidence_text:
A weakly supervised deep learning model for OSCC diagnosis and lesion highlighting in histopathology images.

Background

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the predominant histopathological subtype of oral malignancies, and histopathology-based diagnosis remains central to clinical management. With the rapid development of digital pathology and deep learning, automated analysis of histopathology images has shown considerable potential for improving screening efficiency and reducing inter-observer variability. However, in both public datasets and real-world research settings, only image-level labels are commonly available, whereas region-level annotations are often lacking. This limitation makes weakly supervised modeling necessary and also restricts rigorous validation of spatial interpretability.

Methods

To address these challenges, we developed a weakly supervised deep learning framework based on patch-level representation learning and multiple-instance aggregation for image-level OSCC diagnosis with exploratory heatmap visualization. Specifically, histopathology images were divided into patches and encoded into feature embeddings. UNI 2, a recently developed pathology foundation model with highly competitive performance in contemporary computational pathology benchmarks, was adopted as the primary feature extractor to obtain informative patch representations. ResNet-50 was additionally implemented as a conventional baseline encoder for comparative evaluation. A self-attention-based multiple-instance aggregation module was then introduced to capture dependencies among instances within each patch set and to generate binary OSCC predictions.

Results

In five-fold cross-validation, the UNI-2-based model achieved a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9919, compared with 0.9899 for the ResNet-50 baseline. On the independent external validation cohort, UNI 2 further achieved an AUC of 0.9992, outperforming ResNet-50, which achieved an AUC of 0.9564. As an exploratory interpretability analysis, attention responses were visualized as heatmaps to inspect model focus patterns and support qualitative error review, without assuming verified lesion-level correspondence in the absence of region-level annotations.

Conclusions

This framework demonstrates strong image-level diagnostic performance for OSCC and provides exploratory visualization for qualitative model review without requiring additional fine-grained annotations, offering a reusable technical pathway for weakly supervised OSCC histopathology modeling and future multicenter validation.

evidence_text: Knowledge-enhanced pretraining for vision-language pathology foundation model on cancer diagnosis. Vision-language foundation models have shown great promise in computational pathology but remain primarily data-driven, lacking explicit integration of medical knowledge. We introduce knowledge-enhanced pathology (KEEP), a foundation model that systematically incorporates disease knowledge into pretraining for cancer diagnosis. Background Accurate risk stratification remains essential for guiding cancer management, yet conventional clinicopathological factors and many whole-slide image (WSI)-based deep learning models incompletely capture interpretable tissue-level spatial heterogeneity.
