Mouse models All animal-related procedures were conducted strictly following the guidelines and approvals set forth by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC# 202300101) at New York University Langone Health. RIM3 melanoma cells expressing shSCR or shNf1 were injected subcutaneously into the flank of six-week-old nude mice (Jackson Laboratory, RRID: IMSR_JAX:002019) or syngeneic C57BL/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory, RRID: IMSR_JAX:000664). Male mice were used because the sex of the mouse from which the RIM3 cell line was originally derived was not reported. For tumor-growth studies, mice were injected with1 × 10⁶ cells, whereas 2 × 10⁵ cells were used for treatment studies. Tumor dimensions were measured using digital calipers, and tumor volume was calculated as V = (π/6) x L x W 2 ), where L represents tumor length and W represents tumor width. For longitudinal tumor-growth studies, treatment was initiated when tumors reached approximately 100–200 mm³. Mice were then randomly assigned to vehicle control, afatinib, anti–PD-1, or combined afatinib plus anti–PD-1 treatment groups, with 12 mice per group, and treated for up to four weeks. For flow-cytometric endpoint studies, tumors were allowed to reach approximately 500 mm³ before mice were randomly assigned to the same treatment groups. 5–7 mice were treated for one week, after which tumors were collected for flow-cytometric analysis. Afatinib (MedChemExpress, BIBW 2992, Cat. No. HY-10261) was administered by oral gavage at 20 mg/kg five days per week. Anti–PD-1 antibody (Bio X Cell, anti-mouse CD279, Cat. No. BE0146) was administered by intraperitoneal injection at 10 mg/kg twice weekly. Mice were monitored for changes in body weight, general condition, and other signs of treatment-related toxicity daily. Animals were excluded only according to predefined criteria, including severe weight loss, and six animals were excluded. Tumor-growth curves are presented as mean ± SEM. For each mouse, the area under the tumor-growth curve (AUC) was calculated using the trapezoidal rule, and differences in AUC between treatment groups were assessed using two-sided unpaired t-tests. Mice were euthanized when tumor volume exceeded 2,000 mm 3 or when a predefined experimental endpoint was reached. Overall survival was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier analysis, and survival curves were compared using the log-rank test. A two-sided P  < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Melanoma tissues are organized into 12 spatially defined meta-niches To determine whether and how NF1 loss affects immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance, we used two tissue microarrays (TMAs) comprising samples from 32 patients with melanoma, including 17 NF1 Mut and 15 NF1 WT tumors (Fig.  1 A, Table S1). Because each patient contributed two tissue cores, these TMAs contained 64 cores (34 NF1 Mut and 30 NF1 WT ). We profiled 42 of these cores using the 10X Genomics 5 K Xenium platform. After image processing, cell segmentation, and rigorous quality control, we excluded cells with fewer than 50 transcripts and cores with fewer than 5000 cells. We batch-corrected and normalized the data across independent tissues, creating an integrated data set of 1,003,604 high-quality cells from 39 cores (20 NF1 Mut and 19 NF1 WT ). Louvain clustering separated melanoma cells from B cells, T cells, myeloid cells, plasma cells, epithelial cells, and other stromal cell types (Fig.  1 B), which were then annotated based on lineage-defining marker gene expression (Fig.  1 C). Although these cell populations were detected across most melanoma samples, their spatial distributions varied markedly between tumors (Fig.  1 D), suggesting that each tumor contains multiple specialized niches whose composition and organization may influence pathological features and therapy response. I Representative FOV images of MNs identified in melanoma patients To characterize these niches in greater detail, we re-clustered cells within each major lineage based on gene expression, identifying 18 distinct cell types, including five melanoma cell states (Fig. 1 E-F, Figure S1A). We identified melanoma cells with melanocytic, proliferative, intermediate, neural crest (NC)-like, and mesenchymal (MES) features, consistent with previous reports [ 25 ]. Immune populations included cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells, regulatory T cells (Treg), M2-like macrophages, interferon (IFN)-stimulated macrophages, activated myeloid cells, B cells, and plasma cells. Stromal populations included cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) with myofibroblastic (myCAF) or inflammatory (iCAF) features, as well as pericytes, endothelial cells, and epithelial cells. We mapped cell-type identities and transcriptional programs back to each tissue core, retrieved each cell’s centroid, and analyzed their neighborhoods within a 40-µm radius using a fast radius-based nearest-neighbor search (frNN) [ 18 ]. K-means clustering [ 19 ] grouped these neighborhoods into 12 frequently occurring meta-niches (MNs), which we defined as cellular spatial neighborhood patterns observed across multiple independent tissue samples (Fig. 1 G). Each MN was annotated according to its most prevalent cell types and broadly categorized as melanoma-rich, immune-rich, stromal-rich, or vascular-rich. Notably, each cell type appeared across multiple MNs (Figure S1B), indicating that cell identity alone does not determine niche architecture. Although individual patients exhibited significant variability in MN composition (Figure S1C), with some tissues dominated by melanoma-rich niches, the identified MNs were generally consistent across the cohort. Several MNs were found in all samples, while others appeared in more than 50% of cases (Fig.  1 H-I). These results suggest that, despite differences in niche abundance among patients, the main spatial MN programs reflect recurring TME states rather than isolated, patient-specific patterns. Overall, these data demonstrate that melanoma tissues are highly compartmentalized, with distinct cell types forming recurring MNs, and that each tumor contains multiple MNs in proportions unique to each patient. NF1-loss links meta-niche remodeling to immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance To determine whether variation in MN composition was associated with cancer-driving mutations, we compared NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanoma tissues. Although these tissues contained the same major cell populations (Figure S2A), NF1 Mut melanomas contained significantly more NC-like melanoma cells (Figure S2B-C). NF1 Mut melanomas were also significantly enriched in MNs dominated by NC-like melanoma cells, immune-suppressive M2-like macrophages, immune-suppressive iCAFs, and regulatory T cells (Fig.  2 A-B, S2D-F). Conversely, NF1 Mut melanomas were depleted of MNs enriched for cytotoxic T cells, Tregs, and IFN-activated macrophages, as well as MNs enriched in pericytes and endothelial cells (Fig.  2 A, C, S2D-F). These results suggest that NF1 loss reshapes the assembly of cells into specific MNs, potentially contributing to immune evasion. Dot size represents −log10 of two-sided exact permutation test comparing tissue level MN fractions between R and NR Cell-cell communication analyses using CellChat [ 20 ] support this idea. NC-like melanoma cells communicated more extensively with melanoma cells in other states, stromal and immune cells within MN2 (NC + M2 + CAF) of NF1 Mut than NF1 WT melanoma (Fig. 2 D). Myelin protein zero (MPZ), which has been associated with tumor progression, invasion, and metastasis [ 26 ], was the predominant and most characteristic signaling pathway active within MN2 (Figure S2G). Cell-cell communication within MN6 (iCAFs+M2) was generally much stronger in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT melanoma (Fig. 2 E). Furthermore, interactions between mesenchymal melanoma cells and CAFs were consistently stronger in MN2, MN6, and MN3 of NF1 Mut than NF1 WT melanoma tissues (Fig. 2 D-F). In contrast, melanoma-immune cell interactions, especially those between activated macrophages and pericytes or endothelial cells, were stronger within the immune-active MN3 (IFN-myeloid + T cell) in NF1 WT than in NF1 Mut tumors (Fig.  2 F). Differential cell-cell communication analyses within this immune-active MN3 revealed a greater number of receptor-ligand interactions among cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, regulatory T cells, and activated macrophages in NF1 WT than in NF1 Mut tumors (Fig.  2 G). Conversely, signaling interactions between melanoma cells and CAFs in MN3 were higher in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT tumors. CXCL signaling was significantly elevated in MN3 of NF1 WT tumors, whereas MPZ, Cell Adhesion Molecule (CADM), Protease-Activated Receptor (PAR), and Heparan Sulfate Proteoglycans (HSPG) signaling were increased in MN3 of NF1 Mut tumors (Figure S2H). These data are consistent with a more angiogenic and immunosuppressed tumor microenvironment (TME) in NF1 Mut compared to NF1 WT melanoma. Some differences in cell-cell communication between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanomas were not restricted to specific meta-niches; instead, they were evident globally across tissues. NC-like melanoma cells signaled extensively to iCAFs and mesenchymal melanoma cells, while myCAFs engaged in collagen and laminin signaling with NC-like melanoma cells, in NF1 Mut but not NF1 WT melanoma (Figure S3A-B). Conversely, myCAFs showed fewer interactions with cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT tumors. These differences in cell-to-cell communication were accompanied by broader signaling changes across NF1 Mut compared to NF1 WT melanoma. NF1 Mut melanoma exhibited increased EGF signaling in mesenchymal melanoma cells and iCAFs; significantly higher levels of collagen, laminin, TGFβ, KIT, prostaglandin, VEGF, PDGF, and L1CAM signaling in the TME, where CXCL signaling was decreased (Figure S3C-E). It also showed increased signaling for PDGF, EGF, TGFβ, KIT, VEGF, ADGR-A, ADGR-D, tenascin, and laminin in myCAFs and iCAFs. Overall, these findings indicate that NF1 Mut melanoma is characterized by heightened stromal and growth factor signaling, a more fibrotic microenvironment, reduced vascular signals, and diminished immune-cell interactions. The immunosuppressive TME in this NF1 Mut melanoma cohort indicated that some tumors could be resistant to ICIs. To determine whether the spatial composition of MNs correlates with anti-PD1 or other ICI response data, we stratified our NF1 Mut melanoma cohort into 7 responder (R) and 11 non-responder (NR), and our NF1 WT melanomas into 9 R and 9 NR tissues. By comparing the fraction of each MN between R and NR we uncovered distinct response-associated patterns in NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanomas (Fig. 2 H). The MN2 (NC + M2 + CAF) was highly enriched in NF1 Mut but not NF1 WT tumors that didn’t respond to ICI or anti-PD1 (Fig. 2 I). myCAFs and mesenchymal melanoma cells were also enriched in the NF1 Mut NR group. In contrast, MN3 (IFN-myeloid + T cell) and MN9 (Inter+Prol+Melan) were enriched in the NF1 WT NR group. MN4 (vasc+perivascular) was more abundant in the R group. These data suggest that NC-like melanoma cells, as well as myCAFs, M2-like macrophages, and Tregs, may contribute to ICI resistance in NF1 Mut melanoma, consistent with their well-established immunosuppressive functions [ 27 – 29 ]. They also suggest that MNs orchestrated by melanoma cells that lost NF1 may function as spatially organized, immunosuppressive microenvironments that become enriched in NF1 Mut melanoma tissues that don’t respond to PD-1 or other ICIs. NF1 mutant tumors accumulate dysfunctional CD8 + T cells The selective enrichment of immune-suppressive MNs suggests that NF1 loss could alter the spatial structure of the tumor microenvironment, broadly impairing anti-tumor immunity. To test this idea, we examined global differences in immune cell organization and CD8 + T cell function in NF1 Mut melanoma by measuring distances between melanoma cells and nearby cell types. This neighborhood analysis showed that NF1 Mut melanoma cells are closer to CAFs, Tregs, M2-like macrophages, and pericytes, but are farther from cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, CXCL13 + CD8 + T cells, or endothelial cells compared to NF1 WT melanoma cells within tumors (Fig.  3 A-B). To rule out the impact of tissue sampling differences on the spatial results, we compared the total cell counts, tissue area, cellular density, and the average number of melanoma neighbors between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT tissue samples and found no differences in these parameters (Figure S4A). These findings suggest that the microenvironment surrounding NF1 Mut melanoma cells is depleted of immune cells but rich in CAFs, while NF1 WT melanoma tissues are more infiltrated by CD8 + T cells and other immune cell types. The few CD8 + T cells that infiltrated NF1 Mut tumors expressed significantly less FYN, GZMB, IRF1, TNFRSF1B, TNFSF4, and TNFRSF9 (Fig.  3 F). They were also enriched in pathways associated with decreased cytokine production, reduced T cell activation and differentiation, and diminished T cell-mediated killing of cancer cells (Fig.  3 G, Table S2). To validate these data with an independent method, we stained the same cohort with a custom 45-plex antibody panel. We imaged 56 tissues on the Akoya-PhenoCycler platform and used HALO software to quantify, segment, and annotate 1,079,175 single cells. This approach captured melanoma cells, CAFs, endothelial cells, dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, CD4 + T cells, CD8 + T cells, memory T cells, NK cells, and B cells. After quality control, we retained 1,052,420 cells from 49 samples. These immunostainings confirmed that NF1 Mut melanoma tissues contained fewer cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and a higher regulatory T cell-to-CD8 + T cell ratio. Furthermore, markers of cytotoxic (GZMB + ), memory (CD45RO + ), exhausted (PD-1 + , TOX + ), and activated/proliferating (Ki67 + ) CD8 + T cells were significantly decreased in NF1 Mut melanoma tissues (Fig. 3 H, I). Consistent with these results, imputation of gene expression data of skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM) that were generated by the Cancer Genome Atlas Network (TCGA) [ 13 ] with CIBERSORTx [ 30 ], using single-cell RNA sequencing data from Tirosh et al. [ 31 ] as a reference, also detected significantly fewer CD8 + T cells in NF1 Mut melanoma samples than in NF1 WT melanomas (Figure S4B). To test functional engagement of CD8 + T cells in immune responses, we measured intratumoral CD4 + T cell/CD8 + T cell/DC immune triads, which are crucial for ICI responses [ 32 ]. We quantified the presence of these triads using proximity scores based on distances between CD4 + T cells, CD8 + T cells, and DCs (CD11c + , HLA.DR + , CD14 − , CD68 − , SOX10 − ) and observed significantly fewer CD4 + T cell/CD8 + T cell/DC immune complexes in NF1 Mut melanoma tissues compared to NF1 WT melanoma tissues (Figure S4C-D). Moreover, these complexes were significantly higher in tumors of patients who responded to PD-1 inhibitors (Figure S4E). NF1 loss results in decreased expression of melanoma antigen presentation mechanisms Our analyses uncovered distinct immune evasion strategies in NF1 WT and NF1 Mut melanomas. NF1 WT tumors were enriched for immune-active MNs, in which CD8 + T cells followed a classical activation, memory formation, and exhaustion trajectory. By contrast, NF1 Mut melanomas were dominated by immune-silenced MNs, with broadly attenuated CD8 + T cell states and reduced tumor immune interactions. Consistent with these observations, inflammatory cytokine ( IL1B , IL6 , IL12A/B , IL17A , IL18 , TNF , IFNG , IFNA1 , IFNB1 ), chemokine ( CXCL9 , CXCL10 , CXCL11 , CXCL13 ), and chemokine receptor ( CCR5 , CCR7 , CXCR3 , CXCR4 , CXCR5 ) expression scores were significantly lower in the NF1 Mut tumor immune microenvironment (Fig.  4 A). These changes also correlated with suppressed immune-stimulatory ( CD80 , CD86 , ICOS , CD28 , and TNFRSF9 ), and immune-inhibitory checkpoint ( PDCD1 , CD274 , CTLA4 , LAG3 , HAVCR2 , TIGIT , and VSIR ) gene expression scores. These differential expression data suggest that NF1 Mut melanomas may be less effectively recognized by immune cells, suggesting impaired antigen presentation rather than dominant checkpoint-mediated inhibition. Our highly multiplexed IHC analyses detected significantly lower HLA expression in NF1 Mut melanoma cells (Fig. 4 B-C). This reduced HLA expression correlates directly (r s = 0.8355) with fewer CD8 + T cells in tumor tissues (Fig. 4 D). In addition to HLA, our Xenium data showed lower expression of TAP1 , TAP2 , CANX , and CIITA in NF1 Mu t melanoma cells compared with NF1 WT melanoma cells (Fig. 4 E). TAP1 and TAP2 are required for transporting peptides from the cytoplasm to MHC-I, and CIITA controls MHC-II expression and thus antigen presentation [ 34 , 35 ]. To test whether NF1 loss directly caused reduced HLA expression in NF1 Mut melanoma, we transduced A375 and SK-MEL-28 melanoma cells with non-targeting control short-hairpin RNAs (shSCR) or NF1 -inhibiting short-hairpin RNAs (shNF1) (Fig.  4 F). Differential gene expression analyses showed significantly lower expression of HLA-A , HLA-B , HLA-C , HLA − F , HLA − G , HLA − DMA , HLA − DMB , HLA−DPA1 , and HLA−DPB1 in shNF1-transduced A375 cells compared with shSCR controls (Fig.  4 G). Furthermore, NF1 -knockdown A375 and SK-MEL-28 cells expressed less MHC-I on their cell surface, and SK-MEL-28 cells also expressed less MHC-II, compared with shSCR-expressing control cells, even after IFN-ɣ stimulation (Fig. 4H). These data demonstrate that NF1 loss reduces HLA expression and that IFN-γ stimulation cannot fully restore it. EGF-EGFR signaling is enriched in NF1 -mutant melanoma meta-niches and mediates immune evasion To identify signaling pathways hyperactivated in NF1 Mut melanoma with reduced HLA expression and amenable to therapeutic targeting, we conducted gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) on transcripts differentially expressed in melanoma, stromal, and myeloid cells between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT tumors. These analyses revealed transcriptional programs enriched in NF1 Mut melanoma cells, including EMT, UV response, hypoxia, TGFβ, and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) signaling (Figure S5A). These pathways were predicted based on significantly increased NOTCH1 , SOX2 , NGFR , ERBB2 , EGFR , TGFB2 , TGBR2 , VEGFA , VEGFC , and PDGFRB expression (Figure S5B). Conversely, NF1 WT melanoma cells were enriched for inflammatory responses, IFN-α/ɣ responses, IL2-STAT5, and IL6-STAT3 signaling, based on elevated IL10, IL21, IFNG, IFNL1, IFNA17, and TNFSF18 expression. Furthermore, CAFs we identified in NF1 Mut melanoma upregulated genes involved in cell division, cell-cycle regulation, and EGF signaling (Figure S5C). They also downregulated genes involved in antigen processing, antigen presentation, cytokine production, inflammatory responses, T cell activation, and adaptive immune responses. Similarly, myeloid cells we identified in NF1 Mut melanoma tissues expressed transcripts associated with heightened growth factor responsiveness, increased TGFβ receptor signaling, reduced inflammatory responses, dampened immune effector processes, and diminished cytokine and immune responses (Figure S5D). Notably, EGF signaling was elevated not only in NF1 Mut melanoma cells, as we recently reported [ 8 , 10 ], but also in CAFs surrounding these NF1 Mut melanoma cells, as predicted by CellChat (Figure S3C-E). Cell-level differences in these pathways between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanoma were also observed at the MN level (Fig.  5 A). EGFR expression was more prevalent in NF1 Mut tumors across most MNs (Fig.  5 B), with the highest enrichment in NF1 Mut melanomas that didn’t respond to andti-PD-1-based therapies (Fig.  5 C, S6A). To identify biological programs associated with elevated EGFR expression in NF1 Mut tumors, we computed differential pathway enrichment scores between NF1 Mut and NF1 WT melanomas. These scores correlated directly with EMT, hypoxia, and TGFβ signaling, and indirectly with inflammation, IFN responses, IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling, IL2-STAT5 signaling, and p53 signaling (Fig.  5 D). EGFR inhibition induces an immune response that synergizes with immune checkpoint inhibitors in an NF1 -depleted syngeneic melanoma mouse model The increased expression of EGFR in NF1 Mut melanomas and its association with immune evasion mechanisms suggest that EGFR inhibition could reactivate tumor immunity and thereby improve responses to ICI therapy. To test this hypothesis, we used syngeneic RIM-3 cells [ 41 ] isolated from a melanoma that developed in Tyr::Nras Q61K Cdkn2a Fl/Fl mice [ 22 ]. sh Nf1 knockdown decreased NF1 expression and increased Egfr expression in RIM-3 cells (Fig. 6 I-J) and significantly accelerated their growth rate (Fig. 6 K). These results are consistent with our recent data on human melanoma short-term cultures and xenograft models [ 10 ] and now allow us to functionally test how NF1 loss and/or EGFR activation affect immune evasion and ICI responses. To do this, we first knocked down Egfr in shNf1-expressing RIM-3 cells and used RNA-seq to identify gene sets regulated by EGFR. We found a significant decrease in Egfr expression, along with increased expression of genes required for antigen presentation and NK and T cell activation (Fig. 6 L). Pathway analyses also revealed increased IFN-α and IFN-ɣ responses, while TNF-α signaling via NFκB, EMT, and TGFβ signaling were downregulated as a result of EGFR inhibition (Fig. 6 M). We observed similar changes in HLA expression when we compared shEGFR -expressing human NF1 Mut melanoma cell lines with shSCR-expressing cell lines (Fig. 6 N) or when we treated short-term cultures (STCs) from human NF1 Mut melanoma patients with the EGFR inhibitor afatinib (Fig. 6 O) [ 42 ]. Furthermore, MHC-I expression increased even more when we treated NF1 Mut melanoma cells with afatinib and IFN-ɣ than with IFN-ɣ alone (Fig. 6 P). These data demonstrate that increased EGFR signaling compromises antigen presentation in NF1 Mut melanoma cells, and these changes could contribute to immune evasion, defective T cell infiltration, impaired cytotoxic immune tetrad formation, and thus resistance to ICI therapy. To assess whether NF1 loss affects immune evasion, we subcutaneously transplanted equal numbers of RIM-3 cells expressing shSCR or shNf1 into immunocompromised Nude mice or syngeneic C57BL/6J mice and compared tumor initiation rates. Although both shSCR- and shNf1-expressing RIM-3 cells initiated tumors at similar rates in Nude mice (Fig.  7 A), only shNf1-expressing RIM-3 cells formed tumors in C57BL/6J mice (Fig.  7 B). This result supports the notion that NF1 loss enhances immune evasion, consistent with our spatial transcriptomic results from human melanoma tissues. The anti-PD-1 antibody did not significantly inhibit tumor growth on its own, suggesting that shNf1-expressing RIM-3 cells are ICI-resistant (Fig. 7 D). However, afatinib significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with vehicle control, consistent with results from recently reported PDX models [ 10 ]. Combining afatinib with an anti-PD-1 antibody further enhanced the tumor-inhibitory effect of afatinib in the shNf1-expressing RIM-3 model. These responses led to prolonged survival in tumor-bearing mice treated with afatinib monotherapy or afatinib plus anti-PD-1 until the experimental endpoint, whereas mice treated with vehicle control or anti-PD-1 monotherapy reached their humane endpoints sooner due to their rapid growth rates (Fig. 7 E). To determine how these therapies affect immune responses in these tumors, we treated an independent cohort of NF1-depleted RIM-3 melanoma-bearing mice for one week and analyzed changes in myeloid and lymphoid cells by flow cytometry (FACS). We stained single-cell suspensions with antibody panels to detect and quantify T cell populations (CD45, CD4, FOXP3, CD8, CD44, GZMB, Ki67, TIM-3, and PD-1) and myeloid cell populations (CD45, NK-1.1, I-A/I-E, F4/80, CD11b, CD11c, Ly-6 C, and Ly-6G). Our FACS data revealed that afatinib treatment alone did not affect tumor-infiltrating CD4 + T cells or CD8 + T cells. In contrast, PD-1 inhibition increased CD4 + T cell ( p = 0.0582) and CD8 + T cell ( p = 0.0742) infiltration, although the response was variable and not statistically significant. By contrast, combined inhibition of EGFR and PD-1 led to a statistically significant increase in tumor-infiltrating CD4 + T cells ( p = 0.0123) and CD8 + T cells ( p = 0.0035), as well as a change in the CD8 + T cell/Treg ratio ( p = 0.0030). Among T cell activity markers, GZMB increased ( p = 0.053) in tumors treated with afatinib and anti-PD-1, but not in tumors treated with afatinib or anti-PD-1 alone (Fig. 7 F-G). These results indicate that combination therapy improves the T cell immune response, whereas anti-PD-1 or afatinib alone has no significant effect. Furthermore, afatinib treatment significantly increased neutrophil ( p = 0.0203) and NK cell ( p = 0.0258) infiltration in Nf1 knockdown tumors (Fig. 7 H-I), perhaps due to upregulation of Ulbp1 [ 43 ] (Fig. 6 K). Anti-PD-1 antibodies had no significant effect on these cells, but effects on NK cells ( p = 0.0363), neutrophils ( p = 0.0305), and monocytes ( p = 0.0166) were augmented by combination therapy (Fig. 7 H, I). In conclusion, our data indicate that increased EGFR expression resulting from NF1 loss leads to immune evasion and, consequently, ICI resistance. Therefore, combining EGFR inhibition with ICI therapy would be a rational approach to improve clinical outcomes in patients with NF1 Mut melanoma. Discussion We deployed spatial transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of human melanomas, complemented by functional preclinical models, to define the multicellular architecture of the TME and to reveal its link to immune evasion and immunotherapy response. We identified 12 recurrent MNs as spatially correlated assemblies of transcriptionally distinct melanoma cells that consistently interact with specific stromal and immune populations across samples and patients. These MNs comprise melanoma cells in diverse states, along with subsets of CAFs, endothelial cells, T cells, myeloid populations, and other stromal cells, revealing modular spatial ecosystems that may underlie clinical heterogeneity. Given the unmet need for more effective treatment of NF1 Mut melanoma [ 8 – 11 ], we focused on how NF1 loss shapes TME organization. We report that NF1 Mut tumors were enriched for MNs marked by heightened EGF–EGFR signaling, NC-like dedifferentiation, more abundant CAFs, a collagen-rich extracellular matrix, and spatial patterns consistent with T cell exclusion. In contrast, NF1 WT tumors exhibited greater infiltration by active, exhausted, and memory CD8 + T cells. Our data also reveal that NF1 loss promotes EGFR expression and activation, thereby reducing MHC class I and MHC class II antigen presentation on melanoma cells and, in turn, promoting immune evasion. Consistent with these findings, we observed decreased HLA presentation in NF1 Mut tumors and an inverse correlation between EGFR expression and intratumoral CD8 + T cell density. Our spatial analyses identified fewer MNs containing cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, activated macrophages, and Tregs, as well as fewer intratumoral CD4 + T cell/CD8 + T cell/DC immune triads [ 32 ]. Such an immune landscape is more consistent with impaired antigen presentation and T cell exclusion than with activation–exhaustion dynamics, in which exhausted and memory T cells would be expected to accumulate as more readily seen in NF1 WT melanoma tissues. These results refine prior reports that emphasized PD-L1 upregulation as the dominant immune evasion mechanism in NF1 Mut melanoma [ 44 ]. Although increased PD-L1 surface expression has been observed in NF1-depleted cultures [ 44 ], and desmoplastic melanoma (a rare melanoma subtype typically associated with NF1 mutations, a high tumor mutational burden, and favorable response to immunotherapy [ 5 ]), our spatial analyses of intact tissues also identify a more complex and immunologically “silent” phenotype in a significant subset of NF1 Mut melanomas that do not respond to ICIs. Our spatial analyses suggest that CAFs could function as central orchestrators of the NF1 Mut TME. Melanoma cells are in closer spatial proximity to CAFs in NF1 Mut than in NF1 WT tumors, and their extracellular matrix is more collagen-rich. Ligand–receptor analyses indicated significantly stronger interactions of CAF populations with melanoma cells and other neighboring stromal and immune cells in NF1 Mut tumors. Together, these data suggest that NF1 loss remodels the extracellular matrix and amplifies CAF-driven signaling [ 45 ], creating an immune-suppressive, pro-angiogenic niche that physically and functionally restricts lymphocyte access to tumor cells. Our results also extend the broader literature implicating EGFR in tumor immune evasion across other solid tumors [ 46 – 48 ], highlighting this pathway as a potential target for combination therapy in NF1 Mut melanoma. EGFR was enriched in MNs associated with heightened oncogenic signaling and immune escape. Increased EGFR expression also correlated with immune-evasive transcriptional programs in NF1 Mut melanoma. Functionally, we found that EGFR inhibition can restore the expression of genes required for antigen presentation in NF1 Mut melanoma cells and enhance anti-tumor immunity. In addition to upregulating the MHC machinery [ 49 ], EGFR inhibition increased ULBP1 expression, potentially facilitating NK cell recruitment and innate immune responses [ 50 ]. These observations, together with the more permissive immune context in NF1 WT tumors, support a therapeutic strategy that combines EGFR inhibition with PD-1 inhibitors to overcome antigen presentation defects and immune cell exclusion, thereby improving therapeutic responses in patients with NF1 Mut melanoma [ 51 ]. Results from our syngeneic mouse model support the feasibility and enhanced efficacy of this combinatorial treatment approach. Our work has immediate implications for clinical translation. First, it delineates genotype-specific spatial ecosystems in melanoma, linking NF1 loss to an EGFR-dependent immune-evasive program marked by diminished antigen presentation, CAF-driven matrix remodeling, and T cell exclusion. Second, it identifies EGFR inhibition as a rational partner to PD-1 blockade in NF1 Mut disease, providing a mechanistic basis for combination therapy. Third, it highlights spatially resolved biomarkers, including EGFR activity, HLA antigen presentation signatures, CAF density and proximity, collagen enrichment, and T cell exclusion metrics, that could guide patient stratification and pharmacodynamic monitoring. Although NF1 Mut melanoma has been associated with immunosuppressive features, NF1 mutations do not define a uniformly immune checkpoint inhibitor–resistant subtype, as clinical response rates remain broadly comparable to those reported for other genetic melanoma subtypes [ 6 , 9 , 10 ]. NF1 loss also results in increased RAS/MAPK pathway activity [ 11 ], providing a rationale for MAPK-directed therapy. However, the clinical activity of MEK and related MAPK pathway inhibitors in NF1 Mut has been limited [ 52 ], potentially due to incomplete pathway suppression, adaptive reactivation of the pathway, and compensatory receptor tyrosine kinase signaling. Our results implicate EGFR/ERBB signaling as a potential adaptive dependency in NF1 Mut melanoma. Thus, EGFR inhibition may complement rather than replace MAPK-directed therapy, and combined EGFR and RAS/MAPK pathway inhibition may provide more effective suppression of tumor-intrinsic signaling. Whether and how immunotherapy should be incorporated into such combinations remains to be determined. Our preclinical data provide a rationale for combining EGFR inhibition with immune checkpoint blockade. However, additional studies will be necessary to directly compare EGFR inhibition with combinatorial EGFR-RAS or EGFR-MEK inhibition and their combinations with ICIs to determine the most effective therapeutic strategy. We acknowledge some limitations. The Xenium panel tests only ~ 5,000 genes and some signaling pathways may have been missed. Although our dataset presents the largest spatial multi-omic comparison of NF1 Mut and NF1 WT tissues to date, larger patient cohorts will need to be analyzed to better assess the effects of variant-specific NF1 mutations and co-occurring driver mutations. Finally, the TME programs we describe might reflect convergent signaling pathways downstream of NF1 loss or EGFR activation, and similar outcomes could result from alternative mechanisms. Although these mechanisms might be identified in our spatial transcriptomic data, their testing may require additional preclinical model development. Conclusion In conclusion, NF1 loss is associated with spatially distinct meta-niches in melanoma characterized by reduced MHC antigen presentation, CAF enrichment, matrix remodeling, and T cell exclusion, features collectively associated with immune evasion. By linking these features to EGFR-dependent programs and demonstrating that EGFR inhibition can restore tumor immunogenicity, our findings provide a rationale for biomarker-driven clinical trials combining EGFR inhibitors with PD-1 blockade in NF1 Mut melanoma, or for adding EGFR inhibitors if NF1 Mut melanomas do not respond to PD-1 monotherapy. evidence_text:
DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies.    Figure 1   Illustration of DeSpaST in uncovering cell-level gene expression. (a) Workflow of DeSpaST: The DeSpaST model integrates histology images with spatial transcriptomics (ST), encompassing cell segmentation, extraction of cell features, construction of cellular graphic structures, and the application of Graphic Convolution blocks for the precise deconvolution of cell-level gene expression. (b) Illustration of DeSpaST's application to human breast cancer tissue. Two genes  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  are shown as examples. From left to right includes H&E image, H&E image with pathologist annotations, DeSpaST  ERBB2  gene expression, Visium  ERBB2  gene expression, TESLA  ERBB2  gene expression, DeSpaST  MS4A1  gene expression, Visium  MS4A1  gene expression, and TESLA  MS4A1  gene expression. (c) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of orange box in panel b H&E image. (d) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of red box in panel (b) H&E image.            Multi-panel scientific figure showing the DeSpaST workflow and its application to breast cancer tissue. The workflow combines H&E histology, spatial transcriptomics, cell segmentation, cellular graph construction, and graph convolution to predict cell-level gene expression. Tissue maps compare H&E images, pathologist annotations, and ERBB2 and MS4A1 expression from DeSpaST, Visium, and TESLA, with zoomed regions highlighting tumor and immune-cell boundaries.         DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication. Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts.
