Protocol for integrated multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium and MACSima. Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  Multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on a single tissue section    •  Detailed Xenium and MACSima workflow protocol for single-section spatial multi-omics    •  Registration and integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data at single-cell level      Publisher’s note: Undertaking any experimental protocol requires adherence to local institutional guidelines for laboratory safety and ethics.    Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Dec 18.       Before you begin   Protocol overview  This protocol describes multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on the same tissue section using Xenium (10x Genomics) and MACSima Imaging Cyclic Staining (MICS, Miltenyi Biotec). The workflow was established using human tonsil and tumor tissue sections; however, it can be adapted to other tissue types with appropriate optimization of RNA probe panels, antibody panels, and tissue processing conditions.    Innovation  This protocol introduces a novel workflow for multimodal spatial profiling by integrating Xenium spatial transcriptomics with highly multiplexed protein imaging using MICS on the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarray (TMA) section. Alternative multimodal workflows have demonstrated the combination of Xenium with other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, including PhenoCycler and COMET.  1   ,   2   Building upon these advances, this protocol provides the first detailed experimental and computational workflow for integrating Xenium with the current-generation MACSima platform, which supports significantly higher antibody plexity than comparable technologies. This workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima analysis includes optimized requirements and procedures for sample processing, antigen retrieval, and iterative cyclic immunofluorescence that preserve tissue integrity and enable single-cell RNA and protein measurements on the same section. In addition to the experimental workflow, this protocol provides scripts for accurate registration of Xenium and MACSima imaging data, enabling direct correlation of transcriptomic and proteomic features within the same spatial framework. Importantly, both the laboratory workflow and computational approach can be adapted to other spatial multi-omics combinations, offering a flexible framework for integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data. Together, these advances address key technical challenges in spatial multi-omics and provide a reproducible and scalable approach for multimodal tissue analysis.    Institutional permissions  Experiments involving human-derived tissues require approval from the appropriate institutional ethics committee. Researchers must ensure that ethical approval is obtained and that informed consent is secured from all donors prior to sample collection. All specimens used in this study (see  key resources table ) were obtained with informed consent and handled in accordance with institutional regulations and approved protocols.    Tissue selection and preparation 
   1.  Obtain FFPE TMA samples with preserved morphology and RNA integrity.   
          CRITICAL:  Following proper handling, storage, preparation and sectioning of the FFPE tissues according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ) is critical to ensure preservation of morphology and RNA integrity.  
   2.  Optimize sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time for the block and floating time of the sections in the water bath of the Section Transfer System (STS) before mounting on slides to prevent cutting artefacts.    3.  Assess tissue quality, morphology and RNA integrity of the blocks prior to mounting on Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.    4.  Place sections on Xenium slides and store them according to standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).   a.  If the tissue blocks are of optimal quality, section them at 4–6 μm thickness using a microtome and mount the sections on Xenium slides.    b.  Dry the slides appropriately as per standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).      
          Pause point:  Slides can be stored at room temperature (RT, 20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in tubes with desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and Xenium workflow.  
   Xenium assay version compatibility 
    Note:   The workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima is compatible with the v1 as well as the 5K Prime Xenium assay versions. It is also compatible with the Xenium In situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation which has now become standard in the Xenium workflows. Since the MACSima workflow uses directly conjugated antibodies, the antibodies in the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit do not pose a risk of cross-detection (10x Genomics,  CG000750 ).  
   Xenium probe panel design 
   5.  Select a pre-designed Xenium probe panel and/or design a custom Xenium probe panel (to be used as a standalone panel or as an add-on to the pre-designed panel) targeting genes of interest relevant to the biological question.    6.  Validate the custom probe panel performance in control samples, if available.   
    Note:   Perform add-on panel design in line with the guidelines provided in the  Technical Note: Xenium Add-on Panel Design  (10x Genomics,  CG000643 ). Transcript abundance and cell type specificity should be taken into consideration when designing a panel.  
    Note:   Reference to existing single-cell RNA-seq data, ideally from matched sample types, can guide panel design by enabling identification of cell type specific genes and transcript abundance.  
    Note:   The custom probe panel performance can be cross-validated post-Xenium run by comparing with existing single-cell RNA-seq and / or Xenium datasets for sensitivity in terms of number of transcripts detected and for specificity in terms of biologically relevant co-expression patterns of different genes.  3    
   Antibody panel design for MACSima 
   7.  Select antibodies targeting proteins of interest for multiplex imaging and check for compatibility of antibodies with the respective sample type (FFPE).    8.  Optimize antibody concentrations and staining conditions in a mock Xenium-MACSima experiment using control samples, if available, to test the compatibility of sequential Xenium and MACSima staining (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).   
          CRITICAL:  Antibodies must be tested for compatibility within the Xenium-MACSima workflow (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).  
          CRITICAL:  Ensure that tissue processing conditions, such as working in an RNase-free environment, sectioning thickness, and optimal slide recovery and antigen retrieval conditions post-Xenium are compatible with both Xenium RNA detection and downstream protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Check for tissue integrity after post-Xenium imaging slide recovery (steps 12 and 13 in the  step-by-step method details ) before continuing with the protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Optimize post-Xenium antigen retrieval conditions to achieve sufficient epitope accessibility for protein staining while preserving tissue integrity. Harsh antigen retrieval conditions can compromise tissue integrity and spatial registration between modalities.  
   Instrument and software preparation 
   9.  Prepare the Xenium Analyzer instrument and required reagents according to manufacturer guidelines (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).    10.  Prepare the MACSima imaging system for cyclic staining and imaging. Install the MACS iQ View software on a data-analysis workstation.    11.  Install the scripts for the registration workflow, including required software dependencies ( Table 1 ).   a.  Clone the repository.  >git clone https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium.git    b.  Create the venv environment.  >python3 -m venv macsima_xenium    c.  Activate the venv environment.  >source macsima_xenium/bin/activate    d.  Install the Python package for the Xenium-MACSima analysis workflow from its repository in GitHub.  >pip install ./MACSimaXenium/    Note:   Ensure sufficient data storage and computational resources for handling large imaging datasets (see requirements listed in  materials and equipment ).        
   Table 1   Packages and resources required for data processing      Package or Resource  Version  IDENTIFIER  Reference      Python  ≥3.11   https://www.python.org/  RRID: SCR_008394  Programming language  Python Software Foundation    xenium_macsima_core_registration  1.0.0   https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium/   This protocol    harpy-analysis  ≥0.4.2   https://github.com/saeyslab/harpy   Rombaut et al.  4      Bioio  ≥3.3.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio   Brown et al.  5      bioio-ome-tiff  ≥1.4.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio-ome-tiff   Brown et al.  5      opencv-python-headless  ≥4.13.0.92   https://github.com/opencv/opencv-python   Alekhin et al.  6          Upstream data preparation (prerequisites)  The registration workflow in this protocol assumes that single-cell data and Xenium-MACSima region of interest (ROI) correspondences have been established beforehand. The following upstream processing steps are performed once per slide before the per-core registration loop and are summarized here for context. The code for these steps is experiment-specific and is not included in the shared repository; however, the analysis workflow follows standard practices using scanpy  7   and the Segment Anything Model (SAM).  8      12.  Build AnnData  9   feature matrix.   a.  Load each Xenium output folder by reading the transcript table (transcripts.parquet).    b.  Filter for quality value (QV) ≥ 20, remove control probes, and aggregate transcript counts per nucleus using nucleus boundary polygons (nucleus_boundaries.parquet).    c.  Store the resulting count matrix, centroid coordinates, and nucleus areas as an AnnData object.       13.  Segment TMA cores.   a.  Identify individual TMA cores using the Segment Anything Model (SAM1, ViT-H) applied to a 2D cell density histogram (binned centroids at approximately 50 μm per pixel). Each detected mask corresponds to one TMA core.    b.  Assign a position label to each cell according to which mask their centroid falls within and flag cells outside all masks with is_in_core = False.       14.  Perform quality filtering.   a.  Remove cells that are not assigned to a core and filter the remaining cells according to transcript counts and/or size.          Note:   A commonly used approach for cell-level quality filtering is to exclude cells with fewer than ten transcripts and genes expressed in less than five cells ( https://squidpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/tutorials/tutorial_xenium.html ).  10   However, transcript counts per cell are dependent both on the tissue and gene panel  11   and thus the use of more or less stringent thresholds taking into account also the area of the cell might be required.  12   Finally, a visual inspection of the spatial distribution of the excluded cells can help to identify biases in the filtering by highlighting the presence of spatially organized clusters of excluded cells.  11       15.  Match the TMA cores between Xenium and MACSima data.   a.  Match the Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers manually by comparing a spatial scatter plot of Xenium cell positions (colored by core position) with the MACSima ROI overview image.    b.  Write this mapping as a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.         Planning of multimodal data integration  This protocol describes the cross-modal alignment of Xenium spatial transcriptomics data (10x Genomics) with MACSima multiplexed cyclic immunofluorescence imaging data (Miltenyi Biotec) for TMA samples. Integration is performed per TMA core and produces multi-modal SpatialData  13   objects saved as Zarr  14   archives.           CRITICAL:  Accurate image registration is essential for reliable analysis of RNA and protein data at single-cell resolution.     Data requirements 
   16.  Provide Xenium and MACSima data sets, along with mappings that link Xenium cells to TMA cores and Xenium TMA cores to MACSima ROIs ( Table 2 ).   
          CRITICAL:  Maintain consistent orientation and handling of tissue sections and ROIs throughout the workflow.

MACSima folder  Path to the preprocessed MACSima folder generated after stitching and background subtraction with the MACS iQ View software.  16      Xenium-MACSima ROI matching CSV file  The Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers are mapped in a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.     Step-by-step method details 
    Note:   The protocol was optimized for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with Cell Segmentation Staining, using a Prime 5K Human pan Tissue and Pathways panel (10x Genomics, PN-1000724) and a custom 100-gene add-on panel. For alternative Xenium workflow formats, workflow parameters may require adaptation. Xenium processing should always be performed according to the corresponding manufacturer-recommended protocols. In addition, performance of downstream antibody staining following Xenium processing may vary depending on the selected Xenium assay configuration.  
  Preparation of FFPE TMA sections 
          Timing: 3 days when performing steps consecutively. Approximately 1.5 days are required for sectioning optimization, slide mounting, drying, and quality assessment. Another day is required for sectioning, mounting to Xenium slides, and drying. Half a day is required for deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of sections.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA samples for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow, including sectioning of the FFPE blocks, tissue mounting, deparaffinization, and decrosslinking of sections. Sample preparation is performed according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).           CRITICAL:  Sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time of the FFPE TMA block in ice-cold water, should be optimized depending on tissue type, degree of dehydration, and the age of the paraffin block. Similarly, the floating time of sections in the water bath prior to mounting on Xenium slides needs to be adjusted to prevent wrinkling, folding, or tearing of the sections.     1.  Assess tissue quality and RNA integrity.    Note:   Evaluate tissue quality and RNA integrity of the FFPE TMA samples prior to placement of sections onto Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.     a.  Mount serial sections on SuperFrost Plus slides and deparaffinize according to the standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).    b.  Perform DAPI and H&E staining as outlined in the demonstrated protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Appendix).    c.  Image the slide to assess nuclear integrity, tissue morphology, sectioning artefacts, and the presence of necrotic or degraded regions.    d.  For RNA quality assessment, collect approximately four 10 μm sections (for samples ≤ 6.5 × 6.5 mm) for RNA extraction and DV200 analysis.          CRITICAL:  Samples with DV200 values below 30 % are considered suboptimal and may result in reduced median transcript counts per cell in downstream Xenium analysis.         2.  Section the FFPE TMA block and dry the sections.          CRITICAL:  During sectioning, maintain RNase-free conditions by wiping the microtome with RNase Zap ™ solution and filling the water bath of the STS with nuclease-free water.     a.  Prepare the FFPE TMA block for sectioning by rehydrating it in ice-cold Milli-Q water for a previously optimized duration (typically 10–30 min, depending on tissue type and degree of dehydration).    b.  Trim the block until the area of interest is fully exposed. For previously sectioned TMA blocks, discard the first 5–10 sections to obtain uniformly hydrated and intact tissue sections prior to collection.    c.  Section FFPE TMA block at a thickness of 5 μm using a microtome. Let the sections slide via the STS into its water bath filled with nuclease-free water and maintained at 42°C–45°C.    d.  Incubate the sections in the water bath for a previously optimized duration (typically 10 s to 3 min for most FFPE tissues) to allow the section to fully flatten and to minimize wrinkles, folds, or tearing prior to mounting.          CRITICAL:  Excessive incubation times in the water bath may lead to tissue distortion or reduced adherence during downstream processing.      e.  From the water bath, mount the sections carefully onto the Xenium slides (10× Genomics, PN-1000465), within the designated sample area.          CRITICAL:  Avoid placing the sections covering the fiducials, specifically the top and bottom fiducials.            CRITICAL:  Monitor the section adhesion on Xenium slides throughout the workflow to ensure that sections remain intact and properly attached during all processing steps.      f.  Following section placement, incubate the slides at 42°C for 3 h to promote adhesion of the sections to the Xenium slide surface.    g.  After incubation, place the slides in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing desiccant and store them overnight (16–24 h) at RT (20°C–25°C) to allow complete drying of the tissue sections.          Pause point:  Following section mounting, Xenium slides can be stored at RT (20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in the presence of desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and further processing with the Xenium workflow.         3.  Perform deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of the sections.   a.  Incubate the slides at 60°C for 2 h, followed by cooling at RT (20°C–25°C) for 7 min prior to further processing.    b.  Sequentially incubate the slides in two Coplin jars containing xylene for 10 min each.    c.  Perform two washes in 100 % ethanol for 3 min each.    d.  Perform two washes in 96 % ethanol for 3 min each.    e.  Perform one wash in 70 % ethanol for 3 min.    f.  Perform a final rinse in nuclease-free water for 20 s.    Note:   Xylene and ethanol incubation steps should be performed in a fume hood.      g.  Assemble the slides into Xenium cassettes.    h.  Perform decrosslinking using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000720) (included in the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  kit, 10x Genomics, PN-1000742).    i.  Immediately proceed with the Xenium in situ gene expression workflow.         Probe hybridization for Xenium Prime  in situ  gene expression 
          Timing: 2–3 days; with the Xenium  in situ  multimodal cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 3 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, and cell segmentation staining. Day 3 includes post-staining washes, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining. Without cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 2 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining.   
 This section describes the preparation of deparaffinized and decrosslinked FFPE TMA sections for the Xenium workflow, enabling subsequent imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer. The entire workflow is performed according to the  Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation  user guide (10x Genomics,  CG000760 ) using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  reagents (10× Genomics, PN-1000742).    4.  Perform priming and probe hybridization.   a.  Hybridize priming oligos to decrosslinked RNA.    b.  Perform RNase treatment and a polishing reaction to release the RNA strand from the hybridized oligos, thereby enabling subsequent hybridization of Xenium probes to the target RNA (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).    c.  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, C1000) using the Xenium Prime 5K probes ( Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay  kit, 10× Genomics, PN-1000671) together with an optional custom human add-on panel comprising up to 100 additional genes.       5.  Perform post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification.   a.  Perform post-hybridization washes to remove unbound probes, followed by ligation of hybridized probes, and enzymatic rolling circle amplification to generate amplified signal products for downstream imaging.       6.  Perform optional multimodal cell segmentation staining.   a.  To facilitate morphology-based cell segmentation, perform overnight (16–24 h) staining using the Xenium cell segmentation staining reagents, which label nuclei, cell boundaries, and intracellular RNA-rich regions according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).       7.  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclear staining.   a.  After amplification (and optional cell segmentation staining), perform autofluorescence quenching, brief drying at 37°C for 5 min and subsequent nuclear staining according to the manufacturer’s instructions.    b.  Upon completion of the workflow, store the slides in 0.05 % PBST until imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer.                Pause point:  After completion of the Xenium sample preparation workflow and prior to loading onto the Xenium Analyzer, slides can be stored in 0.05 % PBST at 4°C in the dark for up to 1 week using a new Xenium cassette lid.  This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA sections for MICS after the Xenium run and includes quencher removal, antigen retrieval, DAPI pre-staining, and dust particle removal. Following Xenium imaging, perform quencher removal as recommended in  Xenium In Situ Gene Expression – Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining  (10x Genomics,  CG000613 ) to reduce residual Xenium-associated background signals and improve compatibility with downstream cyclic immunofluorescence imaging using MACSima.    12.  Remove the quencher (see  problem 1  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  In a fume hood, prepare quencher removal solution by weighing 17.4 mg sodium hydrosulfite and transfer it to a conical tube containing 10 mL Milli-Q water.    b.  Cap the tube tightly and vortex for 10 s until the reagent is fully dissolved.    c.  Keep the solution at RT (20°C–25°C) until use.          CRITICAL:  Prepare quencher removal solution immediately before each use to ensure optimal performance, as its effectiveness decreases after 10 min.      Note:   Because sodium hydrosulfite is hazardous, prepare the solution in a fume hood.      Note:   Vortexing may be performed outside the fume hood if the tube is tightly capped.      Note:   Do not use alternative chemicals for quencher removal.      d.  Add 10 mL quencher removal solution into the slide mailer.    e.  Prepare three slide mailers with 10 mL Milli-Q water each.    f.  Gently immerse Xenium slide into the slide mailer with quencher removal solution and incubate for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).    g.  Immerse slide in each Milli-Q water containing slide mailer for 1 min, then move to the next one.    h.  Transfer the Xenium slide into a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with MACSima Running buffer until further use.    Note:   Alternatively, transfer Xenium slide into a MACSwell One Small imaging frame ( Figure 1 A, right) and add 1.5 mL quencher removal solution. After 10 min incubation at RT (20°C–25°C), wash slide with 1.5 mL Milli-Q water three times, waiting for 1 min each time.      Note:   Residual purple staining after Xenium processing indicates the presence of autofluorescence quencher and should disappear following successful quencher removal ( Figure 1 B).         13.  Perform heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER).   a.  Prepare the 10× stock solution of TEC antigen retrieval buffer at pH 9.0.    Note:   The 10x stock solution can be stored at 4°C for up to 3 months.      b.  Immediately before use, dilute the 10x stock to 1x working solution.    c.  Adjust the pH to 9.0.    d.  Preheat the 1× working solution to 95°C in a pressure cooker.    e.  Place the Xenium slide in a slide mailer and immerse it in the preheated TEC buffer. Incubate for 20 min at 95°C.          CRITICAL:  Ensure the slide is fully submerged and does not touch the pressure cooker container.            CRITICAL:  Avoid using open-bottom slide mailers, as air bubbles could directly contact the tissue section and cause partial lifting or detachment from the slide surface.      Note:   Depending on the antibody panel, alternative antigen retrieval buffers may be required (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).      f.  After incubation, remove the pressure cooker container and transfer it to a pre-cooled water bath (ice-cold) for cooling.    g.  When the buffer has reached RT (20°C–25°C), carefully remove the slide from the buffer.    h.  Dry the edges with a lint-free wipe to remove excess liquid.    i.  Mount the slide onto a MACSwell One Small imaging frame.    Note:   The MACSwell One Small imaging frame accommodates the Xenium imaging area optimally and enables complete coverage of the imaged region ( Figure 1 A).      j.  Add 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer.       14.  Pre-stain the sample with DAPI and remove dust particles.   a.  Incubate the Xenium slide with DAPI staining solution at a 1:5 dilution using MACSima Running Buffer (final concentration 1 μg/mL) in the dark for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).          CRITICAL:  Protect the slide from light during DAPI incubation to prevent photobleaching.      Note:   Ensure the staining solution fully covers the section.      b.  Wash the slides three times with 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer to remove excess dye.    c.  Check the TMA section under bright transmitted light to ensure there are no dust particles or debris in the experimental area.    d.  Remove any visible dust or debris, as these can interfere with imaging quality.    e.  Cover the slide with a final experimental volume of 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer and seal with pierceable aluminum foil.    Note:   Clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 2-propanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.            Pause point:  Store slides in running buffer at 4°C for ≤1 week. Register antibodies and define the reagent panel.   a.  Under the Reagent Definition tab, register pre-validated Miltenyi Biotec antibodies using the integrated reagent registration system or manually enter reagent information.    Note:   Pre-validation data for the antibodies is provided to confirm compatibility with acetone-, PFA-fixed, or FFPE tissues; however, they have not been tested for compatibility after Xenium.      b.  Add non-Miltenyi antibodies by specifying antibody type, species reactivity, antigen target, fixation compatibility, and fluorochrome assignment.    c.  Create reagent panels by combining antibodies from the reagent inventory into predefined staining panels.    d.  Review fluorochrome assignments and reagent compatibility prior to experiment setup.          CRITICAL:  Use fluorochromes compatible with cyclic imaging workflows (e.g., FITC, PE, APC) and directly conjugated primary antibodies to avoid issues when using the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit.            CRITICAL:  Include DAPI staining in regular intervals (e.g., every 3–4 imaging cycles) to facilitate reliable image registration and alignment across staining cycles for the MACSima images.      Note:   Evaluate antibody compatibility, for example by performing a mock Xenium experiment followed by a MACSima run (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). Note:   Antibody compatibility should be assessed based on specificity, signal-to-background ratio, reproducibility, and preservation of the expected staining pattern after Xenium processing. Compatible antibodies show the expected cellular and subcellular localization, clear separation of positive signals from background, and staining consistent with previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation and reference databases (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). Set up the cyclic imaging procedure.   a.  Open the Procedure Creation tab and create a new procedure from an existing template or generate a new procedure.    b.  Add reagent panels and/or individual antibodies to the procedure.    c.  Adjust staining and imaging parameters as needed, including dilution factor, incubation time, exposure settings, bleaching conditions, and wash parameters.    d.  Recalculate imaging cycles after all reagents and parameters have been defined or assign the antibodies to the individual cycles manually.    Note:   When manually assigning antibodies to imaging cycles, consider the following guidelines:     i.  Avoid placing multiple markers targeting the same cell type in the same cycle.    ii.  Preferably place low-abundance, transiently expressed, activation-dependent markers, cytokines, and chemokines in earlier cycles, as their detection can be more challenging.    iii.  Place abundant, constitutively expressed, or structural proteins in later cycles, as they provide more robust signals.    iv.  Evaluate receptors and ligands individually based on antigen abundance, subcellular localization, and expected staining performance.    v.  Avoid FITC for broadly expressed or critical phenotyping markers because of its relatively low photostability and potential signal loss during image acquisition.    vi.  For alternative fluorochromes (e.g., Alexa Fluor dyes), empirically determine the bleaching intensity required for efficient signal removal or perform at least two bleaching cycles before staining with the subsequent conjugated antibody in that channel.    vii.  Avoid combining strongly expressed FITC signals with weak PE signals in the same cycle to minimize spectral overlap and signal interference. Export the pipetting scheme for antibody preparation and documentation purposes from the Reagent rack Info tab.       20.  Prepare the antibody plate.   a.  Dispense antibodies into a compatible deepwell reagent plate, distributing them into the designated wells according to the generated pipetting scheme.      Note:   The cell-type annotations and obs_name_orig identifiers are generated during upstream processing (see  before you begin ). The obs_name_orig field links each cell to its original Xenium cell boundary polygon.     26.  Load Xenium core mappings.   a.  Load the H5AD file, filter to the target slide and position, and retain only cells flagged as is_in_core.       27.  Load Xenium Spatial Data.   a.  Load cell/nucleus boundaries, cell labels, transcripts, expression matrix, and the morphology focus images from the Xenium output folder.       28.  Perform the per-core Registration Loop ( Figures 6 C and 6D).   a.  For each position-ROI pair, execute Steps 29–37 below. Pairs where the output Zarr folder already exists are automatically skipped.       29.  Align Observation Tables.   a.  Join annotated metadata with the Xenium cell table by cell_id/obs_name_orig. Filter to the highlighted position and set obsm['spatial'] from centroid coordinates (cell_centroid_x, cell_centroid_y).       30.  Load the MACSima images.   a.  Load the DAPI channel for the first cycle as well as all other non-DAPI and non-background channels.       31.  Compute Core Bounding Box.   a.  Derive the ROI bounding box in pixel coordinates from the spatial extent of the aligned cell table.       32.  Transform Cell/Nucleus Boundary Polygons and crop the Xenium dataset.   a.  Scale each polygon by the transform_factor (micrometers to pixels).    b.  Translate it by subtracting the bounding box origin multiplied by scale_factor, placing the boundaries in the same coordinate space as the full-resolution images.       33.  Perform a Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)-Based Image Registration.  19     a.  Perform downscaling by scale_factor, using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().  20      b.  Apply Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE)  21   with skimage.exposure.equalize_adapthist()  22   with default parameters: clip_limit = 0.01, kernel_size = 1/8 of image dimensions.    c.  Convert pixel values to uint8.    Note:   The downscaling by scale_factor = 3 reduces runtime and suppresses high-frequency photon noise during feature detection. If registration fails or produces poor results, try scale_factor = 2 for higher-resolution feature detection or adjust CLAHE parameters.  21        d.  Detect SIFT key points and match descriptors with Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN)  23   (Parameters: KD-tree, 5 trees, 50 checks).    e.  Apply Lowe’s ratio test  19   with threshold 0.5 to retain high-confidence matches.    f.  Compute a 2D affine transformation from the surviving inlier matches using spatialdata.transformations.get_transformation_between_landmarks().    g.  Scale the translation components by scale_factor to obtain the full-resolution affine transformation matrix.    h.  Apply the full-resolution affine transformation to the entire MACSima image using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().       34. A poorly registered core will show systematic lateral or rotational offsets between the channels. When processing a large number of slides, these metrics could facilitate the identification of potentially misaligned cores for further evaluation by virtual inspection or manual adjustment. Expected outcomes  Successful implementation of this protocol results in the generation of a multimodal spatial dataset containing both transcriptomic and proteomic information from the same FFPE TMA section. The wet-lab workflow provides practical guidance for the critical experimental steps required for successful Xenium and MICS procedures, including tissue preparation, Xenium processing, post-Xenium slide recovery, antigen retrieval, antibody staining, and multiplexed imaging. Important considerations and troubleshooting insights are provided throughout to help users optimize tissue integrity, RNA and protein signal quality, and overall assay performance. Following Xenium spatial transcriptomics and subsequent MICS, users obtain high-resolution spatial maps of RNA transcripts and protein markers while preserving tissue morphology and spatial context. The experimental workflow enables detection of thousands of RNA targets using the Xenium platform together with highly multiplexed protein profiling using MICS. The workflow is expected to enable comprehensive multimodal characterization of individual cells by combining Xenium transcriptomic information with highly multiplexed and customizable protein profiling. The increased antibody plexity and flexibility of MACSima compared with the protein-detection capabilities of Xenium and other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, such as PhenoCycler and COMET, enable broader phenotypic and functional characterization, particularly in complex immune and tumor microenvironments. Following image registration and protein channel intensity quantification, transcriptomic and proteomic measurements are linked at single-cell resolution, generating a combined RNA-protein expression matrix for each cell together with its spatial coordinates within the tissue. The resulting dataset can be used to identify and characterize cellular phenotypes, investigate cell states, study cell-cell interactions, and explore tissue organization by integrating complementary transcriptomic and proteomic information. In addition, the image registration and data integration framework provided in this protocol can be adapted to combine Xenium data with other multiplex imaging modalities.  Users should expect preservation of tissue integrity throughout the workflow, successful recovery of Xenium-processed slides for downstream protein imaging, and generation of registered multimodal datasets suitable for downstream spatial and single-cell analyses. Depending on tissue quality, RNA integrity, antibody performance, and imaging conditions, signal intensity and the number of detected transcripts or proteins may vary between samples.  After step 35 (SpatialData assembly), the output Zarr store contains aligned images from both modalities, transformed cell and nucleus segmentation polygons ( Figure 7 D), the gene expression count matrix with cell-type annotations, and spatially filtered transcript coordinates. The data can be visualized interactively with napari using the napari-spatialdata plugin, where all layers overlay correctly in a shared coordinate space.  After step 36 (protein quantification,  Figure 6 D), each cell in registration.aligned_data[”rna_protein_table”].X contains numeric columns for each MACSima antibody. A cross-modal concordance between RNA-based cell-type annotations and protein measurements can serve as an additional quality metric for the overall registration and quantification workflow. This concordance could be visually explored by plotting heatmaps showing the expression of corresponding RNA and protein markers for each of the identified cells using standard tools such as scanpy.  7   The correlation coefficients between transcript counts and mean protein expression per cell for pairs of corresponding markers can also be used for a quantitative evaluation of the concordance between RNA and protein measurements.  2    After step 37 (registration quality assessment), the color overlay should show white overlap at nuclear positions, with minimal red-only or green-only fringes ( Figure 7 C).    Quantification and statistical analysis  The per-cell protein quantification (step 36,  Figure 6 D) yields absolute fluorescence intensity values (mean of aligned pixel values within each cell mask). These values are instrument- and acquisition-specific and should be used for within-experiment comparisons. Cross-experiment normalization (e.g., percentile normalization or z-score per channel) may be necessary when integrating multiple MACSima runs. It is important to note that errors in per-cell protein quantification could substantially affect downstream analysis. Per-cell protein quantification depends on accurate image registration and cell segmentation, as fluorescence intensity is calculated from the pixels within each cell mask. The sensitivity to segmentation errors may vary according to subcellular localization: nuclear markers are generally less affected by small changes in cell boundaries, whereas membrane-associated markers may be more sensitive to segmentation inaccuracies, particularly at cell-cell interfaces. Cytoplasmic markers typically show intermediate sensitivity. Applications requiring improved or alternative segmentation, advanced segmentation approaches can be evaluated and compared with the default segmentation approach to assess their suitability for the respective tissue and marker composition. Therefore, segmentation quality and image alignment should be carefully assessed before interpreting per-cell fluorescence intensities.  The combined RNA and protein measurements are stored in a single AnnData table within the SpatialData Zarr store. Downstream analyses, including joint RNA and protein cell-type classification, ligand-receptor interaction inference, and spatial neighborhood analysis, can be performed using standard tools (e.g., scanpy,  7   squidpy,  28   LIANA  29  ) applied to the exported AnnData table.    Limitations  Antibody performance may vary between tissue types. For example, we observed tissue-dependent variation in staining performance in the data generated in the scope of this workflow. Therefore, as described in  before you begin  (step 7) and in  problem 2  in  troubleshooting , antibody performance should be validated in the tissue type of interest e.g., by performing a mock Xenium-MACSima.  The SIFT-based registration relies on sufficient structural similarity between the Xenium DAPI morphology focus image and the MACSima DAPI staining. If tissue morphology is substantially altered between the two acquisitions (e.g., due to tissue loss, folding, or deformation during antigen retrieval), registration may fail or produce locally poor alignment. In such cases, non-rigid (deformable) registration methods may be required but are not implemented in this workflow (see  problem 6  in  troubleshooting ).  The per-cell protein quantification uses the Xenium cell segmentation labels projected onto the MACSima images. Any residual registration error directly propagates into protein allocation. Cells at the boundary of registration artifacts or at the tissue edge may receive inaccurate protein measurements.  The current computational workflow performs image registration of MACSima images to the Xenium coordinate system. As with any image transformation and resampling procedure, image registration involves interpolation of pixel values. Therefore, minor changes in pixel intensities may occur in the registered images. In our experience, these effects were not observed to materially impact the intended downstream analyses, including RNA-protein based cell annotation and spatial characterization of tissue microenvironments.  The scripts process each TMA core independently. Cross-core normalization of protein signal intensities is not performed automatically and must be applied by the user if comparing protein levels across cores or slides, due to the technical variation within staining intensities. There are several normalization methods (e.g., Y score, ComBat, MxNorm or mean division) that can fail to consider skewed patterns that arise from this type of data. Thus, we recommend using a more reliable non-parametric normalization methods that can be employed in both pixel and feature level, such as UniForm.  30      Troubleshooting   Problem 1: Insufficient quencher removal after Xenium-processing (related to step 12 in the protocol)  Occasionally, incomplete removal of the Xenium autofluorescence quencher using quencher removal solution (10 mM sodium hydrosulfite) may be observed, indicated by persistent lilac discoloration of the tissue section ( Figure 1 ).    Potential solution 
   •  Verify that the sodium hydrosulfite solution was freshly prepared at a final concentration of 10 mM prior to use.    •  If quencher removal was insufficient, repeat this step with freshly prepared quencher removal solution and use it immediately after preparation.   
   Problem 2: Low/insufficient antigen staining intensity (related to before you begin step 8 and step 13 in the protocol)  Xenium-processed slides may exhibit reduced or absent staining for previously established antigen markers during MICS imaging. Compatibility of an antibody clone with standard MACSima workflows does not necessarily guarantee successful staining performance on post-Xenium tissue sections.    Potential solution 
   •  Confirm proper antibody storage conditions and expiration dates, and assess antibody performance using appropriate control tissues.    •  Optimize HIER by extending the incubation time up to 60 min, ensuring that slides remain fully submerged throughout the retrieval process, and testing alternative antigen retrieval buffers (e.g., pH 6).    •  Evaluate alternative antibody clones or, where applicable, fluorescently label validated unlabeled primary immunohistochemistry antibodies to enable compatibility with MICS.    •  We suggest performing a mock Xenium run on a consecutive section to test and optimize antibody clones and establish panels that are suitable for post-Xenium MICS experiments mimicking v1 or 5k panel conditions. Note that the mock experiment should be considered a pre-screening approach rather than a substitute for validation following the complete Xenium workflow.   ○  For the mock Xenium run, mount a serial section (from the same block as the section used for the Xenium-MACSima experiment) onto a blank Xenium slide.   -  Perform sectioning of the block and initial sample preparation comprising deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking as described in steps 1–3.    -  Perform the subsequent steps, including hybridization, post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification, using only the buffer components from previously used  Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000460), but omit the enzymes.    -  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler as described in step 4, using the hybridization mix without a probe panel.    -  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining as described in step 7.    -  Following sample preparation, setup the samples on the Xenium Analyzer according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ) as described in step 8. Prepare all the buffers as mentioned in the above user guide. Decoding reagents are replaced with plates containing 1x PBS. Start the run and define ROIs as mentioned in step 9.    -  After the mock Xenium run is complete, replace the buffer on the slides with 0.05 % PBST and store at 4°C until quencher removal and subsequent MICS imaging (step 12 onwards).       ○  Alternatively, a mock Xenium run can also be performed in an off-the-Xenium-Analyzer setting. In this case, mount the serial section onto a SuperFrost Plus slide. The sample preparation workflow from deparaffinization to nuclei staining is exactly as mentioned above. Following sample preparation, incubate slides in Probe Removal Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C) followed by Wash Buffer (30 min at RT, 20°C–25°C), at least 4 cycles each, to mimic buffer exposure during the Xenium Analyzer processing. Buffers are prepared as per the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).       •  An antibody should be considered compatible when it fulfills the following criteria (see  Figure 3 ):   ○  Specific staining pattern: Signal is restricted to the expected cell population and subcellular localization.    ○  High signal-to-background ratio: Positive cells are clearly distinguishable from surrounding tissue with minimal nonspecific background.    ○  Reproducible performance: Comparable staining is observed across technical replicates or appropriate control tissues.    ○  Preserved staining after Xenium processing: The staining pattern is consistent with the expected biology, previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation, and comparable to reference databases.       •  The resulting images ( Figure 3 ) allow users to identify antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C, 3D, 3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria.   
   Problem 3: Autofocus failure with large ROIs during MICS (related to step 22 in the protocol)  Selecting tissue sections that cover the entire Xenium imageable area as a single, large ROI during ROI definition on the MACSima instrument occasionally resulted in autofocus instability during imaging. Such issues manifested as blurry FOVs or blurry images in the output folders ( Figure 5 ). In our experience, ROIs larger than approximately 100 FOVs were more prone to the aforementioned focusing issues.    Potential solution 
   •  Divide large imaging areas into smaller ROIs to improve autofocus performance and overall image quality.    •  Select the image contrast-based focusing approach instead of constant height-based focusing for your MICS experiment.    •  Cover the MACSwell frame with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to prevent evaporation and drying of the sample during extended imaging cycles, as insufficient liquid coverage may lead to autofocus and imaging issues.    •  If the tissue to be imaged is larger than the above-mentioned limitation, consider splitting it into several (non-overlapping) ROIs.    •  For TMAs, every core should be imaged as a separate ROI.    •  We suggest using the slides from a mock Xenium run to test suitable ROI sizes and decide on the best autofocusing method.   
   Problem 4: SIFT registration fails or produces identity affine matrix  A failed or bad quality registration could be due to the identification of too few matching keypoints between the Xenium and MACSima DAPI images.    Potential solution  Verify that the correct DAPI file is used (cycle-0 stained DAPI with “_S_” flag, not the baseline “_B_“ image). Try reducing scale_factor from 3 to 2 for higher-resolution feature detection. If images have very low contrast, adjust the CLAHE parameters in preprocess_reg().  21   Confirm that the Xenium morphology focus images contain the expected core region by visually inspecting the cropped image.    Problem 5: Xenium positions do not match MACSima ROI position  If some Xenium positions do not match the MACSima ROI positions, these cores were probably not captured during MACSima scanning (e.g., edge cores or tissue damage).    Potential solution  Do not include these positions in the roi_map_file CSV file, so that they are skipped in the full-slide processing script (“match_rois_cores_fullslide.py”).    Problem 6: Variable registration offset across the tissue  The presence of a misalignment between the Xenium DAPI image and the registered MACSima image that is not constant in magnitude and direction across the image shows that a global affine transformation is insufficient to register the images correctly. A visual inspection of the overlaid Xenium and registered MACSima DAPI image allows for the easy identification of this issue by showing a non-uniform alignment quality across the image. This heterogeneous misalignment is more common for larger ROIs and typically arises from tissue deformation or folding between acquisitions, lens distortion in either imaging system, different tissue mounting geometry, or non-linear shrinkage or expansion of the section.    Potential solution  A non-rigid (deformable) transformation is required.     Note:   Non-rigid (deformable) transformation is not addressed in this protocol, as only a single transformation type was tested. This represents a current limitation; users are advised to adapt the methodology as needed for their specific application. Recommended alternatives are RAMI2D  31   or ST-align.  32       Additional computational problems and diagnostic tips  Other possible computational problems could lead to TMA cores being skipped or output folders not being written due to lack of disk-space ( Table 4 ). For troubleshooting the user can refer to the error message to identify the cause of the problem and correct their workflow or report it as an issue on the GitHub repository associated with this protocol ( https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium ). title: SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics.
xenium_reason: Xenium is explicitly used for validation
evidence_text:
SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics. Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) offers unprecedented opportunities to decipher tissue architecture at subcellular resolution. Consequently, accurate cell segmentation is a fundamental prerequisite for analyzing SST data, as precise transcript assignment is essential for downstream single-cell interpretation. Existing methods often overlook the spatial organization of transcripts, rely on simplified geometric priors, or struggle to coordinate transcript-derived features with morphology-derived spatial guidance. This limitation restricts their adaptability to irregular cell shapes, often leading to transcript misassignment. To address this, we propose SpaCut, a unified deep learning framework designed to effectively integrate transcriptomic feature learning with dynamic morphological guidance. SpaCut comprises a Gene-Wise Attention (GWA) module and a Nuclei-Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. GWA encodes the high-dimensional transcript map and aggregates features across multiple depths. NGAF uses the encoded transcript features to modulate distance-based nuclear softmasks and refine nucleus-anchored cell boundaries through progressive training. Extensive evaluations across seven datasets from diverse platforms (including Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo-seq) demonstrate that SpaCut significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both segmentation accuracy and consistency with single-cell reference data. The source code is available at https://github.com/wenwenmin/SpaCut. Introduction  Elucidating how cells organize into tissues and interact within their environment is fundamental to biomedical research [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ]. Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) technologies enable the measurement of gene expression within intact tissues at subcellular resolution [ 4 ,  5 ]. However, deriving biological insights from these data requires accurately attributing transcripts to individual cells through the segmentation of the spatial domain. The precision of this segmentation directly impacts downstream analyzes, such as cell type annotation and cell–cell communication [ 6 ,  7 ,  8 ]. Specifically, segmentation errors introduce bias: over‐segmentation incorporates extracellular noise or signals from neighboring cells, distorting spatial gene expression patterns; conversely, under‐segmentation results in the loss of valid transcripts, leading to incomplete gene expression profiles. Therefore, accurate cell segmentation is essential for the effective analysis of SST data [ 9 ,  10 ].  Currently, SST technologies vary significantly in key parameters such as resolution and gene profiling capacity [ 11 ]. Imaging‐based platforms, such as Vizgen's MERSCOPE [ 12 ] and 10    ×     Genomics' Xenium [ 13 ], offer high resolution (     ∼  100   nm     ) and capture efficiency for targeted gene panels. Notably, NanoString's CosMx [ 14 ] expands this capability, detecting thousands of genes while maintaining subcellular precision. Meanwhile, sequencing‐based platforms like Stereo‐seq [ 15 ] stand out by offering whole transcriptome analysis, capturing over 10000 genes with a resolution of 0.5      μ  m     . This distinction leads to different data characteristics: imaging methods generally prioritize high capture efficiency for specific gene sets, whereas sequencing methods deliver comprehensive genome‐wide profiles [ 16 ,  17 ]. Consequently, developing a unified cell segmentation method that adapts to these diverse data characteristics and resolutions remains a significant challenge.  Existing cell‐segmentation methods for SST can be broadly grouped into three categories: image‐based, transcript‐based, and integrative image–transcript approaches. Image‐based approaches [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 ] primarily rely on deep neural networks trained on large‐scale annotated cellular images. Leveraging architectures such as U‐Net [ 24 ] or Transformers [ 25 ], these frameworks extract visual features like staining intensity and texture, determining cell boundaries based solely on visual information. Although tools like Cellpose [ 18 ] and StarDist [ 19 ] excel at nuclear detection, they are unable to capture complex gene expression patterns outside the nuclear region. This limitation extends to commercial platforms like 10    ×     Xenium and Vizgen, which rely on similar nuclear‐based strategies. Consequently, they often face challenges such as inaccurately large cells resulting from Xenium's default dilation or transcript loss due to Vizgen's conservative segmentation.  Transcript‐based methods instead infer cellular assignments primarily from molecular distributions. Baysor [ 26 ] utilizes Markov Random Field modeling to partition molecules based on compositional consistency, allowing it to function independently of histological images. Conversely, ProSeg [ 27 ] adopts a simulation‐based Cellular Potts Model. While it uses nuclear centroids for initialization, it primarily drives boundary expansion by optimizing the probabilistic likelihood of transcript distributions. Although these methods excel in regions with poor staining, inferring boundaries solely from transcript distributions often results in imprecise segmentations that do not correspond well to imaging data.  Integrative image–transcript methods seek to overcome the complementary weaknesses of these two categories by incorporating molecular information into morphology‐guided boundary inference. JSTA [ 28 ] jointly optimizes cell segmentation and cell‐type annotation using reference expression profiles, whereas SCS [ 29 ] combines imaging and sequencing data by learning the relative position of each transcript spot to its cell center. BIDCell [ 30 ] introduces biologically informed self‐supervised losses to relate spatial gene expression to nuclear morphology and reference cell‐type information. UCS [ 31 ] adopts a two‐stage nucleus‐anchored framework that combines transcript‐derived foreground features with distance‐based nuclear softmasks. Despite these advances, encoding sparse transcript distributions and adaptively integrating them with nucleus‐derived spatial priors remain challenging.  To address these challenges, we propose SpaCut, a transcript‐aware, nucleus‐guided framework for cell segmentation (Figure  1 ). The Gene–Wise Attention (GWA) module projects raw gene channels into a learned feature space and recalibrates transcript‐derived features to suppress noise and generate a coarse cellular foreground map. The Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module then uses these features to modulate distance‐based nuclear softmasks and refine nucleus‐anchored boundaries according to local transcript distributions. A progressive training strategy first learns foreground localization and subsequently freezes the transcript encoder while optimizing instance‐specific boundary refinement. Benchmarking against representative methods across seven datasets spanning Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo‐seq showed that SpaCut achieved higher segmentation accuracy and greater consistency with single‐cell reference profiles. Designed to leverage both high‐dimensional gene expression maps and nucleus segmentation from nuclei staining, the network first employs a Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module to encode the gene expression data into refined features. This module functions as a robust encoder, capturing spatial context while adaptively re‐weighting gene importance. The encoded features are then utilized in two sequential stages. First, a classification head generates a coarse foreground localization map, distinguishing cellular areas from the background. Simultaneously, discrete nuclei segmentations are smoothed into continuous softmasks via signed distance mapping. Subsequently, the Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) Module integrates the nucleus softmask as a spatial prior. It employs a FiLM‐inspired mechanism where gene features generate a spatial coefficient map to dynamically modulate this prior, guiding the expansion from the nucleus to the precise cellular boundaries. SpaCut adopts a progressive training strategy: it first uses the Weighted Cross‐Entropy Loss (     L  fg     ) to train the foreground localization; it then freezes the encoded features and employs the Weighted Cross‐Entropy Loss (     L  cell     ) to train the NGAF module for individual cell boundary refinement. By jointly optimizing for foreground consistency and individual cell precision, SpaCut effectively produces robust cell segmentation.    2.2.  SpaCut Enables Accurate Cell Segmentation Across Diverse Spatial Transcriptomics Platforms and Tissue Architectures  To comprehensively assess SpaCut's generalization capability, we evaluated its performance across seven datasets spanning four leading SST platforms: 10    ×     Genomics Xenium, NanoString CosMx SMI, Vizgen MERSCOPE, and BGI Stereo‐seq. These datasets cover epithelial, stromal, and neural tissues, capturing a broad range of cellular morphologies and tissue architectures. This diversity introduces substantial segmentation challenges, specifically complex cellular morphologies and varying data quality across different technologies. SpaCut effectively handles this biological and technical variability, achieving accurate and consistent cell segmentation across these highly heterogeneous platforms.  The proposed SpaCut framework demonstrates robust and accurate performance in cell segmentation across diverse SST platforms. In Xenium Human Pancreas and Mouse Colon datasets (Figure  2A,B ), where 10    ×     Genomics annotations serve as the ground truth, SpaCut produces segmentation masks that closely align with reference boundaries. Compared with UCS and Baysor(prior), it yields smoother and biologically coherent boundaries while effectively avoiding the over‐segmentation observed in UCS. Such robust performance is similarly observed in the Xenium Lung Cancer dataset (Figure  2C ), where SpaCut precisely delineates elongated fibroblast‐like cells and irregular stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment, outperforming competing methods that often distort cellular morphology. In the Stereo‐seq Mouse Brain dataset (Figure  2D ), SpaCut maintains compact and morphologically consistent segmentations under sparse transcript density and high spatial resolution—conditions where transformer‐based models such as SCS tend to produce fragmented boundaries. In the Vizgen Ovarian Cancer dataset (Figure  2E ), we leveraged Vizgen's underestimated default segmentation results as “nuclei” inputs to assess cross‐platform adaptability. By reinterpreting segmentation masks as nuclear priors, SpaCut improves transcript coverage and accurately incorporates regions of high gene expression (     P  <  0.001     ), thereby increasing the number of assigned transcripts per cell for downstream analyzes. Finally, in the CosMx Human Pancreas dataset (Figure  2F ), SpaCut achieves results highly consistent with NanoString's full‐cell reference annotations, despite relying solely on nuclear fluorescence and transcript information. Additional same‐region visual comparisons across multiple datasets and platforms are provided in Figures  S1  and  S2 . These panels show that SpaCut retains coherent local boundaries under diverse microscopy backgrounds and transcript‐density patterns. Collectively, these results highlight SpaCut's strong cross‐modality generalization and robust performance under nuclei‐only staining conditions, which is a crucial capability for most SST datasets lacking whole‐cell stains. To quantitatively evaluate segmentation performance, we further analyzed both cell‐level and gene‐level statistics (Figure  5B,C ). At the cell level, five representative metrics—cell count, total transcripts, genes per cell, transcripts per cell, and cell sparsity were used to examine the trade‐off between segmentation outcomes and transcripts capture. Baysor (no prior) tends to over‐segment, producing numerous small cells with sparse transcript counts, while the nuclei dilation method used in the 10    ×     official pipeline generate segment large cells that include background or neighboring signals. In contrast, SpaCut achieves a balanced segmentation profile, recovering a biologically consistent number of cells with stable per‐cell gene and transcript distributions. At the gene level, we compared the proportion of cells expressing each gene between segmented masks and nuclei‐based expression to assess cytoplasmic transcript recovery. Methods with points near the diagonal recover little beyond nuclei, whereas SpaCut shifts more genes above the diagonal, indicating improved cytoplasmic transcript recovery and transcriptome completeness. Across the three Xenium datasets, SpaCut achieved the highest correct cytoplasmic recovery among non‐reference methods (0.6964–0.7324) and the highest assignment F1 (0.7619–0.8371). Although several conservative image‐only methods captured fewer extracellular transcripts, they recovered substantially fewer correct cytoplasmic transcripts. These results support a favorable recovery–contamination balance rather than an advantage driven solely by larger masks (Table  S1  and Figure  S5 ).  Finally, we examined how well each method preserves cellular morphology by correlating nuclear elongation (x‐axis) with cell‐mask elongation (y‐axis) (Figure  5D ). Image‐based models such as Cellpose and Cellpose‐SAM show high morphology correlations but exhibit lower average transcript counts per cell, suggesting that their segmentations primarily follow nuclear boundaries and underrepresent cytoplasmic regions. In contrast, SpaCut shows strong nuclear–cell shape agreement while achieving comparable transcripts per cell than competing methods(Figure  5E ), suggesting improved transcript recovery beyond the nucleus. UCS and BIDCell also display consistent nuclear–cell coupling, whereas Baysor (no prior) exhibits weak correlation and Cell 10X achieves only moderate agreement. Before post‐processing, shuffling or removing transcripts reduced instance F1 from 0.8638 to 0.7389 and 0.7032, respectively, and the full model outperformed fixed‐dilation and analytic‐softmask controls. SpaCut also achieved the largest mean difference between boundary‐expression similarity to the cell's own nucleus and that to adjacent nuclei, although its advantage over fixed dilation was modest. Together, these results support transcript‐dependent boundary refinement beyond simple geometric expansion (Table  S2  and Figures  S6  and  S7 ). Collectively, these analyzes confirm that SpaCut preserves accurate cell morphology while achieving improved transcript capture, producing coherent cell boundaries that reflect both cellular structure and gene expression.    2.5. Impact of Nuclei Segmentation Quality on SpaCut Performance  SpaCut relies on nuclei segmentation as it uses the nuclei as the foundational anchor for reconstructing complete cell boundaries in spatial transcriptomics. Variations in the quality of nuclei segmentation directly affect the accuracy of SpaCut's final cell segmentation results. To systematically evaluate this dependency, we conducted an ablation study using the Xenium Human Lung Cancer dataset, which provides official nuclei and cell segmentation annotations as ground truth. We compared SpaCut's performance across segmentation results obtained from a panel of representative image‐based methods spanning a broad range of segmentation quality from low to high.  As shown in (Figure  7A ), the DAPI‐stained nuclei and corresponding masks highlight the quality gap between the official 10    ×     nuclei masks (Nuclei 10    ×    ), which we use as reference annotations, and lower‐quality methods such as Watershed, which fail to produce reliable instance‐level nuclei segmentations. When these segmentation results were used as initialization inputs for SpaCut, their quality directly influenced the accuracy of the inferred cell boundaries. Using the official 10    ×     nuclei input(Nuclei 10    ×    ), SpaCut generated cell boundaries that closely matched the Cell 10    ×     reference, with accurate instance contours and minimal under‐ or over‐segmentation. Conversely, lower‐quality nuclei segmentations fail to adequately delineate nuclear boundaries, thereby impairing SpaCut's ability to infer accurate cell boundaries. To further quantify these observations, we evaluated the relationship between nuclei segmentation quality and SpaCut accuracy along two complementary dimensions. First, algorithmic consistency measures the internal stability of SpaCut outputs by comparing results from different nuclei segmentations against the Nuclei 10    ×     benchmark (Figure  7B ). Under this assessment, high‐quality segmentations such as Cellpose‐SAM and Cellpose achieved strong consistency (F1 = 0.54 and 0.61), while lower‐quality inputs such as SAM and Watershed showed substantial divergence (F1 = 0.35 and 0.18). Second, biological accuracy evaluates the alignment of SpaCut outputs with the official Cell 10    ×     cell boundary annotations. Under this criterion, SpaCut achieved its highest accuracy when initialized with Nuclei 10    ×     (F1 = 0.85), whereas inputs from less accurate segmentations resulted in a marked decline in performance.  Together, these results show that nuclei segmentation quality is a primary factor controlling SpaCut's segmentation accuracy. When nuclei are well segmented, their locations and extents provide reliable anchors for SpaCut to place cell boundaries in complex tissue regions. SpaCut refines the cell candidate associated with each supplied nuclear anchor and currently does not perform multi‐anchor merging or anchor‐free recovery. Consistently, instance F1 decreased monotonically as 10%–30% of anchors were removed, merged, or split, with missing anchors causing the largest reduction (from 0.8470 to 0.4775 at 30%). These results confirm that upstream nuclear‐mask quality directly constrains cell recovery (Table  S8  and Figures  S14  and  S15 ).    2.7.  Ablation Studies and Computational Performance  We evaluated the contributions of NGAF and GWA through component ablations on three Xenium datasets (Table  S9 ). Within NGAF, removing spatial attention or the concatenation of the original and modulated nuclear softmasks reduced segmentation performance, indicating that both spatially selective aggregation and retention of the nuclear prior contribute to boundary refinement. Within GWA, removing the depthwise‐separable convolution and channel‐recalibration block (DSC_CA) also decreased AJI and F1. Replacing multi‐depth feature fusion with only the deepest feature map caused the largest single‐component reduction on Xenium Human Lung Cancer, lowering AJI and F1 from 0.7465 and 0.9395 to 0.6805 and 0.8871, respectively. Simultaneously removing spatial attention and DSC_CA further degraded performance, particularly on Xenium Mouse Colon. Overall, the complete model achieved the best AJI and F1 on all three datasets, supporting complementary roles for transcript‐feature encoding, multi‐depth aggregation, and nucleus‐guided fusion.  SpaCut also maintained a favorable balance between runtime and segmented‐cell count across the Xenium, Stereo‐seq, and CosMx benchmarks (Figure  S16  and Tables  S10 – S12 ).     3.  Discussion  In this study, we introduce SpaCut, a robust cell segmentation framework for subcellular spatial transcriptomics based on a deep transcript–morphology fusion approach. SpaCut integrates a Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module with a Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. The former encodes high‐dimensional gene expression data to capture spatial context and suppress noise, while the latter dynamically modulates nuclear priors to guide cell boundary expansion based on actual transcriptomic signals. Finally, a progressive training strategy is employed to synergize global foreground localization with precise instance‐level boundary refinement.  We evaluated the effectiveness of SpaCut on seven datasets from four representative platforms, including Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo‐seq. The experimental results show that SpaCut consistently achieves higher segmentation accuracy (F1 score) and instance‐level quality (AJI) than state‐of‐the‐art baselines across various tissues. Beyond these metrics, we validated the biological relevance of our method. Unlike image‐based approaches that rely solely on nuclei, SpaCut leverages gene expression to identify cytoplasmic regions, thereby recovering valid transcripts located outside the nuclear boundary. Furthermore, transcript subsampling experiments demonstrated the model's robustness. SpaCut maintained accurate cell structures even with only 20% of the original transcripts, confirming its ability to handle the signal sparsity and technical noise often found in spatial transcriptomics.  We conducted systematic ablation experiments to dissect the impact of both architectural components and input quality on segmentation outcomes. These studies revealed that the GWA and NGAF modules are mutually indispensable: the former is critical for decoding sparse transcriptomic signals via deep feature aggregation, while the latter is essential for transforming rigid nuclear priors into biologically accurate cell boundaries. Furthermore, we investigated the dependency on nuclear segmentation quality. Our analysis reveals that segmentation performance is significantly correlated with the accuracy of the initial nuclear anchors. While high‐quality nuclei inputs unlock the full potential of SpaCut for precise boundary refinement, suboptimal inputs lead to performance degradation. This observation underscores that reliable nuclear detection serves as a critical prerequisite for the subsequent transcript‐driven expansion. Collectively, these findings validate the efficacy of the dual‐module strategy while highlighting the importance of upstream data quality.  Future work will focus on reducing the dependence on nuclear anchors by incorporating explicit multi‐anchor merging and anchor‐free candidate recovery for tissues containing multinucleated cells or weak or missing nuclear signals. We will also explore confidence‐aware nuclear guidance and adaptive post‐processing to improve robustness when upstream nuclear masks are imperfect.  In summary, SpaCut offers an effective and unified solution for analyzing subcellular spatial transcriptomics data, outperforming state‐of‐the‐art methods in segmentation performance. By integrating transcriptomic and morphological information for robust boundary inference across heterogeneous platforms, SpaCut facilitates more accurate downstream analyzes of tissue heterogeneity and cellular interactions.    4.
