Data Preprocessing  Spatial transcriptomics datasets from multiple platforms were preprocessed to generate standardized gene expression maps and nuclear segmentation masks. Raw transcript coordinates were filtered based on quality scores (QV     ≥     20 for Xenium datasets) and mapped to a regular grid with platform‐specific resolutions (0.5      μ  m      for Stereo‐seq and CosMx, 1      μ  m      for Xenium and MERSCOPE).  For each dataset, we represent the spatial transcriptomics data as a multi‐channel gene expression map      G  ∈   R   H  ×  W  ×  N       , where     H     and     W     represent spatial dimensions and     N     is the number of genes. Each spatial location      (  i  ,  j  )      contains the transcript count for gene     k     as      G   i  j  k      . Nuclear segmentation masks      M  ∈   R   H  ×  W        were obtained either from platform‐provided segmentation (Xenium and MERSCOPE) or from DAPI staining using Cellpose and were spatially aligned with the gene‐expression maps.  For datasets with large gene panels, we compared highly variable genes selected with SCANPY [ 38 ] and genes ranked by mean expression at subset sizes of 500 and 1000. The top 500 expressed genes retained clear spatial structure with limited additional benefit from increasing the subset size and were therefore used to balance spatial information and computational cost (Figure  S17 ).  Large‐scale datasets present unique challenges due to their spatial scale and heterogeneity. The Stereo‐seq Mouse Brain dataset encompasses an entire adult mouse brain slice (approximately 5.3     ×     7.0      m   m  2      ) captured at 0.5      μ  m      resolution, resulting in transcriptomic maps significantly larger than standard imaging‐based platforms. Given this scale, applying uniform gene selection across the entire tissue may overlook regional variations in gene expression patterns. To address this limitation, we partitioned the dataset into smaller, computationally manageable patches of 1200    ×    1200 pixels—adopting the identical patch size configuration used in SCS [ 29 ] to ensure methodological consistency and comparability. Individual models were trained for each patch to capture local transcriptomic characteristics and regional gene expression heterogeneity. For NanoString CosMx datasets, the platform's inherent field‐of‐view (FOV) structure was leveraged for model training. Each FOV was processed independently, with separate models trained to accommodate inter‐regional transcriptomic diversity across different tissue areas. This FOV‐specific approach ensures optimal performance while respecting the platform's natural data organization.    4.3.  Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module  The Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) module encodes the joint spatial transcript map into feature channels for foreground localization. Given a transcript map     G    , we divide it into overlapping patches      {   G   (  p  )    }      of size      h  ×  w      (default      48  ×  48     ), where       G   (  p  )    ∈   R   h  ×  w  ×  N        and     N     is the number of input genes. The input‐gene channels are first projected into a feature space, in which the subsequent channel‐recalibration operations are performed.  To initiate feature extraction, the high‐dimensional input patch is first compressed through three consecutive      1  ×  1      convolutions to reduce channel dimensionality while preserving full spatial resolution, yielding an initial feature map       h  0   ∈   R   h  ×  w  ×  64       . The representation is then hierarchically refined through four encoding stages. In each stage, we first employ a Depthwise Separable Convolution (DSC). Formally, let      h   i  −  1       be the input to the     i    ‐th stage; the intermediate feature       h  ∼   i      is obtained by decomposing the convolution into depthwise (     K   d  w      ) and pointwise (     K   p  w      ) operations:
   (1)       h  ∼   i   =   K   p  w     (   K   d  w     (   h   i  −  1    )   )       This factorization significantly reduces computational cost while preserving fine spatial details essential for modeling subcellular transcript distributions.  Subsequently, global average pooling (GAP) and global max pooling (GMP) summarize the spatial responses of each feature channel. These pooled features are forwarded to a shared multi‐layer perceptron (MLP) to generate feature‐channel recalibration weights. Based on       h  ∼   i     , the weighted output      h  i      is computed as:
   (2)      h  i   =    h  ∼   i   ⊙  σ   MLP  (  GAP   (    h  ∼   i   )   +  GMP   (    h  ∼   i   )   )       where     σ     is the sigmoid activation and     ⊙     denotes element‐wise multiplication. This strategy recalibrates transcript‐derived features and suppresses uninformative responses. No spatial pooling or downsampling is used throughout these stages [ 39 ]; all feature maps preserve the original      h  ×  w      resolution.  To integrate features from different depths, we aggregate the outputs from all encoding stages. We first concatenate the feature maps      {   h  0   ,   h  1   ,   h  2   ,   h  3   ,   h  4   }      to construct a composite feature representation      F  agg     . To suppress redundancy and emphasize informative features, we re‐employ the weighting mechanism formulated in Equation( 2 ), yielding the encoded features      F  enc     :
   (3)      F  enc   =   F  agg   ⊙  σ   MLP  (  GAP   (   F  agg   )   +  GMP   (   F  agg   )   )       The three      1  ×  1      convolutions perform channel projection and dimensionality reduction before attention is applied. The resulting feature‐channel weights are aggregated across encoding depths to form the encoded transcript representation      F  enc     .  Finally, the classification head processes the encoded features      F  enc      through four successive      1  ×  1      convolutional layers followed by a softmax activation, yielding a prediction map       P  fg   ∈   R   h  ×  w  ×  2       . This output comprises two distinct channels: the first channel represents the probability that a given pixel belongs to the background, while the second channel represents the probability that the pixel is part of any cell. For subsequent calculations, we specifically denote       p  ^    i  j       as the predicted foreground probability for the pixel at spatial location      (  i  ,  j  )     .    4.4.  Nucleus Softmask Generation  A critical component of SpaCut is the nucleus softmask, designed to transform discrete nuclei segmentations into continuous probability maps for spatial guidance. Starting with an instance‐level nuclei segmentation     M    , we partition the data into patches      {   M   (  p  )    }      aligned with the spatial transcriptomics input. Each patch is structured as       M   (  p  )    ∈   R   h  ×  w  ×   n  cells        , where      n  cells      indicates the number of nuclei within that patch. Formally, we define       M  c   ∈   R   h  ×  w        (for      c  =  1  ,  ⋯  ,   n  cells      ) as the discrete binary mask corresponding specifically to the     c    ‐th nucleus.  To transform the discrete binary mask      M  c      into a continuous spatial prior, we apply a temperature‐scaled sigmoid function to its Signed Distance Transform (SDT):
   (4)       M  ^   c    (  i  ,  j  )   =  σ       d  signed    (   M  c   ,  i  ,  j  )    τ        where       d  signed    (  ·  )       is the signed distance from pixel      (  i  ,  j  )      to the nearest nuclear boundary (positive inside and negative outside), and     τ     controls transition smoothness (     τ  =  5      by default). This yields        M  ^   c   ∈   (  0  ,  1  )      , which decays continuously from the nuclear interior toward the background (Figure  S18 ).    4.5.  Nuclei‐Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) Module  To explicitly incorporate Nucleus Softmask into gene representations, we design the Nuclei‐guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. As illustrated in Stage 2 (Figure  1 ), this module fuses the encoded gene features      F  enc      with the nucleus softmask       M  ^   c     . Note that the individual softmasks are stacked along the last dimension(corresponding to      n  cells     ). Since all nuclei belong to the same patch, they share the same encoding features      F  enc     , which is broadcasted to match the number of nuclei.  For each nucleus     c    , a FiLM‐inspired projection head [ 40 ], denoted by      ϕ  α      and implemented with three consecutive      1  ×  1      convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU, maps      F  enc      to a spatial coefficient map       α   =   ϕ  α    (   F  enc   )   ∈   R   h  ×  w       . This coefficient modulates the corresponding nuclear softmask:
   (5)       M  ^   mod  c   =    M  ^   c   ⊙   α       The original and modulated softmasks are retained and fused as       F  joint  c   =  Conv   (  Concat   (    M  ^   c   ,    M  ^   mod  c   )   )      . Average and maximum pooling along the channel axis are then concatenated and processed by a      5  ×  5      convolution to obtain a spatial‐attention map. The refined output is computed as:
   (6)      F  out  c   =   F  joint  c   ⊙  σ     Conv   5  ×  5      Concat  (  AvgPool   (   F  joint  c   )   ,   MaxPool   (   F  joint  c   )   )        To generate instance‐level predictions, we project the refined features      F  out  c      via a      1  ×  1      convolution into a dual‐channel probability map       P  c   ∈   R   H  ×  W  ×  2        for the     c    ‐th nucleus, where      c  ∈  {  1  ,  ⋯  ,  C  }      indexes the nuclei identified within the current patch. Let      P  c  bg      and      P  c  cell      denote the two channels of      P  c     , representing the predicted probabilities for the background and the     c    ‐th cell, respectively. These probabilities are normalized via Softmax to satisfy:
   (7)      P  c  bg    (  i  ,  j  )   +   P  c  cell    (  i  ,  j  )   =  1  ,   ∀   (  i  ,  j  )   .      Since multiple background probabilities are generated (one for each nucleus), they are averaged pixel‐wise to form a unified background probability       P  ¯   bg     :
   (8)       P  ¯   bg    (  i  ,  j  )   =   1  C    ∑   c  =  1   C    P  c  bg    (  i  ,  j  )       The final segmentation result for a pixel is determined by selecting the highest probability among the background and each cell in the patch:
   (9)       y  ^    i  ,  j    =   arg max   k  ∈  {  0  ,  ⋯  ,  C  }       P  ¯   bg    (  i  ,  j  )   ,    P  1  cell    (  i  ,  j  )   ,   ⋯  ,    P  C  cell    (  i  ,  j  )    ,      where      k  =  0      denotes the background class, and      k  >  0      assigns the pixel to the     k    ‐th cell.    4.6.  Training Details: Progressive Training Strategy   4.6.1.  Stage 1: Training of the Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module  The training objective for the Gene‐Wise Attention (GWA) Module starts by defining positive and negative samples. For positive samples (foreground), pixels located within nuclei regions (      M   (  p  )    >  0     ) serve as ground truth, ensuring the model accurately identifies areas that belong to cells.  Defining negative samples (background) is more challenging due to the uncertainty in cytoplasmic boundaries. To address this, we employ an adaptive background filtering strategy. First, the nuclei segmentation mask is dilated using a morphological operator     δ     with a      10  ×  10      kernel over four iterations:
   (10)      M  dilated   (  p  )    =   δ   (  4  )     (   M   (  p  )    ,  10  )       This dilation creates an exclusion zone around each nucleus that likely contains cytoplasm. Pixels outside this dilated region are candidates for background. However, not all such pixels are reliable negatives—some may contain diffuse transcripts from nearby cells. To further filter background candidates, we compute the average gene expression in the non‐dilated region:
   (11)       g  ¯   local   =   1    |    Ω  non-dilated    |      ∑    (  i  ,  j  )   ∈   Ω  non-dilated      ∑   k  =  1   N    G   i  j  k    (  p  )        where       Ω  non-dilated   =   {   (  i  ,  j  )   :   M   dilated  ,  i  j    (  p  )    =  0  }      . Only pixels with expression below this local threshold are labeled as background:
   (12)      B   i  j    (  p  )    =       1  ,      if    M   dilated  ,  i  j    (  p  )    =  0   and    ∑   k  =  1   N    G   i  j  k    (  p  )    <    g  ¯   local   ,        0  ,     otherwise.          This formulation ensures that non‐cellular regions (i.e., the negative samples) are accurately classified as background. To prevent the model from learning ambiguous patterns, pixels within the uncertain zone (those that fall neither within the nucleus nor in the confident background) are explicitly excluded from the training objective. The final training set is thus defined as       Ω  train   =   {   (  i  ,  j  )   :   M   i  j    (  p  )    >  0   or    B   i  j    (  p  )    =  1  }      .  The weighted cross‐entropy loss for a single patch is computed as:
   (13)      L  fg   =  −   ∑    (  i  ,  j  )   ∈   Ω  train       w  1    M   i  j    (  p  )    log    p  ^    i  j    +   w  2    B   i  j    (  p  )    log   (  1  −    p  ^    i  j    )        where       p  ^    i  j       is the predicted foreground probability for pixel      (  i  ,  j  )     , and      w  1     ,      w  2      are the weighted parameters that balance the contribution of positive and negative samples. This selective training approach enables the model to learn robust foreground‐background separation while avoiding ambiguous cytoplasmic regions.    4.6.2.  Stage 2: Training of the Nuclei‐guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) Module  In the second stage, the Nuclei‐guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) Module is trained to refine cell boundaries with frozen encoded features      F  enc     . This freezing operation is critical: it prevents the cell‐specific training from corrupting the learned foreground features, ensuring stable and consistent boundary refinement across all cells.  For each cell     c    , positive samples are defined as pixels within the nucleus region (      M   c  ,  i  j    (  p  )    =  1     ). Unlike the first stage, negative samples are now determined by the predictions of Stage 1: pixels with foreground probability below 0.5 (       p  ^    i  j    <  0.5     ) are treated as confident background. Pixels in the uncertain zone (     0.5  ≤    p  ^    i  j    <  1      and outside the nucleus) are again excluded from training, allowing the model to focus on learning clear cell‐specific boundaries without interference from ambiguous regions.  The training region for cell     c     is defined as:
   (14)      Ω  cell   (  c  )    =   {   (  i  ,  j  )   :   M   c  ,  i  j    (  p  )    =  1   or     p  ^    i  j    <  0.5  }       The per‐cell loss is:
   (15)      L  cell   (  c  )    =  −   ∑    (  i  ,  j  )   ∈   Ω  cell   (  c  )        w  3    M   c  ,  i  j    (  p  )    log   P  c  cell    (  i  ,  j  )   +   w  4    (  1  −   M   c  ,  i  j    (  p  )    )   log   P  c  bg    (  i  ,  j  )        where       P  c  cell    (  i  ,  j  )       and       P  c  bg    (  i  ,  j  )       denote the predicted probabilities for the foreground (cell     c    ) and background at pixel      (  i  ,  j  )     . The parameters      w  3      and      w  4      serve as weighting coefficients to balance the contribution of the positive and negative samples. The final loss for a patch containing     C     cells is the average over all cells:
   (16)      L  cell   =   1  C    ∑   c  =  1   C    L  cell   (  c  )        In this formulation,      M   c  ,  i  j    (  p  )       is the binary nucleus mask for cell     c    . This weighted cross‐entropy loss optimizes robust instance‐level separation by accurately distinguishing between the cell interior and predicted background. Crucially, it exploits the stable foreground features learned in Stage 1 to achieve precise boundary refinement.  This progressive optimization strategy sequentially establishes coarse foreground localization and subsequently refines cell boundaries using frozen features, thereby improving segmentation precision by leveraging coarse localization cues to guide accurate cell segmentation.     4.7.  Evaluation Metrics  Model performance was assessed using F1 score and Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI) for instance‐level segmentation quality. To provide a comprehensive evaluation, the F1 score was computed at the instance level across various matching thresholds.  Instance‐level F1 Score: Instead of pixel‐level evaluation, we measure the detection and segmentation accuracy of individual cells. The spatial overlap between a predicted cell mask (    P    ) and a ground truth cell mask (    G    ) is quantified by the Intersection over Union (IoU):
   (17)     IoU   (  P  ,  G  )   =    |  P  ∩  G  |    |  P  ∪  G  |        Given an IoU threshold     τ    , a predicted cell is considered a True Positive (TP) if its maximum IoU with a ground truth cell satisfies      IoU  (  P  ,  G  )  ≥  τ     . Predicted cells that fail to meet this threshold are counted as False Positives (FP), and ground truth cells without a valid matching prediction are counted as False Negatives (FN). Based on these instance‐level counts, Precision, Recall, and the F1 score are calculated as:
   (18)     Precision  =    T  P    T  P  +  F  P         (19)     Recall  =    T  P    T  P  +  F  N         (20)     F1  @  τ  =  2  ·    Precision  ×  Recall    Precision  +  Recall    =    2  ·  T  P    2  ·  T  P  +  F  P  +  F  N        By varying the matching threshold     τ     (e.g., from 0.1 to 0.9), we obtain an F1‐IoU curve that reflects the model's robustness under increasingly strict segmentation criteria.  Aggregated Jaccard Index (AJI): AJI evaluates instance‐level segmentation quality by measuring overlap between predicted and ground truth cell instances:
   (21)     AJI  =     ∑   i  =  1   N    |   G  i   ∩   P   σ  (  i  )    |      ∑   i  =  1   N    |    G  i   ∪   P   σ  (  i  )     |  +    ∑   j  ∈  U     |   P  j   |         where      G  i      represents the     i    ‐th ground truth cell instance,      P  j      denotes the     j    ‐th predicted cell instance,      σ  (  i  )      is the predicted instance with maximum overlap to      G  i     ,     N     is the number of ground truth instances, and     U     is the set of unmatched predicted instances. The AJI ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating better instance‐level segmentation performance.    4.8.  Experiment Settings  Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with PyTorch 2.0.1 [ 41 ] and Python 3.9. The SpaCut framework employed a progressive training strategy optimized by Adam with a learning rate of      10   −  4      . Specifically, the GWA Module was trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 128, while the NGAF module was subsequently trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 1 and frozen encoder features. Loss weights       w  1   ,   w  2   ,   w  3   ,   w  4       were set to 1 to ensure balanced supervision. Data augmentation included random discrete rotation (0     , 90     , 180     , 270     ) and vertical flipping. All experiments were independently repeated five times with different random seeds, and the final results were reported as the mean     ±     standard deviation across runs. SpaCut uses the same post‐processing pipeline as BIDCell [ 30 ], consisting of several standard morphological operations. Standard morphological post‐processing may remove fragmented regions but can also modify correctly delineated boundary pixels. Its effect is therefore condition‐dependent, and it is treated as an optional cleanup step rather than a procedure expected to improve all quantitative metrics. For downstream single‐cell processing, spatial neighborhood analysis, and visualization, we utilized Scanpy [ 38 ] and Squidpy [ 42 ].    4.9.  Baseline Methods  To benchmark SpaCut across complementary segmentation paradigms, we selected eleven representative methods spanning integrative, transcript‐based, and image‐based approaches: BIDCell [ 30 ], Proseg [ 27 ], SCS [ 29 ], UCS [ 31 ], Baysor [ 26 ], DeepCell [ 22 ], SAM [ 21 ], Cellpose [ 18 ], Cellpose‐SAM [ 20 ], StarDist [ 19 ], and MEDIAR [ 23 ]. Their algorithmic principles and execution configurations are summarized below.  
 BIDCell  [ 30 ]: BIDCell is a self‐supervised framework for cell segmentation in subcellular spatial transcriptomics. It integrates biologically informed loss functions with single‐cell RNA‐seq references to model relationships between gene expression and cell morphology. We used the documented Xenium configuration.  
 Proseg  [ 27 ]: Proseg is a probabilistic segmentation method that adapts the Cellular Potts model within a Metropolis–Hastings sampling framework. It infers cell boundaries by optimizing the likelihood of transcript distributions and includes transcript repositioning to reduce spurious co‐expression. The default configuration was used.  
 SCS  [ 29 ]: SCS employs a transformer‐based neural network to combine gene‐expression profiles with high‐resolution imaging information. It learns the relative position of each spot to its corresponding cell center and groups spots through gradient‐flow tracking. We used the default parameters provided by the authors.  
 UCS  [ 31 ]: UCS uses a two‐stage nucleus‐anchored framework. Its first network extracts transcript‐derived foreground features, and its second network combines these features with distance‐based nuclear softmasks for per‐anchor cell prediction. The model was run using the documented implementation and dataset‐specific settings.  
 Baysor  [ 26 ]: Baysor uses a Bayesian mixture model that accounts for spatial morphology and transcriptional composition when assigning molecules to cells. Both spatial‐prior and no‐prior configurations were evaluated using the documented settings.  
 DeepCell  [ 22 ]: DeepCell is a deep‐learning framework for whole‐cell and nuclear segmentation in tissue images. It uses a ResNet50‐based backbone with a feature‐pyramid architecture trained on TissueNet. We used the official pretrained model.  
 SAM  [ 21 ]: The Segment Anything Model uses a Vision Transformer trained on the SA‐1B dataset and provides promptable zero‐shot segmentation. We used the official pretrained weights in the image‐based comparison.  
 Cellpose  [ 18 ]: Cellpose predicts spatial gradient‐flow fields and forms cellular instances by grouping pixels that converge to common sinks. We used the official pretrained weights.  
 Cellpose‐SAM  [ 20 ]: Cellpose‐SAM combines the Cellpose flow‐field formulation with a SAM‐based image encoder to improve generalization across microscopy images. We used the official pretrained model without architecture‐specific retraining.  
 StarDist  [ 19 ]: StarDist represents nuclei as star‐convex polygons and predicts radial distances to their boundaries together with object probabilities. We used the official pretrained weights.  
 MEDIAR  [ 23 ]: MEDIAR is a transformer‐based framework for cell‐instance segmentation in multimodal microscopy images. We evaluated it with the official pretrained model. title: AI-driven multi-omics integration in breast cancer: clinical applications, immunotherapy prediction, and translational challenges.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: AI-driven multi-omics integration in breast cancer: clinical applications, immunotherapy prediction, and translational challenges. Breast cancer remains a major global threat to women's health, and its marked molecular, spatial, and temporal heterogeneity continues to limit the accuracy of early diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment-response prediction. Conventional single-dimensional diagnostic and therapeutic models are often insufficient to capture the dynamic complexity of the tumor microenvironment (TME). In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) provides powerful tools for high-dimensional feature extraction, multimodal data integration, and cross-scale modeling of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. AI-enabled approaches can link microscopic molecular alterations with macroscopic imaging and pathological phenotypes, while also characterizing complex cellular interactions within the TME. This review summarizes current applications of AI-driven multimodal and multi-omics integration in breast cancer, focusing on early detection, precision diagnosis, immunotherapy-response prediction, drug-sensitivity assessment, and prognostic evaluation. We also discuss key translational challenges, including data heterogeneity, batch effects, interpretability, privacy protection, regulatory considerations, and clinical workflow integration. Overall, AI-driven multi-omics strategies offer a promising framework for improving individualized treatment selection and real-time monitoring in breast cancer, although robust prospective validation and multidisciplinary implementation are still required before routine clinical adoption. Compared with previous modality-specific reviews, this article emphasizes cross-modal evidence appraisal, clinical-maturity stratification, data-quality constraints, foundation model opportunities, and regulatory requirements for translating AI-enabled multi-omics from exploratory research to clinically auditable decision support.

evidence_text:
EpiFoundation: A Foundation Model for Single-Cell ATAC-seq via Peak-to-Gene Alignment <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>
                  Foundation models exhibit strong capabilities for downstream tasks by learning generalized representations through self-supervised pre-training on large datasets. While several foundation models have been developed for single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data, there is still a lack of models specifically tailored for single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq), which measures epigenetic information in individual cells. The principal challenge in developing such a model lies in the vast number of scATAC peaks and the significant sparsity of the data, which complicates the formulation of peak-to-peak correlations. To address this challenge, we introduce
                  <jats:bold>EpiFoundation</jats:bold>
                  , a foundation model for learning cell representations from the high-dimensional and sparse space of peaks. Epi-Foundation relies on an innovative cross-modality pre-training procedure with two key technical innovations. First, EpiFoundation exclusively processes the non-zero peak set, thereby enhancing the density of cell-specific information within the input data. Second, EpiFoundation utilizes dense gene expression information to supervise the pretraining process, aligning peak-to-gene correlations. EpiFoundation can handle various types of downstream tasks, including cell-type annotation, batch correction, and gene expression prediction. To train and validate EpiFoundation, we curated
                  <jats:bold>MiniAtlas</jats:bold>
                  , a dataset of 100,000+ single cells with paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data, along with diverse test sets spanning various tissues and cell types for robust evaluation. EpiFoundation demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across multiple tissues and diverse downstream tasks.
                </jats:p>

evidence_text:
Macrophage Signature-Based Prediction of Cancer Treatment Response Using Attention-Weighted Multiple Instance Learning

A bstract

Predicting immunotherapy response from single-cell data remains difficult due to patient-level labels, extreme class imbalance, and highly heterogeneous macrophage states. We present a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework that treats each patient as a bag of macrophage embeddings derived from a single-cell RNA foundation model. The architecture incorporates an attention-based pooling mechanism with reduced model complexity, dropout-enhanced regularization and explicit attention penalties to improve stability in small-sample regimes. To address imbalanced clinical datasets, MIL outputs are optimized with a combined focal loss and supervised contrastive objective that simultaneously sharpens class boundaries and improves representation clustering. Across three cancer datasets, this approach outperforms pseudobulk aggregation, embedding baselines and standard MIL variants. Attention-weighted attribution and transcriptional regulatory analysis reveal distinct macrophage programs, interferon and antigen-presentation networks in responders versus hypoxia-linked regulatory modules in non-responders. This shows the potential of MIL to uncover predictive and mechanistically interpretable immune states.

evidence_text:
X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement Introduction  Targeted in situ transcriptomics platforms such as 10x Genomics Xenium measure hundreds to thousands of genes at subcellular resolution in intact tissue, so that cell types, subtypes and states can be identified in their spatial context ( Janesick et al., 2023 ). They require the user to choose the gene panel before the experiment. The panel is usually chosen from an annotated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) or single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) reference, and the choice determines which cell identities the experiment can resolve. A probe that hybridises to unintended transcripts can also produce misleading spatial signal, so the designed probes need checking.  Several computational methods select markers or probe sets for this purpose: differential-expression rankings such as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test ( Wilcoxon, 1945 ); specificity scores such as COSine similarity-based marker Gene identification (COSG) ( Dai et al., 2022 ); minimal marker combinations such as Necessary and Sufficient Forest (NS-Forest) ( Aevermann et al., 2021 ); and probe-set optimisation such as Spapros ( Kuemmerle et al., 2024 ). Two problems remain. First, single-gene markers are often insufficient for rare populations, closely related subtypes and transient states, and methods that find gene combinations usually reduce each cell type to one combination, which fails if any of its genes is poorly detected. Second, a gene’s detection in a targeted spatial assay differs from its detection in the single-cell reference. Across the ovarian cancer panel studied here, the median gene is detected in Xenium in only about half as many cells as in the matched reference, and the loss varies strongly from gene to gene. A marker that looks excellent in the reference may be nearly invisible in situ. The methods we compare choose genes from the reference as measured and do not model this loss.  Here we present eXtensible Spatial Panel Evaluation And Refinement (X-SPEAR), a framework with two modules. The first is Decision-rule Aggregation for Rare-cell Typing (DART), which learns short Boolean gene rules and selects several gene-disjoint rules for each cell type. Before learning, DART thins the reference to each gene’s measured single-cell-to-Xenium detection rate, so that rules relying on poorly detected genes score poorly and are not chosen. The detection rates come from a  Xenium prior : a previous experiment in which a single-cell reference and a Xenium run were both measured, usually on a different tissue, because a designer never has Xenium data from the target sample before ordering its panel. The second module checks the probes of any panel, whichever method chose it, for predicted off-target transcripts that are expressed in other cell types. The current version targets cell-type marker selection for Xenium. The “X” denotes extensibility, toward other targeted platforms and other selection objectives.  We first ask which Xenium priors help DART, using every combination of prior and target among five paired single-cell and Xenium datasets. We then benchmark DART against the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on three targets (ovarian cancer, mouse brain and cervical cancer), with a deployment rule throughout: nothing measured on the target’s Xenium informs the panel, and its labels are used only for scoring. With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperformed all four methods at matched panel size on every target. Its rules agree with the downstream classifier and name interpretable marker programs. On 45 mouse retinal ganglion cell (RGC) subtypes, held out within a single-cell atlas, DART matched the best methods and led COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance.    2  Results   2.1  X-SPEAR designs a detection-aware panel and checks its probes  X-SPEAR takes an annotated single-cell reference of the tissue to be profiled, together with a Xenium prior, and returns a Xenium gene panel with evidence for classification performance and probe-level off-target risk ( Fig. 1 ). It is a Python package that can be used as a library, from the command line or as a pipeline of twelve stages (below). Panel design with DART proceeds in three steps ( Fig. 2 ).  The first step is detection-aware thinning. For each gene, a keep probability      p   keep       is the ratio of its detection rate (the fraction of cells with a nonzero count) in the Xenium prior’s Xenium run to its detection rate in that experiment’s single-cell reference ( Methods ). Each nonzero count of the single-cell reference is kept with probability      p   keep       and zeroed otherwise, so that the thinned reference reproduces each gene’s expected in situ detection. The prior’s cells need no labels, and the target’s Xenium is never used.  The second step is rule learning. Three learners propose candidate Boolean rules for each cell type: thresholded conjunctions such as     G  e  n  e  A  >   t  1   ∧  G  e  n  e  B  ≤   t  2     , which require one gene to be high and another to be low. The Asymmetric Tree Panel Finder (ATPF), developed here, grows decision trees whose splits isolate one target cell type rather than separating all classes. R ule F it  ( Friedman and Popescu, 2008 ), a rule-ensemble method, is applied to random-forest and gradient-boosted ensembles; it extracts rules from the trees and keeps those with nonzero      L  1     -penalised coefficients.  The third step is orthogonal selection. Candidates are ranked by      F  1      minus a penalty per additional gene, and up to     K     rules are kept per cell type, sharing at most      O   max       genes. The default is gene-disjoint rules        O   max    =  0      . The panel is the union of the selected rules’ genes.  The off-target module reads the probe report that the Xenium Panel Designer returns for a submitted panel, which lists each probe’s predicted off-target genes. For each marker it draws a dotplot of the marker beside its off-target genes across the reference’s cell types. A probe whose off-target genes are expressed in cell types that the marker does not mark would add false signal there and should be replaced; the dotplot shows which probes these are. Because the check needs only the probe report and the reference, it applies to a panel from any selection method ( Section 2.12 ).  X-SPEAR’s pipeline runs these steps as twelve numbered stages, each configured by its own file and each optional ( Fig. 3 ). Stages 00–04 load and prepare the single-cell reference: ingest, quality control, a cap on the cells per cell type, normalisation and, if wanted, an embedding. Stage 06 thins a copy of the reference to the Xenium prior’s detection rates, and stage 07 selects the panel, with DART (as four substages: rule learning, rule scoring, ranking and orthogonal selection) or with one of the other selectors compared here. Stage 10 exports the panel together with the reference bundle that the Xenium Panel Designer takes, and stage 11 checks the probe report it returns. Where a labelled Xenium run of the target exists, stages 05, 08 and 09 load it, label its cells with a classifier trained on the reference and score the labels, as the evaluations in this study do. Every selector writes the same panel file, which is all the later stages read, so the classification, export and off-target stages serve a panel from any method. The interfaces and each stage are described in the  Methods  ( Section 4.1 ).    2.2  Datasets  We used five paired datasets, each with a single-cell reference and a Xenium run, and one single-cell atlas ( Table 1 ). Three pairs serve as  targets , which need cell-type labels on the Xenium cells to score a panel: ovarian cancer, cervical cancer and mouse brain. All five pairs serve as Xenium priors. Ovarian and cervical cancer are the reference cases: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue profiled with the 10x Genomics Chromium Flex assay (Flex) and Xenium Prime 5K on the same tissue block, with 10x’s cell-type annotation of the Xenium cells. Mouse brain adds a fresh-frozen (FF) target of another species. The mouse retina pair supplies a same-species prior for mouse brain; it has no cell-type labels, so it cannot be a target. The breast cancer pair is used only as a prior: its Flex reference and its Xenium run come from different tumours, so it is not suitable as a target. The mouse RGC atlas, with 45 annotated subtypes, has no Xenium counterpart with subtype labels, so it is used for a held-out single-cell benchmark of fine subtypes.  Several other datasets were considered and set aside. A skin melanoma pair was removed because its single-cell reference turned out to be from mouse lemur while its Xenium run was human, so its detection rates measured a species mismatch. A dermatomyositis skin pair had a nearly flat detection profile from a shallow reference and was not validated. A second ovarian cancer Xenium dataset was measured with an earlier 5K panel version lacking about 30% of the genes, and in situ whole-transcriptome Atera data show no detection loss to correct, so neither tests detection-aware design. A human spleen pair was set aside because the source of its Xenium run could not be documented.    2.3  Detection loss is large, gene-specific and reproducible across experiments  A Xenium prior is only useful if a gene’s detection loss measured in one experiment predicts its loss in another. On the ovarian cancer Xenium, the median gene is detected in 52% as many cells as in the matched single-cell reference (4,259 genes detected in at least 0.1% of reference cells), and the loss varies widely between genes ( Fig. 4a ). The loss is reproducible. Per-gene      p   keep       in ovarian and cervical cancer, two different tissues profiled on the same Xenium panel, correlate at Spearman     ρ  =  0.88     over 3,056 shared genes. That is more strongly than the genes’ single-cell detection breadth correlates between the two tissues (    ρ  =  0.62    ), so      p   keep       captures a property of the gene and its probes rather than shared biology ( Fig. 4b ).    2.4  Designing a panel without the target’s Xenium  Every panel in this study is designed and evaluated in the same way ( Fig. 5 ). Three datasets are involved. The  single-cell reference  is annotated single-cell data of the target tissue; the panel is chosen from its genes. The  Xenium prior  supplies per-gene detection rates from a previous experiment that measured both a single-cell reference and a Xenium run; only its detection rates are used. The  target Xenium  is the Xenium run of the target tissue. Its Xenium cells were split into two spatial halves by a checkerboard, and only the held-out half was scored. Nothing from the target Xenium informs the panel. To score a panel, a classifier is trained on the single-cell reference restricted to the panel’s genes, it predicts the cell type of every held-out target Xenium cell, and the predictions are compared with the target’s labels by macro      F  1     , the unweighted mean of the per-cell-type      F  1      scores.    2.5  A Xenium prior helps when it matches the target’s chemistry and species  We first asked which Xenium priors help DART. For each target we designed DART panels with every available prior, and with none, and compared them at the target’s default panel size ( Fig. 6 ;  Methods ). The target’s own Xenium is shown as an upper bound that no designer has before ordering.  The prior that helped most, other than the target’s own, always matched the target’s chemistry and species. For the two human FFPE tumours it was the other tumour, profiled with the same Flex reference and Xenium chemistry: cervical cancer raised ovarian cancer from 0.470 macro-     F  1      without a prior to 0.563, against 0.600 with the target’s own Xenium, and ovarian cancer raised cervical cancer from 0.517 to 0.612 (own 0.666). The breast pair, of the same chemistry but with its reference and Xenium run from different tumours, helped less (0.520 and 0.538). For the fresh-frozen mouse brain, the fresh-frozen mouse retina prior helped (0.643 to 0.673; own 0.700), whereas every human FFPE prior lowered accuracy, by 0.05 to 0.13. Conversely, the two fresh-frozen mouse priors helped ovarian cancer little (+0.011 and +0.025) and lowered cervical cancer (−0.016 and −0.033). A prior from the other species reaches only the genes whose human and mouse symbols agree, about half of the target’s genes ( Methods ). The best results therefore need a prior of the same chemistry and species as the planned experiment, which can come from a different tissue.    2.6  Benchmark against existing marker-selection methods  We then compared DART with four existing methods: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros. Each target used a Xenium prior from a different tissue, chosen by how closely its samples match the target’s and not by any score on the target: for ovarian and cervical cancer, each other (FFPE tissue with a Flex reference and Xenium Prime 5K on the same block), and for mouse brain, the mouse retina pair, the only other mouse pair, which like the target is fresh-frozen tissue with a single-nucleus reference and the mouse 5K panel ( Fig. 7 ). The other methods select genes from the single-cell reference as measured, as they are normally used. Because panel size drives accuracy, DART was run with     K  =  1–10     rules per cell type and the Wilcoxon test and COSG with 1–12 genes per cell type, and methods were compared at matched realised panel size by interpolating along each accuracy curve. NS-Forest’s panel barely changes with its budget (21–24 genes on ovarian cancer and one identical panel on each of the other targets), and Spapros was run at its default size, so neither gives an accuracy curve and DART was compared with them at their own panel sizes.    2.7  DART outperforms existing marker-selection methods  At matched panel size, DART outperformed the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros on every target ( Fig. 8 ;  Table 2 ). On ovarian cancer, the mean advantage over the Wilcoxon test was +0.064 macro-     F  1     , ranging from +0.036 to +0.118 across panel sizes, and DART reached the Wilcoxon test’s best accuracy (0.581 with 144 genes) with 83 genes. On mouse brain the advantage was +0.105, and DART needed 41 genes to match the Wilcoxon test’s best, against its 132. On cervical cancer it was +0.044, with 28 genes against 58. Across the three targets the margins were +0.038 to +0.079 over COSG, +0.099 to +0.175 over NS-Forest and +0.044 to +0.082 over Spapros. When DART’s thinning and rule learning were repeated at four seeds, every margin stayed positive (the smallest was +0.039, over Spapros on ovarian cancer), and the seed-to-seed standard deviation of a margin was 0.005–0.017 ( Methods ).  Two qualifications apply to COSG. First, on mouse brain DART’s lead over COSG is concentrated in small panels: it is +0.041 to +0.217 below about 55 genes, but from about 65 genes upward the two are level (−0.018 to +0.017), and COSG’s best point (0.708 with 120 genes) is slightly above DART’s best (0.703). On cervical, COSG’s best point (0.656 with 72 genes) lies beyond the largest panel on DART’s curve (50 genes). Second, COSG’s accuracy depends on how the reference is normalised; normalising over the full transcriptome rather than the shared gene universe would raise COSG by about 0.015 on ovarian and 0.036 on cervical ( Supplementary S2 ).   Fig. 8a  ranks one panel per method near DART’s default size on each target. DART ranked first on every target and by mean macro-     F  1      (0.610), ahead of Spapros (0.565), COSG (0.558), the Wilcoxon test (0.509) and NS-Forest (0.389). At each method’s own panel size, DART led Spapros by 0.060, COSG by 0.052, the Wilcoxon test by 0.099 and NS-Forest by 0.150 on average over the three targets.  The methods also differ in their compute ( Fig. 8a ;  Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DART splits its rule learning into independent tasks, one per cell type and learner, and runs them on parallel worker processes. It used the most CPU time, 1.2–8.9 core-hours per target against 0.3–1.1 for Spapros and at most 1.8 for the marker selectors, but with eight workers it finished in 12–82 minutes, six to seven times faster than on one core, and its largest process needed at most 6.3 GB of memory. Spapros took 11–28 minutes and needed 16–25 GB, and the Wilcoxon test and COSG finished in under three minutes.    2.8  Per-cell-type accuracy on the target Xenium  The differences in macro-     F  1      come from particular cell types ( Fig. 9 ). On ovarian cancer, DART’s panel gave the highest      F  1      of the five methods for 6 of the 14 cell types and Spapros’s larger panel for 5; DART scored above the Wilcoxon test on 11 types and above NS-Forest on 12. Its largest gain was on T and natural killer (NK) cells (0.50, against 0.14–0.27 for the other methods). It fell furthest behind the best method, by 0.14–0.17, on two tumour states, proliferative and VEGFA-positive tumour cells, which the Wilcoxon test and Spapros separated better. On mouse brain, DART gave the highest      F  1      for 6 of 12 cell types and scored above the Wilcoxon test on 11, most of all on neurons (0.86 against 0.24). The two rarest mouse brain types, macrophages (48 held-out cells) and T cells (36), were poorly classified by every method (     F  1      at most 0.38). On cervical cancer, with six broad cell types, DART’s advantage came from macrophages (0.64, against 0.09–0.30), and it was weakest on squamous carcinoma (0.28, against 0.29–0.43).    2.9  Number of rules per cell type and rule overlap  Two settings control a DART panel:     K    , the number of rules kept per cell type, and      O   max      , the number of genes that two rules of the same cell type may share ( Fig. 10 ). Each additional rule adds genes, so     K     also sets the panel size. macro-     F  1      rose with     K     on every target, steeply from     K  =  1     to     K  =  3     and more slowly afterwards. On ovarian cancer it rose from 0.455 with one rule per type (18 genes) to 0.555 at the default     K  =  4     (58 genes) and 0.623 at     K  =  10     (128 genes); on mouse brain from 0.574 to 0.680 and 0.703; and on cervical cancer from 0.499 to 0.595, reaching 0.643 at     K  =  9     before falling to 0.629 at     K  =  10    . The effect of letting rules share one gene        O   max    =  1       depended on the target. On ovarian cancer it lowered macro-     F  1      at every     K     above 1, by 0.085 at     K  =  4    . On mouse brain the two settings differed by at most 0.024, with no consistent sign. On cervical cancer sharing was better from     K  =  4     upward, by 0.014 at     K  =  4     and 0.043 at     K  =  10    .    2.10  DART’s rules are interpretable and agree with the classifier  Each DART panel comes with explicit rules, such as a gene above a threshold, alone or combined with others. These rules name recognisable marker programs ( Table 3 ). For the interferon-high inflammatory tumour cells of the ovarian cancer reference, DART’s four gene-disjoint rules use  MX1  (in a conjunction that also requires  ESR1  high and  NAMPT  and  CD200  low),  IFIT1 ,  IFIT3  and  DDX58 , all interferon-stimulated genes. The rules for ciliated epithelial cells use cilia genes ( CFAP100 ,  CDHR4 ,  TEKT1 ,  DNAH9 ), those for proliferative tumour cells use cell-cycle genes ( CIP2A ,  RRM2 ,  TYMS ,  TPX2 ), and those for T and natural killer cells use  TRAC ,  CD8A ,  CXCR4  and  IL7R . A ranked gene list carries no threshold and does not say which genes act together.  Panels are deployed with a classifier that never sees the rules, yet the classifier’s coefficients recover them ( Table 4 ). A “    g  e  n  e  >  t    ” condition in a cell type’s rule carries a positive coefficient for that type in 98–100% of cases on the three Xenium targets and in 96.5% across the 45 RGC subtypes. Rule genes carry 2.0–3.0 times the weight of the panel’s other genes, and a cell type’s largest coefficient belongs to one of its rule genes for every cell type of the three targets and for 92% of the RGC subtype panels. The rules are therefore an accurate, human-readable account of why the classifier calls a cell type.    2.11  Fine retinal ganglion cell subtypes  The Xenium targets have 6–14 broad cell types, which a single marker usually separates; on them most DART rules use one gene. RGCs, the projection neurons of the retina, comprise more than 40 transcriptionally related subtypes ( Tran et al., 2019 ;  Sanes and Masland, 2015 ), many without a unique marker. No Xenium dataset has RGC subtype labels, so we evaluated the 45 subtypes of a published atlas by five-fold out-of-fold prediction within the single-cell data ( Methods ): each panel is designed on four folds and scored on the held-out fold. Here 75% of DART’s rules are multi-gene conjunctions, with a mean of 2.4 genes per rule (    K  =  4     panels of the five folds), against 7–15% on the three Xenium targets.  DART, the Wilcoxon test and Spapros reached the same accuracy at matched size, about 0.955 to 0.96 macro-     F  1      from 150 genes upward ( Fig. 11a ): DART scored 0.959 with 184 genes and 0.960 with 223, the Wilcoxon test 0.957 with 191 and 0.958 with 224, and Spapros 0.956 with 175. COSG was 0.04–0.06 lower at matched size and reached 0.945 only with 393 genes, and NS-Forest’s single panel (71 genes) scored 0.879. DART led COSG (+0.028 to +0.037) and NS-Forest (+0.052 to +0.076) in every third of subtype abundance, from the rarest to the commonest, whereas against the Wilcoxon test and Spapros the per-subtype differences stayed within ±0.007 at every abundance ( Fig. 11b ). No single probe was load-bearing, consistent with each subtype being covered by several gene-disjoint rules: among the 230 single-gene knockouts of one fold’s     K  =  4     panel, the largest drop in macro-     F  1      was 0.003.    2.12  Checking a panel’s probes for off-target expression  The off-target check applies to a panel from any method once its probes are designed.  Fig. 12  shows its output for a 176-gene human retina panel designed in a separate study, using the probe report returned by the Xenium Panel Designer and a single-nucleus atlas of the human retina ( Li et al., 2026 ). The probe for the cone marker  CRX  has one predicted off-target,  RPS6KL1 , which is expressed weakly and evenly across the retinal cell classes, so it cannot mimic the cone pattern and the probe can be kept. Three of the probes for the amacrine-cell marker  PAX6  have predicted off-targets. Of those measured in the atlas,  ALX1  is barely expressed, but  PAX2 ,  PAX5  and  PAX8  are strongly expressed in astrocytes, where  PAX6  itself is absent. Those probes could report amacrine-like signal in astrocytes, so they are flagged for replacement.     3  Discussion  X-SPEAR turns an annotated single-cell reference into a Xenium panel without any data from the target sample. It makes three contributions:
    Detection-aware design from a Xenium prior.  The gap between a gene’s detection in a single-cell reference and in Xenium is large, gene-specific and reproducible across tissues. Thinning the reference to a previous experiment’s detection rates anticipates that gap before ordering. The prior should match the planned experiment’s chemistry and species, and it can come from another tissue; a mismatched prior can lower accuracy.     DART.  With a Xenium prior from a different tissue, DART outperforms the Wilcoxon test, COSG, NS-Forest and Spapros at matched panel size on every target we tested, and reaches the Wilcoxon test’s best accuracy with 42–69% fewer genes. Its rules name interpretable marker programs and agree with the classifier that uses the panel. On fine RGC subtypes it matches the best methods, leads COSG and NS-Forest at every subtype abundance, and no single probe is load-bearing.     A method-independent off-target check.  Dotplots of each marker beside its predicted off-target genes show which probes would add signal in the wrong cell types, for a panel chosen by any method.     Two limitations matter most. First, the benefit depends on a suitable Xenium prior: for the best results, the prior should come from the same assay chemistry and the same species as the target. Second, the evaluation labels of the Xenium targets derive from reference-based annotation: 10x’s for ovarian and cervical cancer and our own label transfer for mouse brain. The comparisons are therefore within the reference’s annotation scheme, although an independent annotation of the ovarian section agreed with the evaluation labels on 82.8% of cells at the level of five lineages ( Supplementary S3 ).  The thinning, selection and off-target modules are separable. Other targeted platforms can be supported once a detection profile and a probe-design output exist for them, and the same architecture can host objectives beyond cell-type identification, such as panels that preserve differential expression across conditions or spatial niches.    4  Methods   4.1.  The X-SPEAR software   Interfaces.  X-SPEAR is a Python package (Code availability statement) with three interfaces. As a library,  design_panel  takes an annotated single-cell reference, a dataset configuration and, optionally, a Xenium prior, and returns the panel’s genes, the selected rules (each with its cell type, thresholds, precision and recall) and the full pool of candidate rules.  Panel.reselect  selects again from that pool at another     K     or      O   max       without relearning; this study used it for the RGC panels with     K  =  1–3    .  classify  labels a target’s cells with a panel, and  metrics.evaluate  scores the labels. A dataset configuration, one JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file, names the reference’s cell-type column, the cell types to leave out, and the renames and exclusions that map the target’s labels onto the reference’s. On the command line,  xspear design, xspear classify  and  xspear evaluate  wrap these calls.  xspear prior  lists and exports the Xenium priors shipped with the package,  xspear profile  depth-normalises priors and  xspear kcurve  plots accuracy against     K     ( Supplementary S6 ).  xspear init  writes annotated configuration files for the pipeline, and  xspear run  runs it, in full or for chosen stages.    Pipeline. The stages of the pipeline ( Fig. 3 ) pass files to each other. Every selector writes the panel’s gene list, which is all that stages 08–11 read, and DART also writes its rules. Each stage records its outcome, with the package version and commit, in a run manifest, and a stage does not start if an earlier one failed. Stage 00 loads counts (an AnnData h5ad file or a Matrix Market (MTX) matrix) and can attach Ensembl gene identifiers from a gene transfer format (GTF) file or mygene.info (needed for the export bundle), merge per-cell metadata and assign a group label such as the sample of origin. Stage 01 computes quality metrics and keeps cells with 500–8,000 detected genes and genes detected in at least three cells; it can also filter on mitochondrial fraction and call doublets with Scrublet ( Wolock et al., 2019 ). Stage 02 caps the cells per cell type (3,000, seeded). Stage 03 normalises counts per 10,000, or per median library size, applies     log  (  1  +  x  )     and can flag highly variable genes. Stage 04, off by default, computes principal components, a neighbour graph, a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) ( McInnes et al., 2018 ) and Harmony integration ( Korsunsky et al., 2019 ). Stage 05 loads the target Xenium and its labels, which are used only for scoring. Stage 06 resolves a Xenium prior and thins a copy of the reference to it ( Supplementary S6 ); every data-driven selector of stage 07 uses the thinned copy, and the classifier of stage 08 uses the original. Stage 07 runs DART as four substages, 07a rule learning, 07b rule scoring, 07c ranking and 07d orthogonal selection ( Sections 4.3  and  4.4 ; defaults     K  =  4    ,      O   max    =  0     and 1,000 estimators per ensemble, as in this study). It can instead run the Wilcoxon test, COSG or NS-Forest (10 genes per cell type by default), read a curated marker list, run Spapros or its reference probe sets (principal components, differential expression, highly variable genes and random genes), or adopt an existing panel. Stage 10 writes the panel and, for the Xenium Panel Designer, a reference bundle of counts, gene and cell tables and cell types. Stage 11, off by default, is the off-target check ( Section 4.9 ). This study ran stage 00 to load the references of the three Xenium targets and called the functions behind stages 06, 07 and 11 from its analysis scripts; the capping, splitting and scoring described below are in the paper repository.  Classification and evaluation.  Stage 08 trains a classifier on the reference restricted to the panel and labels the target’s cells. The default is a one-versus-rest logistic regression (    C  =  1    , at most 1,000 iterations, unweighted), as in this study’s scoring; a random forest (500 trees, depth 8) and balanced class weights are options. Reference and target are first normalised over the genes they share, as in this study’s scoring, and so does the library’s  classify ; normalising over the panel’s genes alone, which is what a Xenium run measuring only the panel provides, is an option. Cells can also be labelled by voting with DART’s rules instead of a classifier ( Supplementary S5 ). Stage 09 reports macro-     F  1      and weighted      F  1      over the reference’s cell types, per-type precision, recall and      F  1     , the confusion matrix and the fraction of cells assigned a type. An alternative evaluation built on Spapros’ forest classifier is described in  Supplementary S7 .    Environments.  The analyses ran in Python 3.11.15 with numpy 2.4.6, pandas 2.3.3, SciPy 1.17.1, scikit-learn 1.9.0 ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ), scanpy 1.10.3 ( Wolf et al., 2018 ), anndata 0.12.19, imodels 3.0.0 ( Singh et al., 2021 ), Cython 3.3.0 (for the compiled ATPF criterion), COSG 1.2.0 and NS-Forest 4.1. Spapros 0.1.6 cannot run on numpy 2 or pandas 3, so X-SPEAR runs it in a second environment (numpy 1.26.4, pandas 2.3.3) as a subprocess that returns only the panel file. The package’s installer builds both environments, pinned to lock files of exactly these versions.     4.2.  Datasets and preprocessing   Table 1  lists every dataset. For each target the candidate gene pool is the set of genes measured in both the single-cell reference and the Xenium panel: 4,766 (ovarian cancer), 4,548 (cervical cancer) and 4,791 (mouse brain). Expression is     log  (  1  +  x  )     of counts per 10,000 (CP10k), computed over this shared universe for both modalities before subsetting to a panel. For the benchmark, the reference was capped at 40,000 cells by stratified sampling, keeping small cell types whole, and the selectors were run on a stratified 80% of the capped reference.  The target Xenium cells were divided into design and evaluation halves by a spatial checkerboard, and only the evaluation half was scored: about 183,000 cells for ovarian cancer, 181,000 for cervical cancer and 32,000 for mouse brain. The design half was not used.   Evaluation labels.  For ovarian and cervical cancer, the labels are 10x Genomics’ cell-type annotation, mapped to the reference vocabulary. For cervical cancer, 10x left 56% of cells unassigned, and those cells were excluded. For mouse brain, the labels come from our label transfer, a scaled multinomial logistic regression trained on the reference over the shared genes. The original transfer normalised the reference over its full transcriptome but the Xenium over its panel; rebuilding it with consistent normalisation changed the labels of 18.3% of evaluation cells, and mouse brain results use the rebuilt labels except where noted ( Supplementary S3 ). Labels are used only to score.     4.3  Rule generation   ATPF.  ATPF grows scikit-learn ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) decision trees with a custom precision– recall impurity,     I  (  n  )  =  1  −  P  ×  R    , where    P    is precision and    R    recall. This criterion targets isolation of one cell type rather than global class separation. Root-to-node paths are extracted as candidate rules.    R ule F it .  R ule F it  ( Friedman and Popescu, 2008 ) (imodels 3.0.0) is applied to random-forest and gradient-boosted ensembles. Rules with nonzero coefficients in the      L  1     -penalised logistic model are kept.  Each ATPF tree is grown on a bootstrap sample of the thinned reference, to depth 4, considering the square root of the number of genes at each split. Every root-to-node path, not only those that end in a leaf, is a candidate rule, and rules with the same conditions are merged. The ATPF criterion is a compiled extension of scikit-learn, built for the installed Python and scikit-learn versions. R ule F it  uses imodels’  RuleFitClassifier  on a random forest with balanced class weights or on a gradient-boosted ensemble with 80% subsampling, both of depth 4, with up to 4,000 rules at 1,000 trees. The benchmarks used 1,000 estimators per ensemble. All candidate rules are evaluated on the full thinned design slice to give    P   ,    R    and      F  1      (and      F  β      for     β  =  0.5     and     2    , which are not used). A cell type with fewer than five reference cells is skipped, and a cell type that receives no rule is reported as an error, after which the pipeline stops. Cell types are learned independently and can be spread over worker processes; each learner is seeded per cell type, so the candidate pool does not depend on the number of workers.  Three scoring options, not used in this study, change the candidate pool (stage 07b): discarding rules with a “≤” condition; recording each rule’s      F  1      against each other cell type alone, computed on the cells of the two types, whose minimum can replace one-versus-rest      F  1      in ranking; and rewriting each threshold as the fraction of reference cells at or below it, so that a rule fires at the same rank of any data it is applied to ( Supplementary S5 ).     4.4  Rule ranking and orthogonal selection  ATPF candidates pass a quality gate:     P  ≥  0.75     and     R  ≥  0.50    ; if none pass,     P  ≥  0.45     and     R  ≥  0.30    ; if still none, no gate. The 20 best by      F  1      are then kept for each rule length. The top 40 R ule F it  rules per cell type by penalised      F  1      are kept. Pooled candidates are ranked by a penalised score,
 
 (1) 
   S  =   F  1   −  λ  ⋅  max    0  ,   N   genes    −  1    ,   
 
in two tiers. Rules with      F  1   ≥  0.7     are ranked first, with     λ  =  0.10    , and the rest follow with     λ  =  0.04    . Ties are broken by     |  P  −  R  |     and then by rule length. For each cell type, rules are added greedily in rank order until     K     have been kept. A candidate is skipped if it shares more than      O   max       genes with the rules already chosen for that type, or if all its genes are already among them. Genes may be shared across cell types. The panel is the union of the selected rules’ genes. Defaults are     K  =  4     and      O   max    =  0    ; the selection constants sit on a plateau ( Supplementary S1 ).  The tier threshold, both penalties and the order of tie-breaking can be changed, and the candidate pool can be kept before the quality gate, so that the gate, the number of rules kept per rule length and the R ule F it  top-    N     can be varied without relearning.  Supplementary S1  used these, together with an option that keeps every gene to one cell type, with the types choosing rules in turn. Two further selection modes, not used here, are available from the library: a candidate’s score can be reduced by     λ     times the largest absolute Pearson correlation between its genes and those already on the panel, and a total gene budget can replace     K    , spent first on each type’s best rule that fits and then repeatedly on the rule that most raises its type’s best      F  1      per gene it adds. Selection can also be restricted to the genes the target Xenium measures, or to a list such as the genes that can be ordered on a panel.    4.5  Detection-aware thinning with a Xenium prior  For each gene     g    , a Xenium prior gives
 
 (2) 
    p   keep  ,  g    =  min    1  ,    d  g   xen    /   d  g   sc      ,   
 
where      d  g   xen       and      d  g   sc       are the fractions of all cells with a nonzero count in the prior’s Xenium run and single-cell reference. Before learning, each nonzero entry of the reference count matrix is kept intact with probability      p   keep  ,  g       and set to zero otherwise. This per-entry thinning reproduces the prior’s per-gene detection rate; binomial thinning of individual molecules would not, because it barely changes detection for well-expressed genes. The thinned counts are then normalised as above. The prior is used at its own magnitude and its labels are not used. Genes are matched between prior and reference by gene symbol, and a gene the prior does not cover is not thinned. This study’s ovarian cancer prior ships with X-SPEAR ( Supplementary S6 ).    4.6.  Xenium prior comparison  For each target, DART panels were designed with each Xenium prior, with the target’s own detection profile (an upper bound) and with no prior, exactly as in the benchmark: the same capped reference and design slice, 1,000 estimators per ensemble,     K  =  1–10     and      O   max    =  0    , scored with the benchmark classifier on the held-out target Xenium. The panels designed with each target’s benchmark prior are therefore the benchmark’s DART panels. Here gene symbols were matched ignoring case, so that a prior from the other species reaches the genes whose human and mouse symbols agree (for example human  GFAP  and mouse  Gfap ): 2,139–2,348 of the target’s 4,548–4,791 genes (45–49%). X-SPEAR itself matches symbols exactly, which is the same for priors of the target’s species. Because panel size at a given     K     differs between priors, macro-     F  1      was interpolated along each prior’s curve at the realised sizes of the target’s benchmark panels with     K  =  3–6     (45–83 genes for ovarian cancer, 41–79 for mouse brain and 17–32 for cervical cancer) and averaged.    4.7  Benchmark protocol   Methods compared.  We used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (scanpy 1.10.3 ( Wolf et al., 2018 ); top-    k     genes per cell type), COSG 1.2.0 and NS-Forest 4.1, at     k  ∈  {  1  ,  2  ,  3  ,  4  ,  6  ,  8  ,  10  ,  12  }     genes per cell type for the Wilcoxon test and COSG and     k  ∈  {  2  ,  4  ,  8  }     for NS-Forest. Spapros 0.1.6 ran through X-SPEAR’s Spapros interface, in its own environment ( Section 4.1 ), at its default size; as X-SPEAR prepares it, it saw     log  (  1  +  x  )     CP10k expression with 4,000 highly variable genes flagged. Every method selected from the same cells, the stratified 80% slice of the capped reference ( Section 4.2 ), and from the single-cell reference as measured. DART used the Xenium prior described in  Section 2.6 .    Scoring.  Every panel in this paper, on Xenium and out of fold, was scored by one procedure. The training cells and the test cells are normalised over the genes they share and then restricted to the panel’s genes; a one-versus-rest logistic regression (    C  =  1    , unweighted) is trained on the training cells and predicts every test cell. For the Xenium targets the training cells are the full single-cell reference without thinning and the test cells the held-out target Xenium half. macro-     F  1      averages per-cell-type      F  1      over the reference’s cell types; weighted      F  1      weights each type by its number of held-out cells. Comparisons at matched size interpolate each method’s macro-     F  1      linearly in realised panel size and average the difference over DART’s sizes that lie within the other method’s range. NS-Forest and Spapros give no curve, so DART’s curve was interpolated at their panel sizes; NS-Forest’s margin is the mean over its three budgets.    Seed variability.  The reference thinning and every learner were repeated at four seeds (1, 2, 3 and 42; the benchmark uses 42), and each seed’s DART curve (    K  =  1–6     and     8    ) was compared with the other methods’ panels exactly as in the benchmark. Across seeds, the standard deviation of DART’s margin over a method was 0.005–0.017 macro-     F  1      (0.006–0.008 over the Wilcoxon test), and that of DART’s macro-     F  1      at a single     K     was up to 0.024. A DART panel’s genes partly change between seeds (mean pairwise Jaccard index 0.62–0.74 at     K  =  4    ).    Compute.  Compute was measured on this study’s own runs, one job per target and method on the same cluster. For DART, the Wilcoxon test, COSG and NS-Forest, the job loaded the benchmark’s design slice and timed the method’s selection call exactly as the benchmark makes it (DART with the target’s Xenium prior,     K  =  4    ,      O   max    =  0     and 1,000 estimators; DART and NS-Forest with eight worker processes), recording the wall time of the call, the CPU time of the process and its workers, and the peak memory of the largest process. For Spapros, the scheduler summary of its job gave the same quantities, which also cover loading and preparing the data.     4.8  Single-cell out-of-fold evaluation on RGC subtypes  The RGC atlas (34,029 cells, 45 subtypes) was restricted to the 4,911 genes of the mouse Xenium 5K panel and split into five folds, stratified by subtype (scikit-learn  StratifiedKFold , shuffled, seed 42). For each fold, every method selected its panel from the other four folds only, so the held-out cells never influenced their own panel. Each panel was scored as on Xenium (Benchmark protocol), with the four training folds as the training cells and the held-out fold as the test cells. The predictions of the five folds were pooled, and macro-     F  1      and per-subtype      F  1      were computed over all 34,029 cells. No Xenium prior was used, because there is no Xenium measurement to anticipate. DART was run with     K  =  4     rules per subtype and      O   max    =  0     at 1,000 estimators, and smaller panels were obtained as the first     K  =  1–3     rules of each fold’s     K  =  4     selection; the Wilcoxon test and COSG were run at 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 genes per subtype and NS-Forest at its default, and Spapros was run on each fold’s training cells exactly as for the Xenium targets, at its default size (170–182 genes; a request for 200 genes returned the same panel) and at 50, 100 and 150 genes. Per-subtype differences were compared at near-matched panel sizes ( Fig. 11b ), and subtypes were split into thirds by their number of cells. For the knockout analysis, each gene of a fold’s     K  =  4     panel was removed in turn, the classifier was retrained without it, and the drop in macro-     F  1      on the held-out fold was recorded.    4.9.  Probe off-target check  After probe design, the Xenium Panel Designer returns a probe report listing, for each probe, its predicted off-target genes. X-SPEAR separates probes with and without predicted off-targets, attaches the cell type each marker was selected for, and, for each marker with off-targets, draws a dotplot of the marker and its off-target genes across the cell types of the annotated reference (scanpy; expression as CP10k then     log  (  1  +  x  )    ). The user replaces probes whose off-target genes are expressed in cell types the marker does not mark.  Fig. 12  was drawn this way by X-SPEAR’s off-target stage, with the human retina atlas’s major cell classes (up to 3,000 cells each) as the reference. title: FmH2ST: foundation model-based spatial transcriptomics generation from histological images.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: FmH2ST: foundation model-based spatial transcriptomics generation from histological images. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) reveals gene expression distributions within tissues. Yet, predicting spatial gene expression from histological images still faces the challenges of limited ST data that lack prior knowledge, and insufficient capturing of inter-slice heterogeneity and intra-slice complexity. To tackle these challenges, we introduce FmH2ST, a foundation model-based method for spatial gene expression prediction. Equipped with powerful foundation models pretrained on massive images, FmH2ST employs a dual-branch framework to integrate prior knowledge from foundation model and fine-grained details from spot images. The foundation model branch employs a multilevel feature extraction strategy to obtain enriched features with slice context for capturing inter-slice heterogeneity, and a dual-graph strategy to obtain spatial and semantic enriched features for modeling intra-slice complexity. The spot-specific learning branch leverages multiscale convolutions, Transformer, and graph neural network to extract fine-grained spot features. The outputs of two branches are adaptively fused for better prediction under a collaborative branch learning strategy. Experimental results show FmH2ST outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets. FmH2ST can denoise the raw gene expressions, reveal cancer spatial heterogeneity and gene co-expression patterns, and support the inference of gene regulatory networks. Overall, FmH2ST is effective for predicting ST, with potential applications in clinical diagnostics and personalized treatment.

evidence_text:
Artificial intelligence in thoracic surgery: a narrative review of clinical advances and applications in 2025.

Background and objective

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into thoracic surgery accelerated notably over the course of 2025, transitioning from isolated diagnostic aids toward comprehensive clinical pathway integration. The objective of this narrative review is to synthesize the latest evidence on AI applications across the entire thoracic surgical workflow, organized along the patient care continuum from preoperative assessment through intraoperative execution to postoperative management.

Methods

A PubMed/MEDLINE search was performed on March 6, 2026, and retrieved 378 English-language records published between January 1, 2025 and March 6, 2026. After title and abstract screening, potentially relevant articles underwent full-text review, and studies addressing the clinical applications of AI and related digital technologies across the thoracic surgical pathway were included in this narrative review.

Key content and findings

In the preoperative domain, large-scale foundation models and computational pathology systems have demonstrated strong performance in nodule risk stratification and noninvasive genomic prediction [area under the curve (AUC) >0.900]. Notably, dual-phase computed tomography (CT) systems such as NeoPred have achieved validation for predicting pathological response to neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy. Intraoperatively, augmented reality (AR) navigation has achieved randomized controlled trial (RCT)-level evidence outperforming conventional localization, while generative AI systems have attained expert-level anatomical recognition for surgical video analytics. Postoperatively, wearable continuous monitoring systems and digital therapeutics (DTx) entered prospective clinical validation. Furthermore, large language models (LLMs) emerged as increasingly important tools for automated surgical documentation. Despite these advances, most studies remain retrospective, and domain shift across institutions limits generalizability.

Conclusions

While AI has substantially affected thoracic surgery, important gaps persist regarding prospective validation and regulatory governance. Future priorities must focus on prospective multicenter interventional trials linking AI predictions to standardized clinical action protocols, federated learning architectures to overcome data silos, and the development of specialty-specific guidelines building upon the Artificial Intelligence Organization for Next Generation Surgeons (AIONS) 2025 consensus.
