xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: AI-augmented intraoperative decision-making workflows in diffuse midline glioma biopsy using cryosection pathology. Cryosection pathology is essential for intraoperative diagnosis of diffuse midline gliomas, yet it often leads to diagnostic errors and may prompt unnecessary re-biopsies before completion of the formal molecular assessment. In this study, we propose an AI-augmented framework, CryoAID, for rapid molecular outcome prediction during surgery for patients with diffuse midline glioma. CryoAID integrates a generative model to correct cryosection artefacts and a pathology foundation model to predict molecular statuses directly from cryosection images. We validate CryoAID across multiple cohorts to predict tumoural molecular statuses in the internal (n = 326), external multi-centre (n = 52), and consecutive (n = 68) datasets. In particular, CryoAID accurately predicts major molecular statuses (e.g., ATRX, H3K27M, and TP53) using cryosection images that were previously deemed disqualified for molecular examinations. Beyond tumour cells, CryoAID reveals highly differential clinical features, including glial cell proliferation, abundant cytoplasm, and localised endothelial proliferation. In the retrospective analyses, CryoAID reduces re-biopsy rates by 26.4% and 26.6% in the internal and consecutive datasets, respectively. Our findings demonstrate that the AI-augmented pathology workflow can extract diagnostic value from specimens previously considered non-viable by traditional histopathology. This approach represents a shift towards real-time molecular pathology, potentially reducing re-biopsies and improving diagnostic precision for patients with diffuse midline glioma.

title: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer. Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.

title: Performance of an Artificial Intelligence Foundation Model for Prostate Radiotherapy Segmentation.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text:
Performance of an Artificial Intelligence Foundation Model for Prostate Radiotherapy Segmentation.

Purpose

Radiation therapy is a major treatment modality for localized prostate cancer, and accurate target segmentation is a critical aspect of radiation delivery that can directly affect patient outcomes. We evaluated the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) foundation model in target segmentation tasks for prostate radiotherapy planning.

Methods

AI segmentation using Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2) was evaluated from computed tomography images with varying levels of human intervention, ranging from intervals of every 2nd to every 10th ground truth slice provided as input. Segmentation accuracy was measured using dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for intact and postoperative prostate target delineation.

Results

SAM 2 achieved performance similar to and, in some cases, worse than interpolation in DSC and HD95 for both intact and postoperative prostate cancer patient cases, and the AI segmentation accuracy was significantly better in the intact preoperative patient cases where anatomic boundaries were better defined than postoperative patient cases (P < .01† for intervals 5-10). When sparse ground truth was provided simulating lower levels of human intervention, DSC values decreased from 0.956 to 0.856 in the preoperative setting and from 0.952 to 0.751 in the postoperative setting when the interval between ground truth slices was increased from every 2nd to every 10th slice. Correspondingly, the HD95 increased from 1.817 to 4.436 in the preoperative setting and from 1.988 to 11.02 in the postoperative setting under the same conditions.

Conclusion

Current general-purpose AI foundation models do not outperform existing methods and are likely inadequate for prostate radiotherapy segmentation. Their clinical application will require further understanding of appropriate fine-tuning and task-specific performance.

title: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization
xenium_reason: Xenium is mentioned without evidence of dataset generation or reuse
evidence_text: Learning Discrete Cell and Niche Codes from Spatial Transcriptomics Using Dual Residual Vector Quantization Spatially-resolved transcriptomics (SRT) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution while preserving each cell’s spatial location, enabling the joint study of  cell identity and cellular  niche , the recurring microenvironment that organises tissue function. Existing representation-learning methods typically capture only one of these axes at a time. We present SQUINT, a graph vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) that learns  two disjoint codebooks per cell from a shared architecture: a  cell codebook quantising the per-cell embedding before neighbourhood aggregation, biased toward cell-intrinsic identity, and a  niche codebook quantising the embedding after graph neural network (GNN) aggregation, biased toward spatial context. Both use residual vector quantization, giving a coarse-to-fine discrete-token hierarchy. SQUINT is trained with per-branch negative-binomial reconstruction objectives and three domain-motivated components that we show are crucial: a within-section cosine adjacency loss that anchors the niche codes in the spatial graph, a cross-section contrastive loss on the cell latents that aligns transcriptomically matched cells, and a decoder section covariate that absorbs batch effects. Across three datasets spanning four spatial assays (STARmap, MERFISH, CosMx, Xenium) and four tasks – niche identification, cell-type identification, cross-section integration, and spatial gene-expression imputation in held-out regions – SQUINT outperforms or is competitive with strong baselines on identification and achieves the most faithful cross-section integration. The resulting discrete vocabulary makes tissues directly consumable by transformer-style foundation models and enables one-step query-to-reference atlas mapping via code-distribution similarity, which we demonstrate on a CosMx human non-small-cell lung cancer cohort.

title: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Cellular senescence in human liver under normal aging and cancer. Cellular senescence, a stress-induced program causing stable cell-cycle arrest, is a hallmark of liver aging, fibrosis, and cancer. However, the cell-type-specific mechanisms, spatial organization, and cancer-associated alterations in the liver remain unclear. We profiled 43 normal human livers spanning ages and fibrosis stages using a single-cell multiome, Xenium spatial transcriptomics, and CODEX, complemented by fibrotic mouse models and 24 colorectal cancer liver metastases. We found CDKN1A+ senescent hepatocytes, fibroblasts, cholangiocytes, and endothelial cells associated with age, liver disease, or cancer. Senescence differed between aged and fibrotic livers, with similar patterns in mice. Spatially, CDKN1A+ hepatocytes localized periportally, while SERPINE1+ aging-associated hepatocytes formed spatial clusters, potentially mediated by Claudins and THBS1. Fibrotic regions contained CXCL12+ senescent fibroblasts interacting with CXCR4+ immune cells. Chemotherapy intensified senescence in hepatocytes by 5-fold relative to aging and led to unique CDKN2A+ populations. Across conditions, senescent cells shared AP-1 activation, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and apoptosis resistance, suggesting therapeutic opportunities.

evidence_text: Applying Spatial Transcriptomics to the Human Heart: A Practical Guide for Translational Studies. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell methods are changing the questions we can ask about the human cardiovascular system. In this review, we share lessons learned from applying spatial profiling to human cardiovascular samples. We walk through experimental considerations, sampling, fixation, and ribonucleic acid quality control, then compare sequencing-based and imaging-based platforms within a 2-stage "discovery then validation" framework. We propose a heart-aware analytical pipeline: spatially informed quality control, normalization respecting the outsized transcriptome of cardiomyocytes, thoughtful segmentation, and honest assessment of reproducibility. We consider how spatial data can be woven together with single-cell, epigenomic, and proteomic layers, and look ahead to emerging frontiers including integration with cardiac imaging foundation models. Our hope is that spatially resolved molecular data will reveal new tissue niches to target for precision cardiovascular therapies.

evidence_text: Validation of histopathology-based deep learning algorithms for detection of actionable non-small cell lung cancer biomarkers. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patient management relies on molecular analysis to determine eligibility for targeted therapy. Furthermore, neoadjuvant immunotherapy is primarily suitable in the absence of specific genomic alterations. However, significant challenges remain, including suboptimal molecular testing and patients being assigned to non-optimal treatment strategies. Here, we present AI classifiers for the identification of EGFR, ALK, BRAF and MET alterations directly from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue using CanvOI 1.1, a digital pathology foundation model. Their performance was evaluated on an independent validation dataset of 968 NSCLC samples. The classifiers achieved AUCs of 0.87 for EGFR, 0.96 for ALK, 0.88 for BRAF and 0.83 for MET. Moreover, they demonstrated high accuracy in identifying cases lacking alterations. Our results highlight the potential of deep-learning tools for the detection of NSCLC biomarkers and specifically the identification of tumors without EGFR or ALK driver alterations, supporting more informed clinical decision-making.

evidence_text:
A pre-trained foundation model framework for multiplanar MRI classification of extramural vascular invasion and mesorectal fascia invasion in rectal cancer.

Objectives

Accurate MRI-based identification of extramural vascular invasion (EVI) and mesorectal fascia invasion (MFI) is crucial for risk-stratified rectal cancer treatment. However, subjective visual assessment and inter-institutional variability limit diagnostic consistency. This study developed and evaluated a multi-center, foundation model-driven framework that automatically classifies EVI and MFI on axial and sagittal MRI.

Materials and methods

A total of 331 pre-treatment rectal cancer T2-weighted MRI scans from three European hospitals were retrospectively recruited. A self-supervised frequency domain harmonization strategy was applied to reduce scanner variability. Three classifiers, SeResNet, the universal biomedical pretrained model (UMedPT) with a multilayer perceptron head, and a logistic-regression variant using frozen UMedPT features (UMedPT_LR), were trained (n = 265) and tested (n = 66). Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualized model predictions.

Results

UMedPT_LR achieved the best EVI performance with multiplanar fusion (AUC = 0.82, test set). For MFI, UMedPT trained on axial harmonized images yielded the highest performance (AUC = 0.77). Both tasks outperformed the CHAIMELEON 2024 benchmark (EVI: 0.82 vs 0.74; MFI: 0.77 vs 0.75). Harmonization enhanced MFI classification, and multiplanar fusion further boosted EVI performance. Grad-CAM confirmed biologically plausible attention on peritumoral regions (EVI) and mesorectal fascia margins (MFI).

Conclusion

The proposed foundation model-driven framework, leveraging frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion, achieves state-of-the-art performance for automated EVI and MFI classification on MRI, demonstrating strong generalizability across multiple centers.

Critical relevance statement

Addressing inter-center inconsistencies in rectal cancer MRI, a multiplanar foundation model with cross-scanner harmonization significantly improves the detection of EVI and MFI, potentially standardizing staging and guiding therapy.

Key points

Among the first studies to investigate automated classification of both EVI and MFI using axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI. Foundation model-derived features outperform conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for EVI and MFI classification. Frequency domain harmonization and multiplanar fusion selectively enhance diagnostic performance. Automated prediction of EVI and MFI may support more consistent staging and clinical decision-making across institutions.

evidence_text: A CT Lesion Foundation Model for Non-Invasive Assessment of Hepatocellular Carcinoma Aggressiveness and Prediction of Recurrence Risk.  Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with high recurrence rates following curative resection. Accurate non-invasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and recurrence risk is critical for surgical decision-making and postoperative surveillance, yet remains challenging with conventional imaging modalities. Here, we developed a CT lesion foundation model (LFM), trained via self-supervised learning on 32,120 generic lesion and 6,387 HCC-specific CT patches to capture transferable intra-lesional imaging phenotypes. Across one internal and two external validation cohorts, the sequentially pretrained LFM (LFM-Seq) achieved area under the curve values of 0.916, 0.846, and 0.920 for microvascular invasion (MVI) assessment, and 0.833, 0.885 and 0.795 for pathological grade assessment. The model remained robust under scenarios of limited training data and tumor localization perturbations. Furthermore, LFM-Seq-derived risk scores stratified recurrence-free survival (RFS), yielding an externally validated C-index of 0.701, and remained independently associated with RFS after adjusting for clinicopathological factors. Exploratory biological interpretability analyses showed that LFM-Seq-derived risk phenotypes were associated with suppressed lymphocyte-related immune programs. These results suggest that CT lesion foundation models can support non-invasive and robust characterization of HCC aggressiveness, recurrence risk stratification and discovery of interpretable prognostic imaging biomarkers.

evidence_text: Artificial intelligence across the gastric cancer care continuum: Clinical evidence, multimodal integration, and translation Graphical abstract                     Health sciences     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Nov 20.       Introduction  Gastric cancer continues to impose a substantial global burden despite declining age-standardized incidence and mortality rates in some regions.  1   According to Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2022, stomach cancer accounted for more than 968,000 new cases and nearly 660,000 deaths worldwide,  2   underscoring its status as one of the deadliest common malignancies.  2   The burden remains especially high in East Asia, where organized screening programs and high procedural volumes have made early detection a central clinical priority.  3   Nevertheless, many patients are still diagnosed at locally advanced or metastatic stages.  4   Early lesions may be endoscopically subtle, symptoms are often nonspecific, and the disease exhibits marked histologic, molecular, and spatial heterogeneities. Gastric cancer is, therefore, not only a high-burden disease but also one that is highly prone to error across the clinical pathway.  5    These clinical challenges align closely with the strengths of modern artificial intelligence (AI).  5   Over the past decade, the field has progressed from conventional machine learning models based on limited structured variables to deep neural networks capable of analyzing high-dimensional image data.  5   More recently, the field has moved toward multimodal and foundation model paradigms that learn transferable representations from large, weakly labeled, or unlabeled datasets.  6   In gastric cancer, this transition is especially consequential because management depends on integrating heterogeneous data streams, including white-light and image-enhanced endoscopy, computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), histopathology, immunophenotyping, molecular testing, laboratory findings, and treatment trajectories.  7   Few solid tumors illustrate the need for cross-modal clinical AI as clearly as gastric cancer.  8    Recent reviews suggest that gastric cancer is emerging as one of the most active areas in gastrointestinal oncology for AI translation.  9   A 2024 systematic review focused on gastric adenocarcinoma synthesized studies from PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library and concluded that AI is already reshaping the diagnostic and management pathways.  10   A 2023 systematic review of AI-assisted endoscopy identified 42 original studies and found that deep learning models frequently matched or outperformed endoscopists in tasks related to early gastric neoplasia.  11   The central question is no longer whether AI can recognize patterns in gastric cancer, but whether it can improve real-world decision-making as a trustworthy, equitable, and workflow integrated tool.  12    The present review, therefore, adopts a clinically oriented and translational perspective. Its distinct contribution is to examine AI across the complete gastric cancer care continuum, while explicitly comparing evidence maturity, clinical actionability, workflow compatibility, and regional transportability. It distinguishes near-term deployable systems, including real-time endoscopy and routine-slide pathology, from discovery-oriented technologies such as single-cell analysis, spatial transcriptomics, foundation models, and digital twins. Particular attention is given to multimodal integration, cross-regional generalization, clinician-AI interaction, regulatory governance, and medico-legal responsibility.  13    The scope includes AI applications in prevention and risk stratification, endoscopic detection and characterization, CT and PET/CT staging, digital pathology and biomarker prescreening, prognostic modeling, treatment-response prediction, surgical support, and longitudinal decision support. Four questions guide this review. Which applications currently have the strongest clinical evidence? How do imaging, pathology, multimodal, and omics-based approaches add value beyond endoscopic AI? Which methodological and geographic barriers limit reproducibility and equitable deployment? What validation, workflow, regulatory, and governance requirements are necessary before these systems can improve patient care? ( Figure 1 ).    Figure 1   AI across the gastric cancer care continuum  AI applications span prevention and screening prioritization, endoscopic detection and characterization, imaging-based staging, digital pathology and molecular prescreening, prognostic modeling, treatment allocation, and emerging multimodal decision support. Translational maturity is uneven: a real-time endoscopy CDSS retained external multicenter accuracies of 81.5% for four-class classification and 86.4% for invasion-depth assessment, whereas radiomics for peritoneal metastasis achieved a pooled AUC of 0.89 but substantial heterogeneity (I 2  = 88%).  AI, artificial intelligence; CDSS, clinical decision support system; CT, computed tomography; H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; PET/CT, positron emission tomography/computed tomography.                     Methods   Review design  This article was designed as a structured narrative review addressing the clinical and translational development of AI in gastric cancer. The narrative approach was selected because the evidence spans heterogeneous clinical tasks, data modalities, model architectures, outcome definitions, and study designs that are not suitable for a single pooled quantitative analysis. The conduct and reporting of the review were informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA).  This review was not prospectively registered and not designed as a formal systematic review. Accordingly, it does not claim full compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Transparency was instead strengthened through a reproducible search description, explicit eligibility criteria, structured evidence characterization, and an adapted study-identification framework presented.    Information sources and search strategy  PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for relevant studies published from January 1, 2022 through July 2026. Earlier landmark articles were retained when they established an important clinical or methodological foundation that remained relevant to recent developments. Backward citation searching of major reviews and forward citation tracking of influential original studies were also performed.  Searches used combinations of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to gastric cancer and AI. Representative terms included “gastric cancer,” “gastric adenocarcinoma,” “stomach neoplasm,” “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “neural network,” “radiomics,” “endoscopy,” “computed tomography,” “PET/CT,” “digital pathology,” “whole-slide image,” “multimodal,” “foundation model,” “prognosis,” “treatment response,” “immunotherapy,” “surgery,” and “clinical decision support.”    Eligibility and study selection  Eligible publications included peer-reviewed original clinical studies, prospective or retrospective validation studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical guidelines, methodological reporting guidelines, and regulatory documents relevant to AI applications in gastric adenocarcinoma.  Original studies were prioritized when they included multicenter recruitment, prospective evaluation, independent external validation, clinically actionable endpoints, comparison with clinicians or standard care, calibration analysis, decision curve analysis (DCA), or evaluation within a real or simulated clinical workflow. Studies were excluded from the principal synthesis when they did not report gastric cancer results separately, focused exclusively on non-human experiments without a clinical AI application, described an algorithm without patient-level evaluation or a clinically interpretable endpoint, were conference abstracts or non-peer-reviewed preprints, or lacked sufficient methodological information for critical interpretation.    Evidence appraisal and synthesis  Because of substantial heterogeneity across diagnostic, prognostic, therapeutic, surgical, and implementation studies, a single formal risk-of-bias instrument was not applied to all evidence. Representative studies were instead characterized according to study design, dataset and cohort size, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, proximity to an actionable workflow, and implementation or patient-outcome evidence. These dimensions inform the qualitative evidence-maturity ratings in  Tables 1  and  2 . High model discrimination alone was not considered sufficient evidence of clinical maturity. Results were synthesized by stage of care and modality; no new meta-analysis was performed. AI in gastric cancer diagnosis and subtyping   Endoscopy and imaging-based diagnosis  The most mature application of AI in gastric cancer is endoscopic assistance.  5   This is unsurprising because endoscopy is central to screening, diagnosis, and treatment planning, whereas the visual cues that distinguish inflammation, dysplasia, and early carcinoma are subtle and observer dependent.  4   Recent studies have shown that deep learning systems are being developed not only to flag suspicious lesions on white-light imaging but also to classify lesion type, estimate invasion depth, and assist margin delineation using image enhanced modalities such as narrow-band imaging and linked color imaging.  25   A 2023 systematic review of AI assisted endoscopy that included 42 original studies further supports this view and showed that deep learning is useful for detection, classification, assessment of invasion depth, margin delineation, segmentation, and early lesion recognition.  11    A key translational advance is the shift from static image benchmarking to prospective or near real-time evaluation. In a 2023 endoscopy study, Gong and colleagues developed a deep learning-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) for automated real-time detection and classification of gastric neoplasms.  26   In internal testing, the system achieved a 95.6% lesion detection rate, with 89.7% accuracy for four class histologic categorization and 89.2% accuracy for prediction of invasion depth. In a prospective multicenter external test using images from five institutions, performance remained 81.5% for four class classification and 86.4% for binary assessment of invasion depth.  26   Although the pilot-randomized component did not show a statistically significant difference in lesion detection during screening, the value of the study lies less in peak accuracy than in demonstrating that AI for gastric endoscopy can be evaluated prospectively across institutions.  The field is shifting from a comparison between AI and the endoscopist toward a more realistic collaborative model in which AI supports the endoscopist.  27   A 2023 study reported that AI-assisted interpretation improved the assessment of invasion depth in early gastric cancer.  28   This is an actionable endpoint because the depth of invasion strongly influences the appropriateness of endoscopic resection.  29   External validation in non-Japanese populations is also increasing. For example, a 2023 Singapore-based study evaluated an AI endoscopic system in a distinct population, underscoring that cross-country testing is both feasible and necessary to reduce geographic overfitting.  27   High benchmark performance in a single country dataset is no longer sufficient. Clinical adoption will require robustness to shifts in the lesion spectrum, imaging practice, and background mucosal patterns.  30    Image-enhanced endoscopy represents another promising direction.  31   A 2024 study reported that linked color imaging combined with computer-aided detection improved gastric cancer detection relative to standard approaches, highlighting that performance depends not only on model architecture but also on the diagnostic quality and disease contrast of the input signal.  32   Clinically useful systems will likely be more aware of sequence and context than systems that rely only on individual frames.  26    The principal limitations of endoscopic AI remain retrospective image enrichment, inconsistent patient-level splitting, limited multinational evaluation, and insufficient measurement of false-alert burden and workflow benefit. Future trials should compare endoscopists with and without AI under realistic lesion prevalence and should report per-patient sensitivity, unnecessary biopsy rates, procedure time, subgroup performance, and clinically important missed lesions. As summarized in  Table 1 , endoscopic AI is currently the most translationally mature imaging-related application in gastric cancer, whereas imaging-based staging models remain clinically promising but methodologically less mature.    Imaging AI for staging and metastatic risk  Cross-sectional imaging is central to gastric cancer staging, assessment of resectability, detection of metastatic disease, treatment planning, and response evaluation.  16   Conventional interpretation may, nevertheless, be limited by subtle serosal invasion, small-volume nodal disease, and occult peritoneal dissemination. AI approaches include handcrafted radiomics, deep learning feature extraction, end-to-end image models, and multimodal fusion of imaging with clinical or endoscopic information.  Peritoneal metastasis prediction is among the most extensively studied imaging applications. A 2023 meta-analysis of 10 studies involving 6,199 patients reported a pooled sensitivity of 0.77, specificity of 0.88, and AUC of 0.89 for radiomics-based prediction of peritoneal metastasis.  14   These results suggest clinically relevant signal, but heterogeneity was substantial at I 2  = 88%, probably reflecting differences in the scanner type, contrast timing, image reconstruction, tumor segmentation, feature selection, reference standards, and patient selection.  Individual PET/CT and CT studies have reported stronger performance in selected cohorts. A PET/CT-based multimodal fusion model integrating radiomic and clinical features achieved AUCs of 0.942 in the training cohort and 0.908 in the testing cohort for preoperative peritoneal metastasis prediction.  15   A 2025 CT-radiomics study extracted 1,316 features from tumor and peritumoral regions and reported AUCs of 0.943 and 0.835 in its training and testing cohorts, respectively.  33   The decline between development and testing illustrates why internal estimates should not be interpreted as the expected clinical performance.  Imaging AI is also moving beyond single-modality radiomics. A 2025 study involving 691 patients integrated venous-phase CT and endoscopic images for preoperative pathological staging.  8   The integrated model achieved a test-set AUC of 0.933, with a sensitivity of 0.869 and specificity of 0.840, and outperformed the individual CT and endoscopic models. This supports the rationale for combining complementary information on mural invasion and mucosal appearance, although the study remained retrospective and lacked geographic external validation.  Other imaging applications include prediction of lymph-node metastasis, peritoneal recurrence, treatment response, nutritional risk, and postoperative outcomes.  8   MRI-specific AI evidence in gastric cancer remains comparatively sparse and should not be considered equivalent in maturity to CT or PET/CT. Future studies should use harmonized acquisition protocols, automated quality control and segmentation, independent geographic test cohorts, prespecified clinical thresholds, and direct comparison with conventional staging. Clinical usefulness should be demonstrated through decisions such as staging laparoscopy, neoadjuvant treatment, surgical planning, or surveillance intensity, rather than through AUC alone.    Digital pathology and precision subtyping  Digital pathology has rapidly advanced from basic tumor segmentation to clinically actionable classification and inference.  34   In gastric cancer, this shift is particularly important because routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides contain far more information than is typically extracted in standard practice, including signals related to differentiation, stromal architecture, immune infiltration, vascular invasion, and, in some cases, molecular subtype.  35   Pathology AI is emerging not only as an efficiency tool but also as a scalable platform for treatment-relevant inference from routine histology.  36    An important area of progress is pathology-based prediction of nodal and vascular metastatic risks. In 2024, an interpretable deep learning model trained on H&E whole-slide images from multiple institutions was developed to predict lymph node metastasis in early gastric cancer.  37   This is clinically important because decisions about additional surgery after endoscopic resection often depend on the estimated risk of occult nodal disease, whereas existing pathologic criteria remain imperfect.  29   Another 2024 study developed an ensemble deep learning model to detect lymphovascular invasion on gastric cancer whole-slide images and reported very high discrimination.  38   Together, these studies move pathology AI closer to treatment-escalation support than to passive morphologic assistance. However, their translational value will ultimately depend on whether they provide reproducible, externally validated information beyond established pathologic criteria, rather than merely repackaging familiar morphologic cues in a more complex computational form.  29    Another major advance is low-cost inference of molecular phenotypes from routine H&E slides. A 2025 multicenter retrospective study introduced HER2Net, a deep learning model that predicts human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status directly from H&E whole-slide images.  39   The model was trained on 531 slides from 520 patients and achieved an accuracy of 0.9043 in internal testing and 0.8922 in external multicenter testing.  39   The modest decline in performance between internal and external testing suggests that this approach extends beyond a single-center proof of concept. These findings do not support replacing confirmatory HER2 testing.  17   However, they do support a practical prescreening role that may shorten the turnaround time and reduce unnecessary testing. In the near term, this positions digital pathology more convincingly as a triage and biomarker-enrichment layer than as a wholesale substitute for immunohistochemistry (IHC),  in situ  hybridization (ISH), or broader molecular assays.  34    This principle also applies to other biomarkers. Although the initial demonstration that deep learning can infer microsatellite instability (MSI) directly from gastrointestinal histology predates the 2022–2025 period,  40   recent gastric cancer studies continue to refine this concept through multimodal image-feature extraction and nuclear-segmentation frameworks for MSI and tumor mutational burden (TMB) prediction.  41   More broadly, AI is making the bridge between morphology and genotype increasingly actionable, as subtle tissue architecture may serve as a cost-efficient proxy for complex molecular states.  18   In gastric cancer, this approach may be particularly valuable for MSI, EBV-associated disease, immune-inflamed phenotypes, and resistance-associated signaling states, all of which are relevant to treatment selection and prognosis.  42    Finally, digital pathology is beginning to link morphology to treatment response rather than diagnosis alone.  43   In 2024, a multicenter study developed a deep learning histopathology biomarker—ICIsRS—from whole-slide images to predict response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.  19   Using 313 whole-slide images from 264 patients and 148,181 image patches, the ensemble model achieved AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets.  19   The key point is not the peak AUCs themselves but the finding that routine H&E slides may encode reproducible, treatment-relevant information across datasets.  34   Even after accounting for the optimism that can arise in retrospective image-based studies, this remains one of the clearest recent indications that standard pathology slides may contain clinically exploitable predictors of immunotherapy benefit.  13   However, the central translational question is whether such models can provide stable added value beyond pathologist assessment, standard biomarkers, and existing treatment-selection frameworks.  42   As summarized the most convincing near-term role of digital pathology AI is to support triage, case prioritization, and biomarker enrichment, rather than to replace molecular assays or clinician judgment.  The recent biomarker literature illustrates different levels of translational readiness. HER2Net was developed from 531 slides obtained from 520 patients and achieved accuracies of 0.9043 internally and 0.8922 in external multicenter testing.  39   This supports a potential prescreening role, particularly for prioritizing slides or tissue blocks for confirmatory HER2 testing. However, fixation, staining, scanner platforms, tumor heterogeneity, and reference standards remain important sources of error.  Treatment-response models require more cautious interpretation. The ICIsRS model used 313 whole-slide images from 264 patients and reported AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets for prediction of response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy.  19   Although encouraging, unusually high retrospective performance may reflect selected cohorts, limited event numbers, patch-level sampling, or unmeasured clinical confounding. Prospective studies should determine whether pathology-based enrichment improves treatment allocation beyond established biomarkers such as PD-L1-combined positive score, MSI status, EBV status, HER2, and claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2).  The most defensible near-term use is, therefore, a layered workflow in which AI identifies suspicious tissue, prioritizes cases, estimates biomarker probability, and selects representative regions for confirmatory testing. Final treatment decisions should remain based on validated assays and multidisciplinary interpretation. This positioning may reduce workload and testing inefficiency without prematurely replacing the molecular or immunohistochemical standards.  This translational logic is illustrated in  Figure 2 , which shows how pathology AI is currently better positioned as a triage and biomarker-enrichment layer than as a replacement for molecular assays or clinician judgment.    Figure 2   Near-term clinical role of digital pathology AI in gastric cancer  Digital pathology AI can convert routine H&E slides into non-definitive signals for case triage, biomarker prescreening, biomarker enrichment, and treatment-response enrichment. HER2Net achieved accuracies of 0.9043 internally and 0.8922 in external multicenter testing, while the ICIsRS model reported AUCs of 0.92–1.00 across four testing datasets for first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy. These systems are best positioned as workflow-compatible prioritization layers rather than replacements for confirmatory testing or expert interpretation.  AUC, area under the curve; H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; HER2, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2; ICIsRS, immune checkpoint inhibitors response score; IHC, immunohistochemistry; ISH,  in situ  hybridization; PD-1, programmed cell death protein 1.                      AI in prognostic prediction and risk assessment   Spatial biology, single-cell integration, and multi-omics  The prognostic frontier in gastric cancer is increasingly spatially informed,  44   ,   45   but the available technologies currently serve two distinct translational roles. Spatial pathology AI converts routine or multiplex tissue images into prognostic representations that can be incorporated into existing diagnostic workflows, whereas single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and broader multi-omics approaches mainly function as upstream discovery platforms for identifying biologically grounded features.  43   ,   46   This distinction separates near-term clinical deployment from mechanism-oriented feature discovery without implying that the two approaches are independent.  A pathology-native example is a 2022 NPJ Precision Oncology study that converted multiplex IHC images from 172 patients into cell-graph representations and used graph neural networks to predict survival.  47   The “cell-graph signature” achieved a binary survival AUC of 0.960 ± 0.010 and a ternary C-index of 0.823, outperforming the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM staging system.  48   Beyond performance, the study reframed prognosis as a network property shaped by cell-cell relationships, local immune architecture, and stromal organization, which may capture invasive-front structure and immune exclusion that conventional staging does not fully represent.  21   ,   49   ,   50   ,   51   ,   52    A second clinically scalable direction is virtual biomarker generation.  53   In 2024, a multimodal attention-based system inferred seven prognostically relevant immune markers from non-antibody-stained fluorescence images and produced prognostic stratification comparable to conventional multiplex immunofluorescence.  53   By recovering high-value immune information from a simpler input, this approach illustrates how AI may retain spatial prognostic value while reducing laboratory cost and workflow burden.  54    Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies complement these deployable approaches by resolving malignant cell states, immune ecotypes, stromal programs, and localized signaling niches associated with recurrence, treatment resistance, and survival heterogeneity.  55   Their present value is primarily upstream; they identify mechanism-linked features such as immunosuppressive myeloid states, exhausted T cell niches, invasive epithelial programs, and neutrophil-associated resistance signals that can subsequently be projected into scalable pathology or imaging models.  56   Multi-omics integration extends this discovery layer by linking transcriptomic, proteomic, genomic, and clinicopathologic variables to latent axes such as immune activation, stromal dominance, proliferative drive, and metabolic adaptation.  57    Accordingly, high-resolution omics should currently be viewed as a biologic discovery and feature-distillation layer, rather than as a standalone clinical predictor. Their longer-term contribution will depend on whether reproducible signals can be anchored to routine histology, imaging, and longitudinal clinical data, thereby producing prognostic models that are both scalable and mechanistically interpretable.  58      Multimodal personalized prediction models  Single-modality prediction is increasingly inadequate for a disease as biologically and clinically heterogeneous as gastric cancer.  59   ,   60   A patient’s prognosis is shaped not only by the radiologic extent and histologic phenotype but also by the immune architecture, molecular subtype, frailty, treatment intensity, perioperative events, and the timing of response or recurrence.  4   For this reason, multimodal AI is becoming less an optional technological upgrade and more a necessary design principle for clinically meaningful risk prediction in precision oncology.  7    This transition is already visible in both population-level risk prediction and individualized survival modeling.  61   At the population level, a 2025 machine learning model developed from the Korean National Health Insurance Service cohort analyzed more than 10 million screened adults and identified familiar drivers, including age, male sex,  Helicobacter pylori  infection, smoking, and family history.  62   Notably, logistic regression achieved the best performance.  62   This finding suggests that in structured screening settings, simpler models may remain highly competitive and may even be preferable when transparency, calibration, and transportability are priorities.  44   This is an important corrective in a field that is often biased toward algorithmic complexity. Not every clinically useful model needs to be deep, and, in some settings, the most robust solution may also be the most interpretable.  45    At the postoperative level, complication prediction represents another clinically meaningful application.  63   ,   64   Recent multicenter studies have shown that machine learning models can predict serious or early complications after radical gastrectomy with stable validation performance. These systems are valuable not only because they identify statistical risk but also because they may inform perioperative counseling, prehabilitation intensity, intensive care unit (ICU) triage, nutritional support planning, and tailored postoperative surveillance.  65   In this setting, AI becomes clinically relevant when it changes management intensity, rather than merely generating another abstract probability score.  66    In advanced disease, the field is moving toward treatment-linked survival prediction, rather than static baseline risk estimation.  21   A 2025 systematic review focused on machine learning for gastric cancer survival prediction reflects the maturation of this field.  51   Recent studies have also pointed toward models that integrate pathology, CT radiomics, immune surrogates, and longitudinal treatment variables.  52   The key shift is conceptual. Survival models become more clinically meaningful when they are explicitly linked to decision points, continuously updated as new information accrues, and evaluated not only for discrimination but also for calibration, temporal robustness, and practical utility.  67   Prognostic AI will be most clinically useful when it becomes dynamic, treatment aware, and longitudinally updated. As summarized in  Table 2 , prognostic modeling in gastric cancer is shifting from static, single-modality prediction toward spatially informed and dynamic multimodal risk stratification.  Figure 3  summarizes this paradigm shift from static baseline prediction toward spatially informed and dynamic multimodal risk stratification.    Figure 3   Evolution of prognostic AI in gastric cancer  Prognostic modeling is shifting from static, single-modality baseline prediction toward spatially informed and multimodal risk assessment. A cell-graph model achieved a binary survival AUC of 0.960 and a ternary C-index of 0.823; a nationwide structured-data model in more than 10 million screened adults achieved an AUC of 0.708; and a multicohort radiopathomics model achieved 5-year OS AUCs of 0.857–0.917 in validation cohorts. Routine pathology-derived spatial representations currently have the greatest workflow compatibility, whereas single-cell and multi-omics data mainly provide upstream mechanism-linked features.  AJCC, American Joint Committee on Cancer; AUC, area under the curve; C-index, concordance index; OS, overall survival.                      AI in treatment decision-making and personalized therapy   Treatment response prediction and regimen optimization  A central clinical application of AI in gastric cancer is treatment allocation, rather than diagnosis alone.  22   This is particularly relevant in gastric cancer because systemic treatment increasingly includes biomarker-linked options such as HER2-targeted therapy, PD-1 inhibitors, and combination regimens, whereas response heterogeneity remains substantial.  68   In this setting, the most clinically valuable AI systems are not simply prognostic models. They are treatment-specific predictors that help identify which patients are most likely to be benefited from a particular therapeutic strategy.  69    Digital pathology-based immunotherapy prediction is among the strongest recent developments in this area.  19   In a 2024 multicenter study, a histopathology biomarker derived from whole-slide images was developed from 313 whole-slide images obtained from 264 patients, with 148,181 image patches used for model construction.  19   The ensemble model achieved AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets for predicting response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.  19   Complementary studies have also used interpretable machine learning to predict progression-free response duration to sintilimab plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer.  70   These studies suggest that even routine laboratory variables can support clinically meaningful response models when analyzed with explainable machine learning approaches.  70   These studies place treatment response prediction among the most plausible near-term deployment targets in gastric cancer AI. However, the central methodological challenge is to distinguish a true predictive signal from prognostic enrichment because some models may primarily learn baseline disease severity, rather than treatment-specific benefit.  71   Accordingly, future studies should demonstrate that these systems are genuinely predictive rather than merely correlated with overall outcome.  72    A second important trend is the estimation of immune contexture from noninvasive data. In 2024, investigators developed a machine learning workflow that used contrast-enhanced CT and clinical variables to predict cluster of differentiation 8 (CD8)-positive T cell infiltration in gastric cancer.  73   This is clinically attractive because immune infiltration is prognostic, relevant to treatment response, and difficult to sample repeatedly.  73   If robustly validated, radiology-derived immune proxies could function as repeatable whole-tumor biomarkers for treatment selection, treatment monitoring, and potentially adaptive sequencing of systemic therapy.  74   Their appeal lies in scalability and repeatability, but their clinical utility will depend on whether they maintain reliable correspondence with biologically meaningful immune states across scanners, institutions, and treatment settings.  75    AI may also help optimize upstream prevention strategies related to gastric carcinogenesis. A 2025 Nature Communications study introduced an AI clinician for  Helicobacter pylori  management based on reinforcement learning.  76   The model was trained on 38,049 patients from the European Registry on  Helicobacter pylori  management. In internal validation, AI-recommended therapies achieved a 94.1% eradication success rate, compared with 88.1% for clinician-prescribed therapies that were not aligned with AI recommendations.  76   This represented an absolute improvement of 6.0% and was replicated in an external cohort of 7,186 patients. This is an important development because it extends AI in gastric cancer beyond diagnosis and treatment into carcinogenesis prevention. From a public health perspective, optimized eradication strategies may ultimately have a broader population-level impact than many downstream oncology models. The next practical wave of AI in gastric cancer may, therefore, include prevention-oriented decision support, alongside response stratification and regimen optimization.  77   Key treatment-allocation and prevention-oriented studies are summarized.    Intelligent surgery and intraoperative support  Compared with diagnostic AI, surgical AI in gastric cancer remains at an earlier stage, but evidence is expanding from retrospective video analysis toward workflow parsing, skill analytics, and patient-specific navigation.  78   Most systems still perform foundational perception tasks rather than autonomous guidance, which is an appropriate developmental sequence because reliable recognition of the operative scene is a prerequisite for clinically meaningful intraoperative support.  Concrete evidence is emerging for workflow recognition and skill assessment. A 2024 multicenter study used laparoscopic distal gastrectomy videos from 20 hospitals, annotated the operation into nine phases, and achieved an overall phase-recognition accuracy of 88.8%. Model-derived phase duration and surgical-field development scores also differed between high- and low-skill groups, supporting the automated performance assessment.  79   In parallel, automated instrument recognition in robotic distal gastrectomy showed that patterns of instrument use during infrapyloric lymphadenectomy could distinguish more experienced surgeons from less experienced surgeons.  80   These systems are most immediately relevant to standardized training analytics, workflow monitoring, and objective feedback, rather than procedural autonomy.  AI-assisted navigation has also entered prospective feasibility testing. In a 30-patient study of robotic distal gastrectomy, patient-specific three-dimensional models reconstructed from preoperative CT angiography reproduced all vessels and vascular variations encountered during surgery, and no system-related intraoperative events were reported.  23   Compared with matched controls, the navigation group had numerically shorter anesthesia time (218.6 min vs. 230.3 min), operative time (177.1 min vs. 193.9 min), and console time (129.3 min vs. 147.4 min), although these differences were not statistically significant.  23   Earlier three-dimensional angiographic analyses likewise support the feasibility of patient-specific perigastric vascular mapping before gastrectomy.  81    These examples remain feasibility studies, rather than evidence of improved patient outcomes. Future studies should, therefore, use prospective multicenter comparisons with predefined endpoints such as navigation error, unintended vascular injury, blood loss, operative and console time, lymph-node yield, conversion, pancreatic fistula, anastomotic leakage, and 30-day morbidity. At present, the most defensible role of surgical AI in gastric cancer is to support perception, navigation, workflow standardization, and training while preserving surgeon oversight.    Drug discovery and therapeutic simulation  AI is beginning to influence gastric cancer not only at the level of diagnosis and prognostic assessment but also across the therapeutic development pipeline.  82   In this domain, however, the most credible near-term role of AI in gastric cancer is not fully autonomous  de novo  drug discovery. Instead, its more realistic translational value lies in prioritizing therapeutic hypotheses, optimizing companion diagnostics, enriching biomarker-guided patient selection, and modeling treatment pathways. In gastric cancer, AI is most likely to matter where it improves the matching of therapies to patients within biomarker-defined subgroups.  22    A particularly relevant application is biomarker enrichment for existing and emerging targeted therapies and immunotherapy strategies. In gastric cancer, treatment selection increasingly depends on markers such as HER2, fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), CLDN18.2, and immune phenotypes related to PD-1 and PD-L1.  68   These biomarkers are clinically actionable, but their interpretation is often complicated by intratumoral heterogeneity, variable staining intensity, sampling limitations, and differences in scoring and testing workflows.  83   This is where AI-enhanced digital pathology and multimodal modeling may add the greatest near-term value. By integrating histomorphology, spatial distribution patterns, immunohistochemical signals, and clinicopathologic context, AI could help identify biomarker-enriched regions, flag borderline or potentially discordant cases, prioritize specimens for confirmatory IHC, ISH, or next-generation sequencing (NGS) testing, and improve screening efficiency for biomarker-defined therapeutic pathways.  39   In this sense, AI may strengthen companion diagnostics not by replacing established assays but by making the molecular triage more efficient, more standardized, and more biologically informed.  39    This logic is particularly relevant for HER2-directed therapy, where spatial heterogeneity and incomplete sampling can lead to underrecognition of eligible patients.  84   It is also relevant for FGFR2-directed strategies, where biologically meaningful subgroups may be small and difficult to identify efficiently. It is equally relevant for CLDN18.2-targeted treatment, where accurate stratification depends not only on positivity but also on the extent and distribution of expression. Similarly, for PD-1-based therapy, AI may help move beyond a single-marker view by integrating morphology, immune contexture, and clinical features to identify patients with a higher probability of being benefited than conventional biomarkers alone can provide. As a result, the most immediate impact of AI in this area may lie less in inventing new drugs and more in improving patient enrichment, reducing missed eligibility, and refining trial matching for therapies that are already clinically or developmentally relevant in gastric cancer.  22    A second important opportunity is therapeutic simulation, particularly in the context of treatment sequencing. Gastric cancer management increasingly involves multiple layers of decision-making, including perioperative therapy, first-line systemic treatment, later-line targeted options, and biomarker-driven immunotherapy combinations.  85   In this setting, AI could evolve into a decision-support layer that models likely outcomes under different treatment pathways using integrated pathology, imaging, laboratory, molecular, and longitudinal clinical data. This does not yet amount to a fully realized digital twin, and evidence that is specific to gastric cancer is not yet sufficiently mature to support strong clinical claims.  86   Even so, the concept remains highly relevant. Rather than treating each therapy choice as an isolated event, AI may help estimate which sequence or combination strategy is most appropriate for a given patient, especially when biomarker overlap, borderline eligibility, or competing treatment priorities complicate decision-making.  86   Its most plausible role is to support sequence selection when biomarker overlap, borderline eligibility, or competing priorities complicate treatment choice.  The most defensible near-term role of AI in this domain is to improve companion diagnostics, strengthen patient enrichment, and refine treatment matching rather than to pursue autonomous drug invention.  87   Framed in this way, drug discovery and therapeutic simulation become less of a speculative future addition and more of a clinically relevant extension of precision oncology in gastric cancer. Challenges, limitations, and ethical considerations   Data heterogeneity and bias  Despite rapid progress, gastric cancer AI remains fundamentally constrained by heterogeneity in both data generation and disease representation.  88   Endoscopy datasets vary according to processor generation, image-enhancement mode, insufflation technique, bowel preparation quality, lesion prevalence, annotation practice, and operator behavior.  88   Imaging datasets differ across scanner vendors, contrast protocols, reconstruction parameters, and segmentation workflows. Pathology data are affected by stain variation, scanner settings, section thickness, processing pipelines that are specific to individual institutions, and labeling conventions. These factors are major sources of instability that can inflate retrospective performance and weaken generalizability.  66    An additional and often underappreciated issue is label quality. Many gastric cancer AI models, particularly in digital pathology, rely on weak labels such as diagnoses made at the slide level, treatment labels, or outcome labels that may not correspond precisely to the most informative microscopic regions.  89   This creates a risk of label noise because models may learn from partially misaligned or biologically diluted supervision, rather than from signals that are truly specific to the lesion. In pathology, this problem is especially relevant when only biomarker status or response outcomes are available at the case level, which forces algorithms to infer regional importance indirectly.  89   Similar concerns apply in imaging studies when radiologic endpoints are derived from imperfect reference standards or when segmentation boundaries vary substantially across annotators.  66    Methodological bias can also arise from data handling itself. In retrospective radiomics and image-based deep learning studies, data leakage remains a recurrent concern, particularly when image splitting is performed at the image, patch, or lesion level rather than strictly at the patient level, or when preprocessing steps inadvertently expose information from the test set.  90   Such leakage can lead to overly optimistic estimates of performance that do not survive external validation.  66   In addition, class imbalance and prevalence shift are common in gastric cancer AI because early neoplastic lesions, occult metastasis, rare molecular subtypes, and treatment responders may represent only a minority of cases. A model trained in a highly enriched research cohort may, therefore, perform poorly when applied to real-world populations with different disease prevalence, referral patterns, or lesion spectra.  A second major issue is geographic imbalance. Much of the strongest gastric cancer AI literature originates from East Asian cohorts because of the region’s high disease burden, organized screening, and concentrated digital data resources. However, models optimized in high-incidence settings may not transfer directly to lower-incidence populations with different lesion spectra, background gastritis patterns, molecular subtype prevalence, referral pathways, and disease prevalence.  85   External studies in Singapore and European  Helicobacter pylori  cohorts show that cross-regional transfer is feasible, but multinational evaluation under explicit distribution shift remains uncommon.  91    Targeted strategies should operate across the data, model, evaluation, and deployment levels. First, international consortia should prospectively collect regionally diverse cohorts, using harmonized acquisition protocols, annotation standards, endpoint definitions, and core metadata on ethnicity, geography, device, operator, and care pathway. Second, development studies should use patient-level splitting and report leave-one-center-out or leave-one-country-out validation, temporal validation, and region-stratified performance, rather than relying only on random internal splits.  66   ,   92   ,   93   Third, domain-generalization and transfer learning methods should be combined with privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) or federated benchmarking so that models can be trained or evaluated across institutions without centralizing raw patient data.  94   These approaches must still be audited for non-identically distributed data and subgroup-specific failure. Fourth, deployment in a new region should include local recalibration, prespecified threshold selection, uncertainty or out-of-distribution flagging, and continuous monitoring for prevalence and performance drift. Finally, comparative prospective studies should test clinician-alone workflow versus clinician-AI workflow in the target population and report subgroup fairness, calibration, net clinical benefit, and patient- or workflow-level outcomes.  91      Global evidence landscape and equity  The geographic distribution of gastric cancer AI research reflects major differences in disease incidence, screening policy, procedural volume, digital infrastructure, and data availability. East Asia contributes much of the strongest evidence because Japan, South Korea, and China combine high case volumes, experienced endoscopists, organized or risk-based screening, and large institutional image repositories. These conditions have supported real-time endoscopic systems, invasion-depth classifiers, radiomics models, digital pathology tools, and surgical-video datasets.  External evaluation outside original development settings remains uncommon. A Singapore-based study demonstrated the feasibility of evaluating a gastric-neoplasia endoscopy model in a population and clinical environment distinct from its Japanese development setting.  27   Such studies are essential because lesion prevalence, background mucosal disease, endoscopy practice, and referral patterns may alter performance. Validation in a second Asian country, however, does not, by itself, establish global transportability.  In Europe, registry-based prevention models, digital pathology cohorts, and multimodal analyses are increasingly relevant. The European Registry on  Helicobacter pylori  management supported the development of an AI clinician for eradication treatment selection,  76   while implementation is also shaped by medical-device legislation, data-protection requirements, and the European Union AI Act. In North America, gastric cancer-specific prospective deployment studies remain less common because population-wide endoscopic screening is not routine; much of the evidence derives from tertiary centers, public molecular resources, or pan-cancer pathology frameworks.  Low- and middle-income countries face shortages of endoscopists, pathology specialists, digital scanners, modern processors, stable connectivity, and referral capacity.  95   AI may support triage and training, but importing a computationally intensive model trained in a high-resource setting could widen disparities. Priorities should include locally relevant datasets, affordable or offline models, compatibility with existing equipment, workforce training, evaluation under local prevalence, and clear referral pathways. The appropriate system for a high-volume East Asian screening center may, therefore, differ substantially from that required in a rural or resource-constrained hospital.    Explainability, trust, and clinical acceptance High discrimination alone is not sufficient for clinical adoption.  66   Many gastric cancer AI systems remain black box predictors, and commonly used post-hoc visualization tools such as Grad CAM or SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), although useful for inspection, do not, by themselves, establish causal faithfulness or clinical reliability.  96   In high-stakes contexts, such as judging invasion depth, deciding on additional surgery or selecting immunotherapy, clinicians need explanations that are not merely visually persuasive but also biologically coherent, operationally relevant, and auditable within a clinical responsibility framework.  66    A useful distinction can be made between attention-based explanation and mechanism-linked explanation. Attention maps indicate where a model appears to focus. By contrast, mechanism-linked explanations connect predictions to recognizable pathobiology, such as stromal remodeling, immune exclusion, vascular invasion, or biomarker-enriched tissue regions. Gastric cancer is particularly well suited to this shift because pathologists and endoscopists already interpret structured morphologic cues in routine practice.  66   The more closely the AI explanations align with this domain knowledge, the more likely they are to support clinician trust, meaningful audit, and responsible deployment.  97   In practice, explainability will matter only if model representations remain clinically legible and relevant to decision-making.  97    However, trust is not determined by explainability alone. Human factor risks must also be considered.  98   Even a well-performing model can create automation bias if clinicians begin to rely too heavily on AI suggestions, especially in time-pressured settings such as endoscopy or intraoperative support.  98   Conversely, poorly calibrated or poorly integrated tools may be ignored altogether, leading to underuse, even when they are potentially beneficial.  98   Repeated low-value alerts may also produce alert fatigue and reduce attention to truly important prompts.  99   Over the longer term, overdependence on automated assistance could contribute to deskilling if core interpretive abilities are gradually displaced rather than supported.  For these reasons, clinical acceptance depends not only on whether a model is understandable but also on whether it is introduced in a way that preserves appropriate human oversight.  98   Gastric cancer AI systems should, therefore, be designed to support trust calibration rather than blind trust.  100   Clinicians should understand when a model is likely to be reliable, when uncertainty is high, and when override or independent review is appropriate. In mature deployment, the most acceptable systems will be those that enhance expert judgment without narrowing clinical vigilance or eroding professional competence.  Validation, regulation, and clinical utility  Most gastric cancer AI studies remain retrospective, and this is the principal limitation on evidence maturity.  5   The 2023 real-time endoscopy CDSS is notable because it included prospective multicenter external testing, whereas many otherwise high-performing systems remain confined to retrospective datasets.  26   Similarly, the radiomics meta-analysis for peritoneal metastasis reported an AUC of 0.89 but a substantial heterogeneity (I 2  = 88%).  14   These examples show that model availability is no longer the main constraint; the priority is the consistent clinical evaluation.  Several representative studies show why strong discrimination should not be equated with clinical maturity. The peritoneal-metastasis radiomics meta-analysis reported an AUC of 0.89 but a heterogeneity (I 2 ) of 88%.  14   In the real-time endoscopy CDSS, four-class accuracy declined from 89.7% internally to 81.5% in multicenter external testing.  32   HER2Net declined from 0.9043 internal accuracy to 0.8922 external accuracy,  53   while the ICIsRS model reported retrospective AUCs as high as 1.00 without prospective treatment-allocation evidence.  19   In a national cohort of more than 10 million screened adults, logistic regression outperformed more complex machine learning approaches.  62   These examples support external validation, calibration, realistic prevalence, and comparison with simpler models and standard practice.  Clinical evaluation should be reported in a standardized, task-appropriate framework. For detection and classification, studies should report sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPVs and NPVs, respectively), AUCs, and performance at prespecified operating thresholds, with per-patient and per-lesion results where relevant. For time-to-event prediction, the C-index and time-dependent AUCs should be accompanied by calibration plots, calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and Brier score. Across all tasks, discrimination should be complemented by decision-curve net benefit, comparison with the established clinical models and clinician performance, and the workflow outcomes such as examination time, alert burden, missed-lesion rate, treatment reclassification, complications, or patient outcomes. Robustness reporting should include geographic, temporal, device, operator, and clinically relevant subgroup analyses.  93    A clinically credible evidence pathway should progress from patient-level internal validation to external geographic and temporal validation, followed by silent prospective testing, comparative or interventional workflow evaluation, and post-deployment surveillance.  93   Each stage should have a predefined deployment claim, locked or tightly governed model updates, and explicit criteria for acceptable calibration, subgroup performance, and clinical utility. This staged approach helps distinguish an academically strong model from a system that is ready to influence care.  Regulatory challenges compound the evidentiary problem. Adaptive or multimodal systems that actively support decisions require clearer controls for data provenance, model updates, human oversight, cybersecurity, and post-deployment monitoring than static triage tools. Real-world adoption also depends on reimbursement and medicolegal responsibility; even a well-validated system may not diffuse if institutions lack a payment pathway, implementation resources, or agreement on accountability when AI-assisted recommendations contribute to error.  101    Accordingly, evidence standards should prioritize calibration, clinical net benefit, usability, fairness, economic feasibility, and accountability, in addition to technical accuracy.  101   The central translational question is not whether an algorithm performs well retrospectively, but whether a clearly defined AI-assisted workflow improves decisions or outcomes safely in the intended population.
