Clinical implementation and translational considerations   Workflow and information-system integration  Clinical implementation should begin with a clearly defined intended use. The same algorithm requires different evidence and workflow designs depending on whether it functions as a second reader, triage tool, diagnostic classifier, risk calculator, or treatment recommendation system. Deployment should specify when the model is activated, which data are required, what output is generated, which clinician receives the output, and what action is expected.  Real-time endoscopic AI requires direct integration with the endoscopy video stream and sufficiently low latency to permit immediate reinspection. Alert presentation must balance sensitivity against distraction and false-positive burden. Systems should record whether alerts were reviewed, accepted, or overridden and should maintain a clear fallback workflow when AI is unavailable.  Imaging AI should be embedded within picture-archiving and communication systems (PACSs), rather than requiring manual export to a separate platform. Digital pathology AI should similarly integrate with whole-slide viewers, laboratory information systems (LISs), and pathology reporting. Multimodal models require standardized data definitions, units, acquisition times, and missing-data handling across hospital information systems (HISs) and electronic health records (EHRs). Deployed systems should maintain model-version records, audit trails, access controls, cybersecurity safeguards, and downtime procedures. Silent prospective deployment can identify integration failures before predictions influence care.    Clinician training, human factors, and adoption  Clinician adoption cannot be inferred from technical performance alone. Before deployment, endoscopists, radiologists, pathologists, surgeons, nurses, and information-technology personnel should receive role-specific training on intended use, operating thresholds, known failure modes, uncertainty, escalation procedures, and circumstances in which the model should not be used.  Human-AI interaction should be evaluated directly because a model may improve some clinicians, while distracting or misleading others. Studies should compare clinicians with and without AI and report disagreement patterns, override rates, alert burden, interpretation time, and automation-related errors. Institutions should designate clinical and technical owners and regularly review errors, near misses, subgroup performance, user feedback, and drift.    Regulation, model updating, and medico-legal responsibility  Regulatory requirements depend on intended use, autonomy, and risk. In the United States, AI-enabled medical devices may be evaluated through 510(k),  de novo , or premarket approval pathways. FDA guidance permits a predetermined change control plan to describe anticipated modifications, validation procedures, and impact assessments before controlled updates are implemented. In the European Union, medical AI may be governed by medical-device legislation, together with the high-risk requirements of the AI Act, including risk management, data quality, transparency, human oversight, robustness, and post-market monitoring.  Responsibility should not be assigned solely to the clinician who views an AI output. Developers are responsible for design, documentation, validation, and controlled updating; healthcare institutions are responsible for local validation, integration, training, access control, and monitoring; clinical departments should define appropriate-use and escalation pathways; and clinicians remain responsible for interpreting outputs in the context of the individual patient. Institutions should establish procedures for documenting AI-assisted decisions, reporting adverse events, investigating systematic errors, and suspending a model when performance deteriorates.    Illustrative clinical workflow scenarios  Scenario 1: During gastroscopy, an AI system highlights a subtle mucosal abnormality. The endoscopist re-examines the area with white-light and image-enhanced imaging and decides whether biopsy or surveillance is appropriate. The AI prompts additional inspection but does not establish the diagnosis. Relevant outcomes include the miss rate, unnecessary biopsy rate, procedure time, and performance across experience levels.  Scenario 2: After a gastric cancer biopsy is scanned, a pathology model estimates the probability of HER2 positivity, MSI, or another treatment-relevant phenotype and identifies representative tumor regions. High-probability or uncertain cases are prioritized for confirmatory IHC, ISH, or molecular testing. Evaluation should include the turnaround time, missed eligible patients, safely deprioritized tests, and cost per correctly identified biomarker-positive patient.  Scenario 3: A CT model identifies a high probability of occult peritoneal metastasis despite the absence of definite radiologic nodules. The result is reviewed at a multidisciplinary meeting, together with conventional staging, and may prompt staging laparoscopy before definitive surgery. The clinically relevant endpoint is whether model-informed assessment reduces non-therapeutic surgery without causing excessive invasive testing.     Future perspectives: integration, trustworthiness, and equity   Multimodal foundation models and generalist clinical AI  A plausible next phase is the broader use of foundation models and multimodal learning, but their clinical value remains conditional.  20   Recent advances in pathology pretraining and biomedical vision language modeling suggest that large, pretrained backbones may support multiple downstream tasks more efficiently than separate models trained from scratch for each application. In gastric cancer, this raises an important possibility. Tasks such as lesion detection, HER2-related prescreening, survival estimation, and treatment response stratification may increasingly be built on shared pretrained representations with task-specific adaptation, rather than on isolated single-purpose models.  26    Even so, this possibility should not be overstated. The practical value of foundation models lies less in being universal solvers than in improving label efficiency, transferability, and cross-modal alignment, particularly in clinically fragmented data environments.  101   Clinically, the most useful systems are likely to be oriented toward multidisciplinary teams and constrained to specific tasks, rather than being fully general.  6   Because gastric cancer management is inherently multidisciplinary, an AI assistant that synthesizes lesion appearance, imaging stage, pathologic risk, biomarker probability, and patient frailty is a more realistic near-term goal than a fully general clinical agent with open-ended functions.  102    Whether such systems become clinically meaningful will depend on more than model size; their outputs must be calibrated, responsive to uncertainty, and aligned with real decision points, rather than merely appearing technically impressive in retrospective benchmarks.  45   In practice, multimodal foundation models will matter only if they improve decision quality under prospective evaluation at the workflow level. Accordingly, the most defensible expectation is not that larger models will automatically transform care but that carefully governed multimodal backbones may become useful infrastructure for selected clinical tasks if domain adaptation, interpretability, and deployment governance are handled well.  13      Deeply embedded explainable and mechanism-aware AI  A likely next step is the gradual incorporation of more mechanistic structure into clinically relevant models.  47   In gastric cancer, recent work suggests that this transition is feasible. Cell graph survival models, virtual multiplex immune phenotyping, and explainable treatment response systems all move beyond black box pattern recognition toward representations that are more closely tied to tissue biology.  19   These developments do not yet establish a new standard of care, but they indicate that the mechanistic structure can increasingly be incorporated into predictive models.  The value of this shift extends beyond clinician trust. Models built around biologically meaningful intermediate states, such as immune exclusion patterns, stromal organization, invasive front architecture, or spatial ecologies that are relevant to treatment, may prove less brittle than systems relying heavily on image statistics that are specific to a given site or on incidental correlations.  50   This is particularly relevant in gastric cancer, where morphologic variability across scanners, institutions, and populations can be substantial.  24   If biologically anchored abstractions are reproducible across settings, they may support better transportability and more stable external performance than models optimized mainly for internal benchmark accuracy.  103    At the same time, AI that is designed to be mechanism aware should not be framed as an automatic solution to generalizability or trust.  96   Its advantages will depend on whether the proposed biologic intermediates are reproducible, measurable across datasets, and meaningfully connected to clinical decisions.  104   In that sense, the near-term goal is not to replace conventional predictive models with fully mechanistic systems but to progressively incorporate more biologically legible structure into models that are already clinically relevant. In gastric cancer, the most clinically valuable systems may be those that are both accurate and biologically legible.  96      Democratization, prevention, and digital twins  If implemented carefully, AI may help reduce inequities in gastric cancer care, particularly by extending decision support to settings with limited specialist resources.  105   Risk models developed from routine structured data, affordable pathology prescreening for molecular markers, and noninvasive imaging surrogates for immune contexture could all help broaden access to more stratified care.  62   In gastric cancer, this is important because disease burden is unevenly distributed, and access to expert endoscopy, molecular profiling, and subspecialty pathology remains uneven across regions and institutions.  2    The most realistic gains in this area are likely to come from scalable triage, prevention-focused support, and biomarker prioritization that is sensitive to resource constraints, rather than from highly sophisticated fully integrated platforms.  105   In other words, the most transformative AI applications may not be the most technically complex, but rather the ones that improve access to high-quality decision-making at scale.  106   This makes prevention and early risk stratification especially important. When AI supports  Helicobacter pylori  management, screening prioritization, or affordable enrichment for confirmatory testing, its impact on public health may exceed that of some later-stage oncology tools, provided that these systems remain usable in settings with fewer resources.  76    A more distant possibility is the development of practical digital twins for gastric cancer. These would be patient-specific computational models that estimate likely outcomes under different treatment strategies using multimodal longitudinal data.  107   However, this should still be viewed as a conditional and relatively distant objective, rather than an imminent clinical reality. At present, the evidence base does not support routine digital twinning in gastric cancer, and several prerequisites remain underdeveloped. These include stable longitudinal data capture, reliable multimodal integration, validated updating of treatment response, and governance frameworks for iterative decision support. For now, digital twins should be regarded as a conditional long-term objective rather than a near-term clinical reality.  108   ,   109       Conclusions  Evidence reviewed here supports five immediate priorities for gastric cancer AI. First, future studies should progress from single-center retrospective development to prospective, multicenter, and multiregional evaluation. Second, discrimination should be reported together with calibration, prespecified threshold performance, decision-curve net benefit, and clinically relevant subgroup results. Third, AI-assisted care should be compared directly with existing workflows and with clinician performance without AI. Fourth, trials should evaluate workflow efficiency, safety, resource use, cost effectiveness, and patient-level outcomes, rather than model accuracy alone. Fifth, deployment should include local validation, version control, uncertainty management, post-market surveillance, and predefined responsibility for errors and model updates.  Across domains, priority should shift from additional retrospective model development to prospective, comparative evaluation of clearly defined AI-assisted workflows. Multiregional validation, standardized metrics, local calibration, and monitoring under distribution shift will determine whether apparently strong models deliver reproducible clinical benefit. If these requirements are met, gastric cancer could become a leading example of AI progressing from retrospective pattern recognition to clinically accountable precision medicine. evidence_text:
An MRI Foundation Model for Versatile Clinical Applications in Gynecological Cancer via Report Metadata Learning Abstract

The application of artificial intelligence in gynecological magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been limited by the scarcity of labeled data and the "task silo" dilemma, resulting in poor generalization ability. We introduced GynoMRFound, the first gynecological MRI foundation model, trained on a large-scale multi-center dataset of 28,755 patients and 435,471 sequences. The model employed a dual-path paradigm combining 3D masked image reconstruction with explicit learning from structured report metadata, enabling accurate visual-semantic alignment without dense annotations. When evaluated across 42 clinical tasks, including diagnosis, staging, subtyping, biomarker prediction, prognosis, report generation, and segmentation, GynoMRFound outperformed baseline methods on 40 tasks under a frozen backbone setting, demonstrating strong generalizability. The model and code were open-sourced, providing a reproducible foundation tool to advance precise diagnosis and treatment in gynecologic oncology.

scMAC: large language model-enhanced single-cell functional priors for completing functional context in bulk T cell receptor repertoires Introduction  Bulk T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing enables scalable, cost-effective immune repertoire profiling in clinical cohorts and immune monitoring [ 1–3 ]. However, bulk TCR data mainly report clonotype identity and clonal abundance without measuring the single-cell transcriptomic states required to infer T cell functional programs [ 4 ]. Paired single-cell RNA/TCR sequencing (scRNA/TCR-seq) addresses this gap by jointly observing TCR identity and transcriptomic states, enabling fine-grained characterization of transcriptome-inferred functional programs such as effector, regulatory, and exhausted states [ 5–8 ]. Nevertheless, single-cell sequencing remains expensive, technically demanding, and difficult to deploy in large cohorts or routine screening. Together, these limitations motivate functional context completion, which we define as using knowledge from paired scRNA/TCR-seq data to infer functional representations reflecting transcriptome-derived T-cell states for TCR clonotypes without matched transcriptomic measurements.  A prerequisite for transferring functional knowledge from paired scRNA/TCR-seq to bulk TCR repertoires is a reliable single-cell functional reference. Single-cell transcriptomes are high-dimensional, sparse and noisy, and distorted cell-state representations can propagate into downstream TCR-to-function mapping [ 9–12 ]. Conventional workflows such as Seurat and Scanpy provide efficient normalization, highly variable gene (HVG) selection and clustering [ 13 ,  14 ], but remain largely driven by expression-derived statistics and fixed HVG feature selection [ 15 ]. Deep representation and foundation-model approaches improve nonlinear embedding learning [ 16 ,  17 ], yet many still rely mainly on expression patterns or broad pretraining, which may limit their adaptability to newly generated or disease-specific datasets [ 18 ]. Recent prior-guided methods incorporate external biological knowledge, such as protein–protein interaction networks in scNET [ 19 ] or large language model (LLM)-derived gene semantic embeddings in GenePT [ 20 ]. However, curated networks have incomplete functional coverage, whereas static gene semantic embeddings are not fully coupled to dataset-specific expression programs. Therefore, functional context completion for bulk TCR repertoires requires a single-cell reference that suppresses technical noise, preserves multi-scale expression patterns, and captures context-relevant gene semantics.  The second challenge is to establish a robust mapping from TCR identity to transcriptome-derived functional states. Existing TCR-oriented models mainly address related but different tasks: sequence- or repertoire-level models support antigen-specificity prediction, disease-associated repertoire classification, and TCR representation learning [ 21–24 ], whereas paired RNA/TCR methods reveal multimodal associations between clonotypes and transcriptomic states in single-cell data [ 7 ,  8 ,  25 ,  26 ]. However, these approaches are not designed to complete functional context for bulk TCR repertoires, where transcriptome measurements are unavailable. Although Complementarity-Determining Region 3 (CDR3) sequence and variable and joining (V/J) gene usage provide TCR molecular identity and antigen-recognition context, they cannot uniquely determine the transcriptomic state, and therefore the functional state, of the corresponding T cell. Similar clonotypes may occupy different functional states under distinct tissue contexts, antigen exposure, activation histories, or microenvironmental cues [ 27 ,  28 ]. Consequently, direct label transfer, sequence-similarity matching, or hard point-to-point cell alignment may overfit noisy single-cell observations and produce unstable TCR-to-function mappings. A robust solution should therefore not rely solely on hard cell-level correspondences, but should learn stable functional structures that allow clone-level predictions to be reliably aggregated for repertoire-level functional composition estimation.  To address these challenges, we propose scMAC, a single-cell-reference-guided framework for completing functional context in bulk TCR repertoires. scMAC first constructs a high-fidelity functional reference by integrating multi-scale expression modeling with LLM-derived gene semantic embeddings, thereby capturing both expression heterogeneity and gene-level functional coherence. scMAC then learns a prototype-guided TCR-to-function mapping from CDR3 sequence and V/J gene usage, combining paired cell-level latent alignment with functional prototype regularization to reduce overfitting to noisy individual-cell observations. By aggregating clone-level functional predictions according to clonal abundance, scMAC supports repertoire-level functional composition estimation from bulk TCR features. We evaluate scMAC on real single-cell and paired RNA/TCR datasets, demonstrating improved fine-grained cell-state representation, gene functional consistency, expression recovery, and disease-relevant pathway analysis, as well as reliable repertoire-level functional composition estimation. Together, scMAC defines and addresses functional context completion for bulk TCR repertoires, providing a practical route for interpreting immune repertoires beyond clonotype identity and clonal abundance.    Methods and materials   Overview of scMAC  scMAC is a two-module framework for completing functional context in bulk TCR repertoires using paired scRNA/TCR-seq data as functional knowledge ( Fig. 1 ). The scMAC-LLM module first constructs a high-fidelity single-cell functional reference by combining multi-scale expression modeling with LLM-derived gene semantic embeddings, thereby reducing noise-induced distortion in transcriptomic representations. The scMAC-MAP module then learns a prototype-guided TCR-to-function mapping from TCRβ CDR3 sequence and V/J gene usage through paired latent alignment and prototype regularization. During inference, it outputs a TCR functional representation and functional probability vector for each clonotype. Clone-level functional predictions can then be aggregated with clonal abundance to estimate repertoire-level functional composition.    Figure 1   Overview of scMAC for functional context completion; scMAC comprises two modules, scMAC-LLM and scMAC-MAP; scMAC-LLM integrates LLM-derived gene embeddings with gene expression to construct a single-cell functional reference; using paired scRNA/TCR-seq data, scMAC-MAP learns TCR-to-function mapping by aligning TCR representations with the corresponding scMAC-LLM-derived cell functional latent embeddings; during inference, bulk TCR repertoire records are mapped to TCR functional representations and functional probabilities; clone-level functional predictions are aggregated with clonal abundance to estimate repertoire-level functional composition.            Workflow of scMAC showing single-cell functional reference construction, TCR-to-function mapping, and repertoire-level functional composition estimation.           Data preprocessing and model inputs  Paired scRNA/TCR-seq data is used for reference construction and mapper training, whereas target bulk TCR repertoires are used only for inference. For scMAC-LLM, raw scRNA-seq counts were quality-controlled, library-size-normalized, and log-transformed by Scanpy (v1.10.3). Results   Experimental setup  To evaluate whether scMAC can transfer single-cell functional knowledge to TCR repertoire analysis, we organized the experiments around two linked questions. First, we assessed whether scMAC-LLM could construct a biologically faithful single-cell functional reference from sparse and noisy scRNA-seq profiles. Second, we evaluated whether scMAC-MAP could transfer this reference to TCR clonotypes and recover functional context from bulk TCR repertoires.   Datasets  The evaluation used five datasets covering single-cell reference construction and TCR-to-function mapping ( Table 1 ) [ 36–39 ]. The datasets were selected to support fair benchmarking across high-quality annotations, immune-cell heterogeneity, complex disease backgrounds, and practical medium-scale sample sizes, while avoiding overlap with the pretraining corpus of scGPT, a single-cell foundation model. The Cancer cell line (CCL), PBMC3K, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and colorectal cancer (CRC) datasets were used to assess reference quality across cell-line separation, peripheral immune annotation, inflammatory perturbation, and heterogeneous tumor microenvironments. CRC-Paired was derived from CRC by retaining T cells with matched transcriptomes and productive TCRβ records, providing the paired supervision required to train and evaluate scMAC-MAP. For CRC-Paired, fine-grained T cell annotations were consolidated into seven major functional states, including Effector, Naive/Memory, Helper, Innate-like, Regulatory, Proliferating, and Exhausted T cells. This grouping was used to define an interpretable and sufficiently supported label space for benchmarking TCR-to-function mapping.    Table 1   Datasets used for evaluation. Evaluation metrics  For single-cell functional reference construction, representation quality was evaluated by clustering learned cell embeddings and measuring adjusted Rand index (ARI), normalized mutual information (NMI), and silhouette index (SI) [ 40 ]. Biological coherence was assessed using GO semantic consistency [ 41 ,  42 ], the proportion of GO-enriched gene clusters, marker-based cell-type classification measured by the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR), and pathway recovery by gene set enrichment analysis [ 43 ].  For TCR-to-function mapping, evaluation was performed at both repertoire and clone levels. Repertoire-level functional composition estimation was assessed using the coefficient of determination ( R  2 ), Bray–Curtis distance, regression slope, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE). Lower Bray–Curtis distance indicates greater overall compositional similarity. Lower sMAPE indicates smaller relative errors and gives greater emphasis to discrepancies in low-abundance functional states. A regression slope closer to 1 indicates lower systematic bias. Clone-level functional annotation was evaluated using accuracy, weighted F1-score, macro precision, macro recall, and macro F1-score.     scMAC-LLM constructs a high-fidelity single-cell functional reference  Because scMAC-MAP uses the scMAC-LLM cell embedding as its single-cell functional reference, the reliability of this reference is central to the framework. We therefore evaluated whether scMAC-LLM could recover biologically meaningful cell-state structures across datasets with varying levels of technical noise, immune perturbation, and annotation granularity. For each method, cell embeddings were clustered with the same Scanpy-based k-nearest-neighbor and Leiden workflow across a unified resolution range, and the resolution with the highest ARI was used for quantitative comparison [ 14 ,  44 ] (Supplementary Methods). Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualization was used as a complementary qualitative assessment [ 45 ].  The CCL dataset provided a noise-sensitive setting with clear cell-line labels. Under the same 5000-HVG input setting, Scanpy split H1975 cells into two separate regions, although they share the same cell-line annotation and are expected to form a coherent cluster. scMAC-LLM (without LLM) improved the structural consistency of the H1975 region, while the full scMAC-LLM model further removed this artifactual separation and recovered a compact H1975 cluster ( Fig. 2a–c ). The CCL metric summary showed that the full scMAC-LLM further improved over the scMAC-LLM (without LLM) variant, particularly for SI, supporting improved local compactness and between-cell-line separation ( Supplementary Fig. S1a ). The scale-attention profile showed that cells from the same cell line tended to share similar scale preferences, whereas different cell lines attended to distinct gene-set scales ( Supplementary Fig. S1b ). These analyses suggest that multi-scale expression modeling improves local structure, and that LLM-guided semantic fusion further sharpens the learned functional reference. Across the four scRNA-seq datasets, scMAC-LLM achieved the highest ARI and NMI among all evaluated reference-construction methods ( Table 3 ). The improvement was observed in cell-line separation, peripheral immune-cell annotation, inflammatory immune perturbation, and the fine-grained CRC tumor microenvironment, indicating that the model was not tuned to a single dataset type. Cross-dataset UMAP comparisons further showed that scMAC-LLM generally produced tighter same-cell-type neighborhoods and sharper boundaries between different cell types, whereas several baselines showed over-fragmented or mixed structures ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Internal CRC analyses further supported the two main scMAC-LLM components. scMAC-LLM (without LLM) and scMAC-LLM (fixed kernel) both reduced reference-construction performance in ARI and NMI, indicating that LLM-guided semantic fusion and adaptive multi-scale expression modeling contributed to the final reference quality ( Supplementary Table S3 ). L‌LM-guided reference learning improves biological coherence and pathway recovery  A useful single-cell functional reference should preserve gene-level relationships and disease-relevant programs, not only separate annotated cells. We therefore evaluated scMAC-LLM by GO-semantic consistency, GO-enriched gene clusters, marker-based AUPR, and pathway recovery (Supplementary Methods).  At the gene-representation level, scMAC-LLM produced embeddings that were more consistent with known GO functional relationships ( Fig. 3a  and  Supplementary Table S5 ). On the COVID-19 dataset, scMAC-LLM achieved the highest agreement between representation-derived gene similarity and GO semantic similarity, with mean and median absolute correlations of 0.162 and 0.151, respectively, outperforming Counts, scNET, and GenePT. GenePT’s competitive median correlation supports the value of LLM-derived gene semantics, whereas scMAC-LLM’s higher mean, median, and maximum correlations suggest that dataset-adaptive semantic fusion yields more biologically informative gene representations. Lysine demethylase 5B (KDM5B) further illustrates this dataset-relevant prioritization. As a histone-modification-related gene implicated in regulatory networks involving angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 in severe COVID-associated comorbidity contexts [ 46 ], KDM5B showed a high GO-consistency correlation in scMAC-LLM (0.490), suggesting that scMAC-LLM can highlight functionally coherent genes relevant to the dataset context. We next asked whether the learned gene representation space organized genes into functionally coherent groups. Because this analysis focused on dataset-adapted gene organization, we compared scMAC-LLM with Counts and scNET, whose gene representations were derived or updated from the target dataset. Across clustering resolutions, scMAC-LLM maintained a high proportion of GO-enriched gene clusters, remaining close to 0.95 as the number of clusters increased, whereas Counts and scNET declined more clearly at higher resolutions ( Fig. 3b ). UMAP visualization further showed that scMAC-LLM formed clearer and more compact functional gene groups than the comparators, supporting the structural coherence of the learned gene representation space ( Fig. 3c–e ).  Expression reconstruction further tested whether the reference preserved cell-type-specific expression signals after denoising. Marker-expression UMAPs first showed that scMAC-LLM clearly recovered cell-type-specific marker patterns across COVID-19 immune cells, indicating that the reconstructed profiles retained visible marker signals rather than only improving aggregate metrics ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). The improvement was particularly evident for CD8+ T cells, where scMAC-LLM improved AUPR to 0.833 compared with 0.798 for Counts and 0.760 for scNET, suggesting better recovery of T-cell marker signals. Finally, pathway recovery was evaluated in terms of pathway significance, enrichment strength (NES), and disease relevance ( Fig. 3f  and  g ). In the COVID-19 dataset, monocyte-versus-background pathway analysis showed that scMAC-LLM identified more significant Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways than Counts (6 versus 4) and recovered key inflammatory pathways with stronger enrichment [ 47 ]. This included interleukin-17 (IL-17) signaling, which is linked to S100A8/9-mediated inflammatory activation [ 48 ,  49 ], and complement and coagulation cascades, a pathway axis closely associated with COVID-19 inflammatory pathology [ 50 ]. Although scNET detected more significant pathways overall, the additional pathways were not necessarily more disease-relevant: it missed IL-17 signaling and returned less context-relevant pathways such as salivary secretion. These results indicate that scMAC-LLM enhanced core immune pathway recovery while reducing nonspecific background signals.  In CRC CD8+ T cells, scMAC-LLM more strongly recovered tumor-associated immune pathways. Antigen processing and presentation, a central anti-tumor immune mechanism [ 28 ,  51 ], achieved the highest enrichment score in scMAC-LLM (NES = 2.74). By contrast, nonspecific stress-related disease pathways, such as Parkinson disease, were prominent in scNET, whereas scMAC-LLM more strongly prioritized tumor-associated immune pathways. Thus, scMAC-LLM improved not only enrichment strength for key immune programs, but also the specificity of pathway interpretation under dynamic disease-state comparisons.  Together, these analyses show that scMAC-LLM constructs a reference that is accurate for cell-state representation and biologically coherent at gene, marker, and pathway levels. This provides a biologically coherent functional reference for downstream TCR-to-function mapping, supporting the use of scMAC-LLM embeddings as functional supervision for scMAC-MAP.    scMAC-MAP enables functional context completion for bulk TCR repertoires  We next evaluated whether scMAC-MAP could complete functional context for TCR-only repertoire records. CRC-Paired was used as a paired validation setting because it provides TCRβ sequences, V/J gene usage, matched transcriptome-derived functional states, and scMAC-LLM-derived functional embeddings for the same T cells. Transcriptomic information was used only to define functional targets and reference proportions; scMAC-MAP inference used only TCRβ sequence and V/J gene usage. Functional states were imbalanced, with proliferative and exhausted T cells each below 1%, making rare-state completion challenging ( Supplementary Fig. S4 ).  We first evaluated whether clone-level functional context completion could recover pseudo-bulk functional composition. In each cross-validation fold, scMAC-MAP predictions for held-out TCR records were aggregated into functional-state proportions, which closely matched the actual single-cell derived reference proportions ( Fig. 4  and  Table 5 ), with an  R  2  of 0.979, a Bray–Curtis distance of 0.075, a regression slope of 0.907, and an sMAPE of 56.332. These results support reliable repertoire-level functional composition estimation from clone-level predictions. Baseline comparisons further showed that the improvement was not merely driven by fitting dominant functional proportions. Compared with DeepLION, which uses TCR sequence features without single-cell functional transfer, scMAC-MAP improved all composition-level metrics, supporting the value of the scMAC-LLM functional reference. MIST achieved slightly better global fit metrics, but its sMAPE was much higher than that of scMAC-MAP (82.053 versus 56.332) and it tended to predict exhausted and proliferative T cells as zero in several folds. ConTCR achieved competitive sMAPE, but weaker  R  2  and slope, suggesting that point-level contrastive alignment was less stable for reconstructing the full functional landscape.  Because repertoire-level aggregation can mask errors in low-abundance functional states, we next evaluated clone-level functional annotation as a higher-resolution assessment of functional context completion. Although MIST obtained the highest overall accuracy (0.752) and weighted F1-score (0.734), its macro F1-score was lower, consistent with a bias toward abundant functional states ( Supplementary Table S6 ). In contrast, scMAC-MAP achieved the highest macro precision (0.393) and macro F1-score (0.383), while maintaining competitive macro recall (0.413). Thus, scMAC-MAP produced more balanced functional assignments across the long-tailed state distribution rather than simply reproducing the dominant effector T cell class.  Ablation analyses linked both downstream validations to the components required for functional context completion. Replacing the scMAC-LLM reference with a Scanpy-derived reference weakened composition recovery and reduced clone-level macro F1 from 0.383 to 0.332, confirming that a high-fidelity single-cell functional reference is important for TCR-to-function mapping. Removing V/J gene usage also degraded composition and clone-level annotation, supporting the contribution of germline segment context beyond CDR3 sequence alone.  Together, repertoire-level functional composition recovery and clone-level functional annotation provide complementary evidence for functional context completion: the former evaluates whether aggregated predictions recover the functional composition, whereas the latter evaluates functional-state predictions for individual TCR records. scMAC-MAP showed strong composition recovery and comparatively balanced clone-level performance, supporting the transfer of single-cell functional knowledge to TCR repertoire analysis.     Discussion  scMAC addresses the absence of functional-state information in bulk TCR repertoires using paired scRNA/TCR-seq as functional reference and supervision, reframing the problem as functional context completion. Conceptually related to reference-based deconvolution methods such as CIBERSORTx [ 52 ], it operates on TCR clonotypes rather than expression mixtures. scMAC first constructs a single-cell functional reference with scMAC-LLM, then uses scMAC-MAP to generate clone-level functional predictions and aggregate them with clonal abundance when repertoire-level functional composition is required.  scMAC-LLM provides the single-cell functional reference for this mapping. By combining multi-scale expression modeling with LLM-derived gene semantics, it improves cell-state representation while preserving gene-level biological coherence in GO consistency, marker recovery, and pathway analyses. The expanded analyses examine NCBI-only versus NCBI-plus-UniProt content and diverse commercial and open-source text-embedding models ( Supplementary Tables S7 and S9 ), supporting a flexible modular design that accommodates different pretrained encoders with frozen upstream encoding and trainable downstream adaptation. The runtime comparison further shows that scMAC-LLM trained much faster than scGPT and scNET on the CRC benchmark while providing stronger biological representation quality than a minimal expression-only model ( Supplementary Table S8 ). These results position scMAC-LLM as a lightweight reference-construction model for newly generated, moderate-scale single-cell datasets.  scMAC-MAP extends this reference to TCR repertoires by completing transcriptome-derived functional context at the clonotype level. Because TCRβ CDR3 sequence and V/J gene usage do not uniquely determine a cell’s transcriptomic state, scMAC-MAP combines paired latent alignment with prototype regularization. The repertoire-level and clone-level results show that the resulting clone-level functional predictions support both clonotype-level interpretation and abundance-weighted repertoire summarization, supporting their use for interpreting whether repertoire shifts reflect effector expansion, memory-like persistence, regulatory enrichment, or exhausted-state accumulation. Across both modules, focused sensitivity analyses show generally stable performance under reasonable variations in key architectural and objective settings ( Supplementary Tables S10 and S11 ).  Several limitations remain. scMAC-MAP is a supervised mapper, not a universal zero-shot model, and therefore depends on paired scRNA/TCR-seq data from a matched or closely related biological context. Performance may decline across tissues, cancer types, treatment settings, or annotation schemes with strong distribution shifts [ 27 ]. In addition, repertoire-level evaluations use pseudo-bulk repertoires derived from held-out paired single-cell data; independent bulk cohorts with orthogonal functional measurements will be needed for broader validation. The TCRβ-only implementation reflects its broad availability in bulk repertoires, while paired TCRαβ information may improve functional specificity. Functional states are defined from discrete single-cell annotations, so the resolution and consistency of functional context completion depend on annotation quality. Broader paired RNA/TCR references across diseases and cohorts will be needed to improve mapping generalizability, while richer multi-source gene descriptions and end-to-end or parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source text-embedding encoders represent potential extensions for scMAC-LLM.    Key Points    scMAC is a single-cell-guided framework for functional context completion in bulk T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires, transferring transcriptome-derived single-cell functional knowledge to TCR clonotypes.    The scMAC-LLM module constructs a biologically coherent single-cell functional reference by combining multi-scale expression modeling with gene semantic embeddings generated by a large language model.    The scMAC-MAP module maps TCRβ complementarity-determining region 3 sequence and variable and joining (V/J) gene usage into the single-cell functional reference constructed by scMAC-LLM using paired latent alignment and prototype regularization.    The scMAC-LLM reference improves cell-state representation, gene-level Gene Ontology semantic consistency, marker recovery, and disease-relevant pathway interpretation across real single-cell datasets.    Pseudo-bulk functional composition recovery and clone-level annotation show that scMAC-MAP produces informative clone-level functional predictions and supports abundance-weighted repertoire aggregation. title: Exhaustive white blood cell extraction and profiling across whole-slide images of blood and bone marrow smears
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Exhaustive white blood cell extraction and profiling across whole-slide images of blood and bone marrow smears Blood and bone marrow smears are central to diagnosing hematological disorders. While whole-slide scanning enables automated single-cell profiling at scale, the computational burden of gigapixel images has confined automated analysis to manually pre-selected regions of interest. Here, we present HemAutomaton, a framework built on neural cellular automata that extracts white blood cells across entire whole-slide images without manual region selection and with minimal annotation requirements. HemAutomaton matches the in-domain detection accuracy of Faster R-CNN while surpassing it under domain shifts, operating at a fraction of the computational cost and with over 10,000-fold fewer parameters. Across three blood cancer cohorts, we extract over 100 million single-cell images and achieve annotation-efficient differential counting via few-shot classification using a pretrained hematology foundation model. Slide-wide spatial analysis uncovers consistent blast-frequency gradients across smears and demonstrates that automated blast counts match expert evaluations within inter-expert variability. Scaling automated profiling from hundreds to tens of thousands of cells per smear overcomes conventional sampling limits and establishes the foundation for more sensitive AI supported hematological assessments.

title: Enhancing foundation model transfer for prostate cancer detection with patch-level contrastive learning.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Enhancing foundation model transfer for prostate cancer detection with patch-level contrastive learning. Accurate localization of prostate cancer on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains challenging due to the subtle appearance of cancer, resulting in missed clinically significant cancers, large inter-reader variability and large numbers of confounders that require biopsy confirmation. Vision foundation models have shown promise, but direct transfer to prostate MRI is challenging due to the substantial domain gap between natural images and prostate MRI and the subtle appearance of prostate cancer. We therefore developed prostate vision contrastive networks (ProViCNet), a weakly supervised model utilizing patch-level contrastive learning on MRI to support MRI-based screening, biopsy targeting and focal treatment planning. ProViCNet was trained and validated (using 4401 patients across six cohorts) as a prostate cancer detection model on MRI. Training labels were biopsy-confirmed radiologist annotations, while the evaluation labels included both biopsy and surgery-confirmed lesions. ProViCNet demonstrated consistent detection and segmentation performance across multiple internal and external validation cohorts, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values ranging from 0.875 to 0.966, and outperforming radiologists in the MRI expert reader study (0.907 versus 0.805, p < 0.01). We also integrated ProViCNet with serum PSA to develop a virtual screening test, which preserved high sensitivity for detecting clinically significant cancers while more than doubling specificity from 15% to 38% (p < 0.001) among men with PSA ≥ 4 ng/mL, thereby potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies. These findings highlight ProViCNet's potential for enhancing the accuracy of prostate cancer diagnosis and reducing unnecessary biopsies.

title: Automated workflow for target volume propagation in online adaptive magnetic resonance guided radiotherapy for lung lesions using foundation models.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text:
Automated workflow for target volume propagation in online adaptive magnetic resonance guided radiotherapy for lung lesions using foundation models.

Background and purpose

This study presents a novel workflow for automated gross tumor volume (GTV) adaptation in online adaptive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided radiotherapy using promptable segmentation foundation models and evaluates its impact on the quality of adapted treatment plans.

Materials and methods

Treatment planning GTV contours in lung cancer patients, treated at an MRI-Linac, were propagated to daily MRI using affine or deformable image registration. Subsequently, propagated contours were refined using MedSAM2 or nnInteractive foundation models. The prompting strategy was optimized using an internal validation dataset (16 patients with single GTV, 143 fractions), and its accuracy was evaluated on internal and external datasets (total of 39 patients with single GTV, 225 fractions). In the dose-volume histogram (DVH) evaluation, daily treatment plans were reoptimized to GTVs and planning target volumes (PTV) generated by the proposed workflow. The resulting DVHs were compared with the originals.

Results

NnInteractive improved the segmentation accuracy significantly compared to affine- and TransMorph-based propagation methods. The Dice similarity coefficient improved by up to 15% compared to affine-based propagation, but only marginal improvements were observed compared to TM-based propagation. The DVH evaluation revealed no systematic degradation of plan quality. Most DVH metrics did not differ significantly from the original treatment plans. In 17 out of 21 cases, 100% of the clinically approved GTV volume remained covered by the prescribed dose after the reoptimization.

Conclusion

The proposed workflow is feasible and enables automated daily GTV adaptation with improved segmentation accuracy and comparable quality of adapted treatment plans.

title: Preoperative 3D morphological phenotyping of hepatocellular carcinoma via a foundation model: a non-invasive biomarker for recurrence risk stratification.

evidence_text:
Preoperative 3D morphological phenotyping of hepatocellular carcinoma via a foundation model: a non-invasive biomarker for recurrence risk stratification.

Background

Imaging features play a central role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) staging, but current systems remain limited in prognostic precision and treatment guidance. Pathological gross classification, which categorises HCC into four subtypes based on tumour margin morphology, represents a morphological surrogate of aggressive tumour behaviour encompassing histological and molecular features and has demonstrated value in predicting prognosis and guiding adjuvant locoregional therapy selection. Importantly, gross classification is assessable through imaging, but its evaluation utterly depends on postoperative pathology and remains subjective, time-consuming and poorly reproducible. We aimed to develop a three-dimensional (3D) Foundation Model-driven system to automatically perform non-invasive morphological phenotyping and to evaluate its prognostic utility.

Methods

A cohort of 551 patients who underwent hepatectomy after gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI from two medical centres was retrospectively analysed. Pathological gross classification served as the reference standard. The 3D MorphStratify Model was built to automatically phenotype 3D gross classification with a dedicated 3D Foundation Model encoder and a channel-aware fusion module. A combined model integrating 3D MorphStratify and Conventional Imaging Predictors (Morph-CIP) was constructed and validated for recurrence risk stratification. The biological rationale linking imaging morphological phenotyping to underlying biology was preliminarily explored.

Results

Eligible patients were divided into a development dataset (n=291), a validation dataset (n=192) and an external test set (n=68). The 3D MorphStratify Model achieved a micro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.932, significantly outperforming senior radiologists (AUC 0.825) with about 40-fold improved efficiency. The imaging-based 3D morphological phenotyping (3D MorphStratify) independently predicted poor recurrence-free survival (RFS, HR 2.16, 95% CI 1.20 to 3.87, p=0.010). The Morph-CIP Model enables risk stratification through training set (AUC 0.836, 0.768, 0.765 for 1-year, 2-year, 3-year RFS), internal test set (AUC 0.816, 0.690, 0.711) and external test set (AUC 0.737, 0.709, 0.702). The high-risk group is characterised by the enrichment of glycolysis and hypoxia signalling pathways.

Conclusion

3D MorphStratify is the first automated 3D morphological phenotyping system for HCC, transforming subjective pathological gross classification into an objective, non-invasive imaging biomarker. The integration of 3D MorphStratify with conventional imaging predictors enables recurrence risk stratification, potentially providing complementary information for prognostic evaluation.

title: Multi-Modal Foundation Model with Whole-Slide Attention Enables Transferrable Digital Pathology at Single-Cell Resolution
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Multi-Modal Foundation Model with Whole-Slide Attention Enables Transferrable Digital Pathology at Single-Cell Resolution Paired histopathology and spatial transcriptomics data are advancing our understanding of tissue biology and disease, but modeling both modalities at single-cell resolution while mapping local and distal cell-cell interdependencies remains computationally prohibitive. Here we introduce TissueFormer, a framework for pretraining foundation models with linear rather than quadratic computational complexity, overcoming a long-standing barrier to modeling long-range dependencies at scale. Trained on over 17 million image-expression pairs from 1.2K tissue slides, TissueFormer excels at predicting spatial gene expression from histology images at cellular resolution and scales to diagnostic tasks at the cell, region, and slide levels. Additionally, by identifying both long and short-range cell-cell interdependencies, our model enables the generation of testable hypotheses about disease mechanisms and staging, as demonstrated in lung fibrosis and breast cancer.

title: Integrating Foundation Model Features into Graph Neural Network and Fusing Predictions with Standard Fine-Tuned Models for Histology Image Classification.
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Integrating Foundation Model Features into Graph Neural Network and Fusing Predictions with Standard Fine-Tuned Models for Histology Image Classification. Histopathological image classification using computational methods such as fine-tuned convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention in recent years. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have also emerged as strong alternatives, often employing CNNs or vision transformers (ViTs) as node feature extractors. However, as these models are usually pre-trained on small-scale natural image datasets, their performance in histopathology tasks can be limited. The introduction of foundation models trained on large-scale histopathological data now enables more effective feature extraction for GNNs. In this work, we integrate recently developed foundation models as feature extractors within a lightweight GNN and compare their performance with standard fine-tuned CNN and ViT models. Furthermore, we explore a prediction fusion approach that combines the outputs of the best-performing GNN and fine-tuned model to evaluate the benefits of complementary representations. Results demonstrate that GNNs utilizing foundation model features outperform those trained with CNN or ViT features and achieve performance comparable to standard fine-tuned CNN and ViT models. The highest overall performance is obtained with the proposed prediction fusion strategy. Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of a Vision Foundation Model Maps the Allometric Scaling Laws of Gastric Tumor Ecology Abstract

Background Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major public health challenge in Chile, exacerbated by a shortage of regional pathologists and population underrepresentation in global AI datasets. While pathology foundation models offer high-sensitivity screening, their deployment is limited by computational demands, domain shifts, and binary classification constraints that overlook complex tumor biology and sampling-scale artifacts. Methods We developed a parameter-efficient workflow using Low-Rank Adaptation on the MUSK vision foundation model (MUSK-LoRA). Using a cohort of 108 GC patients from a high-incidence regional Chilean hospital, we evaluated diagnostic screening performance, incorporating a refiner module to project spatial probability maps. We leveraged the specialized latent space to define 29 automated digital morphotypes via the Leiden algorithm. These units were analyzed using landscape ecology metrics and an allometric scaling framework to quantify morphotype heterogeneity while mathematically decoupling specimen sampling size from true tissue structural scaling properties. Results The adapted MUSK-LoRA ensemble achieved superior performance (ROC-AUC = 0.95, MCC = 0.81), optimizing hold-out sensitivity to 0.996, whereas zero-shot inference showed no predictive value (MCC = -0.02). Latent space partitioning identified 29 stable morphotypes (Q = 0.74) that segregated classical histological subtypes without molecular labels. Spatial mapping revealed that morphotype richness and Shannon diversity significantly correlate with T-stage and invasion depth (p < 0.001). Crucially, extracting sample-size-corrected net allometric residuals (∆LMS) successfully eliminated sampling area biases, revealing that corrected microenvironmental disorganization correlates with anatomical tumor staging (p < 0.001) independently of late-stage systemic mortality factors (p = 0.809). Conclusions Efficient local adaptation of foundation models provides a scalable path toward technological sovereignty in resource-constrained networks. By shifting from binary detection to an allometrically corrected ecological paradigm, this workflow introduces a precise framework for patient stratification tailored to regional epidemiological realities.

evidence_text: Towards robust foundation models for digital pathology. Biomedical Foundation Models (FMs) are transforming AI-enabled healthcare research and entering clinical validation. However, their susceptibility to learning non-biological features - including variations in laboratory procedures and scanner hardware - poses risks for clinical deployment. We introduce PathoROB, a public benchmark quantifying FM robustness to non-biological features. Representation-level robustness is assessed using the robustness index, while output-level robustness is evaluated across clinically relevant settings, including patch- and slide-level prediction, case retrieval, and clustering tasks. Our experiments reveal robustness deficits across all 20 evaluated FMs, with substantial differences between them. We find that non-robust FM representations can cause major diagnostic downstream errors preventing safe clinical adoption. Using more robust FMs, vision-language alignment, and post-hoc robustification reduces (but does not yet eliminate) the risk of such errors. This work establishes that robustness evaluation is essential for validating pathology FMs before clinical adoption and provides a blueprint for assessing and improving robustness across biomedical domains.

title: Finetuning masking challenges narrow-task evaluation of cell foundation models
xenium_reason: No Xenium text or characteristic Xenium files found
evidence_text: Finetuning masking challenges narrow-task evaluation of cell foundation models Single-cell foundation models are large, self-supervised deep learning networks pretrained on millions of cellular transcriptomes. These models promise to deliver cell representations that are transferable across diverse biological domains and, when used in specific tasks, would outperform narrowly scoped models. A central assumption is that more pretraining data translates to better downstream performance. However, despite its centrality, this assumption remains largely untested. Here, we tested downstream performance on gold-standard benchmarking tasks across massive dataset reductions, showing that performance was largely insensitive to pretraining data size once finetuning was allowed. This trend reveals a finetuning masking effect that offsets differences in representation quality induced by pretraining, making the benefit of additional pretraining scale largely invisible under current benchmark settings. These findings challenge current benchmarking standards, which rely on closed-ended finetuning tasks that are too narrow to expose the full representational value of pretraining. They also challenge the main driving force in single-cell foundation-model development when evaluated through common narrow tasks. We propose that the next generation of foundation models should be assessed less by performance on highly optimised finetuning tasks and more by their ability to support open-ended biological inference, frozen-representation evaluation and zero-shot capability.

TFE3-DualNet: An Interpretable Foundation Model-Based Deep Learning Ensemble for Diagnosing TFE3-Rearranged Renal Cell Carcinoma From Whole-Slide Images in a Two-Center Cohort.

Background

TFE3-rearranged renal cell carcinoma (TFE3-rRCC) is a rare, aggressive subtype that predominantly affects adolescents and young adults. Its marked morphologic heterogeneity can delay recognition and downstream confirmatory testing.

Methods

We assembled a two-center retrospective cohort of patients < 30 years with renal cell carcinoma (n = 228; 59 TFE3-rRCC), using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) as the reference standard. Model development was performed in a development cohort (n = 129), followed by independent external validation (n = 99). We developed TFE3-DualNet, an ensemble of weakly supervised CLAM models trained on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) using patch embeddings extracted from two pathology foundation models (UNI and CHIEF). We compared performance with three immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring methods and a feature-fusion CLAM baseline using concatenated H&E-derived UNI and CHIEF features, and assessed interpretability by attention mapping.

Results

In the external validation cohort, TFE3-DualNet achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.932, with accuracy 0.879, sensitivity 0.893, and specificity 0.873. The model outperformed IHC scoring methods (AUROC 0.793-0.819; all p < 0.05) and exceeded the feature-fusion baseline (AUROC 0.906). Attention hotspots localized to diagnostically relevant tumor regions and showed concordance with TFE3 IHC patterns.

Conclusions

TFE3-DualNet showed encouraging performance as an interpretable H&E WSI-based screening model for TFE3-rRCC in young patients, supporting its potential use to prioritize confirmatory testing and pathologist review in routine diagnostic workflows.

Clinical-imaging fusion model for risk assessment of clinically significant prostate cancer.

Background

Prostate cancer is the second most commonly diagnosed malignancy among men worldwide. Its biological heterogeneity challenges conventional imaging-based risk assessment and complicates biopsy decision-making. Although advanced artificial intelligence may improve risk stratification, medical imaging applications are often limited by small sample sizes. Vision foundation models, with strong transferability in data-constrained settings, offer a promising approach to improving prostate cancer risk assessment, guiding personalized treatment, and reducing overdiagnosis.

Methods

A robust transfer learning framework based on prostate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), termed robust transfer learning model (RTLM), was developed to enable the non-invasive risk assessment of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). RTLM employs a feature-matching transfer strategy to adaptively capture task-relevant abstract knowledge from vision foundation models, thereby enhancing the feature representation capability and robustness of convolutional neural networks. Model performance was evaluated on csPCa MRI data, and a multi-task evaluation was conducted on PD-L1 expression prediction in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to assess the generalizability of the proposed framework. Subsequently, features extracted by the RTLM were used to construct a deep learning signature (DLS), which was then integrated with key clinical variables, including age, serum total PSA level, PSA density, prostate volume, and PI-RADS score, to build the clinical-imaging fusion model (CIFM) for csPCa risk assessment. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), decision curve analysis (DCA), integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and net reclassification improvement (NRI).

Results

The CIFM achieved AUCs of 0.918, 0.890, 0.828, and 0.852 in the training cohort (n = 585), test cohort (n = 310), and two external validation cohorts (n = 510 and n = 94), respectively. Compared with the clinical model and the RTLM, CIFM showed significant improvements in both IDI and NRI (all p < 0.05). Decision curve analysis further demonstrated that CIFM provided greater net clinical benefit.

Conclusion

By effectively leveraging knowledge representations from vision foundation models, RTLM enhances the feature learning capability and robustness of CNNs in small-sample medical imaging tasks. The CIFM, which integrates clinical indicators, demonstrates good accuracy in csPCa risk assessment, suggesting potential generalizability.

Foundation Model-Driven Regions of Interest Classification and Renaming in Cancer Radiotherapy: A Customizable, Retraining-Free Workflow Across Institutions.

Purpose

Inconsistent and institution-specific naming of regions of interest (ROIs) in cancer radiotherapy planning limits interoperability, hinders automation, and introduces ambiguity in clinical workflows. This study aims to develop and evaluate a multistage, foundation model-based workflow for automated ROI classification and standardization in accordance with AAPM Task Group 263 (TG-263) nomenclature, while maintaining flexibility for customization to institution-specific naming conventions.

Materials and methods

A four-stage modular pipeline integrating large language models (LLMs) and a Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) model was developed. The system sequentially performs (1) anatomic site classification, (2) ROI type classification into four categories, (3) standardization based on customizable protocols, and (4) laterality verification via CLIP. The pipeline operates on standard DICOM RTSTRUCT and CT data and requires no model retraining. We evaluated the workflow on 600 patients from three institutions across five disease sites (head and neck, breast, lung, cervix, rectum). Classification and renaming accuracy were assessed at both global and institution-site levels, with error taxonomy used to characterize failure modes.

Results

The workflow achieved an overall ROI type classification accuracy of 99.12% and a renaming accuracy of 97.92%. Classification performance was consistently high across all institutions and sites; renaming accuracy showed minor variation driven by protocol omissions, compound suffix ambiguity, and institution-specific naming conventions. CLIP-based laterality verification corrected all errors in a targeted stress test with deliberate left-right label inversions.

Conclusion

This study demonstrates that foundation language models, augmented by a vision-language module for laterality verification, can robustly automate ROI classification and naming across institutions, offering a customizable and retraining-free solution for standardizing cancer radiotherapy workflows.

evidence_text:
A two-stage foundation model for bladder tumor segmentation: An international multi-site study<sup>☆</sup>.

Background and objective

Accurate bladder tumor segmentation is crucial for muscle invasion assessment, neoadjuvant therapy response evaluation, and bladder preservation decision-making. Manual delineation is time-consuming and observer-dependent, highlighting an unmet clinical need for accurate and automated segmentation, particularly in large multi-site studies. This study aims to (i) develop an automated MRI-based foundation model for bladder tumor segmentation (BLA-T-Seg) using a two-stage framework, in which segmentation is first constrained to the bladder wall, including wall-contiguous tumors and then refined in a second stage focused specifically on the tumor, and (ii) rigorously assess generalizability via multi-site, independent external validation across diverse cohorts.

Methods

This retrospective study included T2-weighted MRI scans from 236 patients with bladder cancer across two international sites. Experienced radiologists manually annotated bladder and tumor regions of interest on T2-weighted images, which served as the ground truth. BLA-T-Seg was developed by adapting the Segment Anything Model (SAM), fine-tuned to segment the bladder in stage 1 and the tumor in stage 2. The primary performance metric was the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), evaluated across five studies (S1-S3: internal; S4-S5: external) and benchmarked against 10 state-of-the-art (SOTA) segmentation architectures.

Results

For stage 1, BLA-T-Seg achieved good-to-excellent performance, with mean DSC values ranging from 0.85 to 0.93. For stage 2, BLA-T-Seg demonstrated moderate-to-good performance, with mean DSC values of 0.74-0.81. Cross-site validation showed minimal performance variation (≤0.01-0.04), confirmed by radar plot analyses. Compared with SOTA models on subset S1, BLA-T-Seg achieved the highest DSC of 0.84, outperforming the next best-performing model, Swin Transformer (DSC: 0.56).

Conclusion

BLA-T-Seg enables accurate and generalizable bladder wall and tumor segmentation and outperforms SOTA alternatives.

evidence_text: A generalizable Hi-C foundation model for chromatin architecture, single-cell and multiomics analysis across species. Nuclear DNA is organized into a three-dimensional (3D) structure that impacts critical cellular processes. However, the integrative analysis of 3D structure (measured by high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C)) and associated epigenomic regulation (for example, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) and chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq)) remains challenging due to the differences in data format, resolution and analytical pipelines. Here we propose HiCFoundation, a foundation model trained on massive Hi-C data for integrative analysis linking chromatin structure to downstream regulatory function. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizability across species on various 3D genome analysis, including reproducibility analysis, resolution enhancement and loop detection. Additionally, HiCFoundation can predict various epigenomic activities from Hi-C to reveal how 3D structure links to regulatory function. Finally, HiCFoundation can easily adapt to single-cell Hi-C data. HiCFoundation thus offers a general, interpretable framework for studying the 3D genome and its functional roles across cell types and species.

title: A Generative Virtual Tissue Model Enables Computational Design of Therapeutic Perturbation Strategies

evidence_text: A Generative Virtual Tissue Model Enables Computational Design of Therapeutic Perturbation Strategies Computational design has transformed many fields of engineering, where simulators can explore millions of candidate design configurations before experimental development and testing. Therapeutic design in biomedicine has resisted computational design approaches because disease progression and therapeutic response emerge from interactions among many cell types within human tissue, governed by biochemical parameters that are largely unknown and potentially unknowable. Here, we introduce the Cell Interaction Foundation Model (CIFM), a virtual tissue model that forward-simulates the transcriptional dynamics of cells in human tissue under arbitrary therapeutic conditions based upon a spatial transcriptomic seed. CIFM is a geometric graph neural network trained by self-supervised masked-transcriptome prediction on millions of cellular microenvironments spanning human tissue types and disease states; generative, auto-regressive, monte-carlo play-out, then, simulates transcriptional dynamics under combinatorial perturbations from a spatial transcriptomic seed. We validate CIFM by showing accuracy gains in gene expression prediction and imputation, disease classification, recapitulation of perturbation responses in prostate cancer models, and recovery of T cell-tumor signaling measured in cell–cell sequencing experiments. Beyond such conventional tasks, CIFM enables target identification and therapeutic design through generative tissue simulation play-outs. Analyzing over 10  6 single and combinatorial perturbations, CIFM designs immunotherapy strategies for cancer and autoimmune disease that exploit combinatorial manipulation of signaling pathways to induce or suppress immune activation. Broadly, CIFM shows how generative artificial intelligence methods can be applied to model emergent behavior in highly interacting biological systems, yielding new approaches to fundamental understanding of tissue behavior as well as large-scale therapeutic design.

evidence_text: Breast Cancer Recurrence Status Assessment in 5 Years Using Multimodal Integrated Learning: A Feasibility Study. Despite advances in breast cancer detection and treatment, recurrence after curative therapy continues to impact long-term survival and quality of life. Therefore, early identification of high-risk patients is crucial to guide personalized treatment and follow-up strategies. Although genomic assays provide valuable prognostic insights, their high cost and limited accessibility hinder widespread adoption in clinical practice. Recent machine learning or deep learning approaches leveraging clinical, imaging, or multimodal data have shown promise but do not reflect real-world clinical scenarios. This study proposes a deep learning-based multimodal framework for predicting 5-year breast cancer recurrence using routinely collected clinical data. The framework consists of three main components. First, we adopted automated tumor segmentation with MedSAM to extract the tumor region from ultrasound images. The radiomics features are extracted from those tumor regions. Second, report features are extracted using a Med-Contrastive Pre-trained Transformers (MedCPT)-based approach incorporating predefined, clinically informed queries. Third, a multimodal integration model jointly processes image, radiomics, clinical features, and report features through modality-specific branches. The image branch employs the Ultrasound Foundation Model (USFM) as the backbone, while structured tabular data is processed using the FT-Transformer architecture. The features of all branches are fused using a mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based classifier, and the entire model is trained using a progressive fusion training strategy. Experimental results confirm the feasibility of using ultrasound images with tumor mask integration for recurrence prediction and demonstrate the additive value of integrating multiple data modalities through the proposed multimodal integration model. The final model for recurrence prediction achieved an AUC of 0.7540, accuracy of 74.61%, sensitivity of 70.41%, and specificity of 76.44%. This feasibility study's findings underscore the potential of the proposed multimodal deep learning framework to provide accessible, accurate, and generalizable recurrence risk prediction using routinely available clinical data, potentially supporting more informed treatment decisions and personalized post-treatment monitoring in real-world clinical practice.

Foundation Model RNAGAN Enhances Biomedical Insight of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Metastasis

ABSTRACT

RNAGAN (version 2.0, https://github.com/ZhaozhengHou-HKU/RNAGAN-2.0.git ) is a published foundation model that analyzes single-cell and bulk-level RNA sequencing samples and enables multiple applications that enhance medical insights. Here we applied this model to Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) as in-context few-short format (i.e., the model was never trained with any NPC data). We conducted all four supported functions, which include sample stratification, vectorization, pseudo data generation, and marker identification. The results were then used for identifying metastatic NPC and to investigate mechanisms associated with NPC metastasis. Examination with stratification showed that the accuracy of RNAGAN results for evaluating the metastasis risk in NPC patients are comparable to or outcompeted recently published risk estimation linear prediction model. Vectorization results present consistency across multiple cohorts and RNAGAN model versions. In the task of identifying markers and mechanisms related to NPC metastasis, incorporating pseudo data substantially enhanced the representativeness of single-cohort-based differential expression (DE) analysis. Moreover, RNAGAN identified metastasis-related marker genes based on single cohort, were concordant with the ground truth obtained across multiple cohorts (p=1.05e-9). Regarding biomedical mechanisms, RNAGAN enabled second-order feature extraction, unveiling a remarkable domination of the protective function of adaptive immune responses (as indicated by IL21R levels) over the hazardous function of chronic, non-resolving innate inflammation (as indicated by S100A8 levels) against NPC metastasis after first-line treatment. This association demonstrates a high degree of consistency with the external cohort. This study demonstrates the utility of the foundation model RNAGAN in uncovering therapeutic insights for novel cancer types without extra training. We reveal a critical spatial mechanism preventing distant metastasis via humoral anti-tumor immunity in NPC. High S100A8 expression by innate antigen-presenting cells (APCs) triggers an inflammatory cascade promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and metastasis. However, when germinal center IL21R + B cells simultaneously colocalize with these innate signals, they override this suppressive tissue stress. Spatial analysis shows that a high S100A8 / IL21R intersection within tumor regions strictly distinguishes treatment responders, whereas non-responders display spatial mismatch or S100A8 + hyper-infiltration. This coordinated innate-adaptive cross-talk sustains functional tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) that mature IgG-secreting plasma cells, which opsonize and eliminate emerging EMT tumor cells before systemic escape. Consequently, while S100A8 alone is an unreliable prognosticator, its spatial colocalization with IL21R is a robust protective indicator overlooked by conventional bulk analysis methods.

evidence_text: PathQC: Determining Molecular and Structural Integrity of Tissues from Histopathological Slides. Quantifying tissue, molecular, and structural integrity is essential for biobank development. However, current assessment methods either involve destructive testing that depletes valuable biospecimens or rely on manual evaluations, which are not scalable and lead to interindividual variation. To overcome these challenges, we present PathQC, a deep-learning framework that directly predicts the tissue RNA Integrity Number (RIN) and the extent of autolysis from hematoxylin and eosin (H & E)-stained whole-slide images of normal tissue biopsies. Advancing over prior QC methods focused on imaging quality control, PathQC provides sample-quality control through the direct quantification of molecular integrity (RIN) and structural degradation (autolysis). PathQC first extracts morphological features from the slide using a recently developed digital pathology foundation model (UNI), followed by a supervised model that learns to predict RNA Integrity Number and autolysis scores from these morphological features. PathQC is trained on and applied to the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) cohort, which comprises 25,306 non-diseased post-mortem samples across 29 tissues from 970 donors, when paired ground-truth RIN and autolysis scores were available. Here, PathQC predicted RIN with an average Pearson correlation of 0.47 and an autolysis score of 0.45, with notably high performance using adrenal gland tissue (R = 0.82) for RIN and colon tissue (R = 0.83) for autolysis. We provide a pan-tissue model for predicting RIN and autolysis scores for new slides from any tissue type (GitHub).
